**Commentary on Surah Sad (38), by al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir)**

Surah Sad is Meccan. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the consensus. Ibn al-Duraysh, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in the *Dala'il* related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Surah Sad was revealed in Mecca." Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in the *Dala'il* related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "When Abu Talib fell ill, a group of the Quraysh, among them Abu Jahl, entered upon him and said: 'Your nephew insults our gods, and does this and that, and says this and that. Would you send for him and forbid him?' So he sent for him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) came and entered the house. Between them and Abu Talib there was the space of one man's seat. Abu Jahl feared that he would sit beside Abu Talib and be above him, so he leapt up and sat in that place. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) found no place near his uncle, so he sat by the door. Abu Talib said to him: 'O my nephew, what is the matter with your people? They complain about you, claiming that you insult their gods and say this and that.' He said: They pressed him with many words. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke and said: 'O uncle, I want them to adopt one word, by which the Arabs will submit to them and the non-Arabs will pay them the jizya.' They were startled by his words and his statement. The people said: 'One word? Yes, by your father, ten!' They said: 'What is it?' He said: 'There is no god but Allah.' They rose in alarm, shaking their garments, saying: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ [Sad 38:5]. Then there was revealed concerning them: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾" [Sad 38:1–8].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Sad﴾. The majority read it with a sukun on the dal, like all the disjoined letters at the beginnings of surahs, since they are pausal forms (ending in sukun when stopped upon).

Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Nasr ibn Asim, Ibn Abi Ablah and Abu al-Simak read it with a kasra on the dal without tanwin. The reason for the kasra is the meeting of two sukuns. It was also said that the reason for the kasra is that it derives from *sada yusadi* (to confront, to oppose), and the meaning is: confront the Qur'an with your deeds, that is, oppose it with your conduct and face it by acting upon it. Al-Nahhas related this from al-Hasan al-Basri and said that he interpreted his recitation this way. And it is related from him that the meaning is: recite it and present yourself to its recitation.

Isa ibn Umar read *ṣāda* with a fatha on the dal. The fatha is due to the meeting of two sukuns. It was also said that it is in the accusative by way of incitement (*al-igra'*).

It was also said that its meaning is: Muhammad has attracted the hearts of creation and won them over until they believed in him. This reading is related from Abu Amr. It is also related from Ibn Abi Ishaq that he read *ṣādi* with a kasra and tanwin, likening this letter to what is not fully declinable among sounds.

Harun al-A'war and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *ṣādu* with a damma without tanwin, in the manner of indeclinable forms such as *mundhu* and *haythu*.

The meaning of *ṣād* has been disputed. Al-Dahhak said: its meaning is "Allah has spoken truly." Ata' said: "Muhammad has spoken truly." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is a sea by which Allah will bring the dead to life between the two blasts. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it is the key to the name of Allah. Qatada said: it is one of the names of Allah. It is related from him that he said: it is one of the names of the Most Gracious. Mujahid said: it is the opening of the surah. It was also said: it is among the things Allah has kept to Himself in knowledge, and this is the truth, as we have mentioned at the opening of Surah al-Baqara.

It was said: it is either a name for the letters enumerated in a fixed pattern for worship, or a name for the surah, or the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative by the implied verb *udhkur* (mention) or *iqra'* (recite). The *wa* in His saying ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ is the *wa* of oath, and swearing by the Qur'an indicates the exaltedness of its rank and the loftiness of its station. The meaning of ﴿full of reminder﴾ is that it contains the reminder in which is the explanation of everything.

Muqatil said: the meaning of ﴿full of reminder﴾ is full of explanation.

Al-Dahhak said: full of honour, as in His saying: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:10], that is, your honour. It was also said: that is, full of admonition.

They differed about what the answer (*jawab*) to this oath is. Al-Zajjaj, al-Kisa'i and the Kufans other than al-Farra' said: it is His saying ﴿Indeed, that is surely true﴾ [Sad 38:64]. Al-Farra' said: we do not find this correct, because it is too far removed from His saying "by the Qur'an." He and Tha'lab preferred that the answer is His saying ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them﴾. Al-Akhfash said: the answer is ﴿Each one of them only denied the messengers, so My punishment was due﴾ [Sad 38:14]. It was also said: the answer is *ṣād*, because its meaning is "true," so it is an answer to the phrase "by the Qur'an," just as you say "truly, by Allah" or "it is necessary, by Allah." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari, and it is also related from Tha'lab and al-Farra'. This is based on the view that the answer of an oath may precede it, and this is weak.

It was also said: the answer is omitted, and the estimate is: "By the Qur'an, full of reminder, you will surely be raised," and the like.

Ibn Atiyya said: its estimate is: "The matter is not as the disbelievers claim." The view that it is omitted is preferable.

It was also said: His saying *ṣād* is itself sworn by, and according to this view the *wa* in ﴿and the Qur'an﴾ is for conjunction with it. Since swearing by the Qur'an indicates its truthfulness, that it is true, and that it is not a place for doubt—

He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾. So He turned away from that, as if He said: there is no doubt in it at all, and the disbelieving polytheists' refusal to accept it was not due to any doubt about it.

Rather, they are in arrogance, that is, in refusing to accept the truth: pride and tyranny.

And *shiqaq* means opposition, that is, refusal to accept the truth. In the language of the Arabs, *'izza* means dominance and overpowering. It is said: "Whoever is mighty plunders," that is, whoever dominates takes spoil. From this comes His saying ﴿and he overpowered me in the discourse﴾ [Sad 38:23], that is, he dominated me. From it is the saying of the poet:

*He overpowers on the road with his two shoulders, as the gambler crouches over the arrows.*

*Shiqaq* is derived from *shiqq* (split, side), and its explanation has already preceded.

Then He, glorified is He, warned them and threatened them with what He did to the disbelievers before them, saying: ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them﴾, meaning the earlier nations destroyed for denying the messengers. That is: how many of the bygone nations did We destroy, who were stronger than these in defence, more powerful and richer in wealth. *Kam* here is the informative *kam* that indicates multiplicity; it is in the position of the accusative governed by *ahlaknā* (We destroyed), as its object. *Min qarn* is the specification. The *min* in ﴿min qablihim﴾ is for the starting point of the limit.

﴿Then they called out, but there was no time for escape﴾. The calling here is the calling for help from them at the descent of punishment upon them, and the time is not a time of escape.

Al-Hasan said: they called out for repentance, but it was not the time of repentance, nor a time when deeds benefit.

*Manas* is the verbal noun of *nāṣa yanūṣu*, meaning escape and withdrawal. *Lāta* in the sense of *laysa* is in the dialect of the people of Yemen.

The grammarians said: it is *lā* in the sense of *laysa*, to which the *tā'* has been added, as in their saying *rubba* and *rubbat*, and *thamma* and *thammat*. Al-Farra' said: *al-nawṣ* is withdrawal, and he recited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*Because of the memory of Layla, when she moved away from you withdrawing?*

He said: it is said: "He withdrew from his opponent, *yanūṣu nawṣan*," that is, fled and swerved.

Al-Farra' also said: it is said: *nāṣa yanūṣu* when he advanced.

It was also said: the meaning is that some of them said to others: "*Manas*!" that is, "Flee and be defeated!" Then when punishment came upon them they said "*manas*," and Allah said: ﴿but there was no time for escape﴾. Sibawayh said: *lāta* is made similar to *laysa*, and its subject is pronoun-implied, that is: "Our time is not a time for escape."

Al-Zajjaj said: the estimate is: "and it is not our time."

Ibn Kaysan said: the view is as Sibawayh said. Its pausal form, according to al-Kisa'i, is with a *hā'*, and al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash held the same.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Akhfash said: the *tā'* is written separated from *ḥīna*, and so it is in the codices.

Abu Ubayd said: it is written joined to *ḥīna*, so it is said *wa-lā taḥīnu*. From this is the saying of Abu Wajza al-Sa'di:

*The ones who bestow, at a time when no one bestows, and the ones who feed, at a time when no one feeds.*

*Ḥīn* may be used without its genitive complement, as the poet said:

*He remembered his love for Layla, a while too late, and grey hair had already cut off the companion.*

Abu Ubayd said: we have not found the Arabs adding this *tā'* except with *ḥīn*, *awān* and *al-ān*.

I say: rather they add it in other than that too, as in the saying of the poet:

*Then you will surely recognise dispositions held in common, and you will surely regret, and there is no time for regret.*

Al-Farra' cited this verse as evidence that some Arabs use it in the genitive. The clause ﴿but there was no time for escape﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *nādaw* (they called out).

The majority read *lāta* with a fatha on the *tā'*. It was also read *lāti* with a kasra, like *jayr*.

﴿And they wondered that a warner from among themselves came to them﴾. That is: the disbelievers, whom Allah described as being in arrogance and opposition, wondered that a warner from among themselves came to them, that is, a messenger from their own selves, warning them of punishment if they persisted in disbelief. *Anna* and what follows it is in the accusative position by removal of the preposition, that is, *min anna jā'ahum* (at the fact that he came to them). This is a new sentence including mention of one kind of their disbelief.

﴿And the disbelievers said: This is a magician, a liar﴾. They said this when they witnessed the miracles he brought, which lie beyond human power. That is: this one who claims prophethood is a magician in what he displays of miracles, and a liar in what he claims, that Allah sent him.

It was said: the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to show anger against them, and that what they said is not dared except by those who plunge deep into disbelief.

Then they denied what he (ﷺ) brought of monotheism, and of his negation of partners with Allah. They said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾, that is, has he turned them into one god and restricted them to Allah, glorified is He? ﴿Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾, that is, a matter utterly astonishing to the utmost degree. Al-Jawhari said: *ʿajīb* is a matter that is wondered at, and likewise *ʿujāb* with a damma and *ʿujjāb* with a shadda is more intense than it. The majority read *ʿujābun* with light pronunciation. Ali, al-Sulami, Isa ibn Umar and Ibn Miqsam read it with the *jīm* doubled.

Muqatil said: *ʿujābun* with light pronunciation is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a. It was said: both *ʿujāb* (light) and *ʿujjāb* (heavy) indicate that he has exceeded the limit in wonder, just as it is said: "the tall one" (*ṭawīl*) is one who has height, and "the very tall" (*ṭiwāl*) is one who has exceeded the limit of height. Al-Jawhari's statement implies that intensification is specific to *ʿujjāb* with the doubled *jīm*, not to the light form. We have already mentioned at the beginning of this surah the reason for the revelation of these verses.

﴿And the chiefs among them went off﴾. What is meant by *al-mala'* (the chiefs) is the nobles, as is established in many places in the commentary on the Mighty Book. That is: they went away from their gathering in which they were with Abu Talib, as has preceded, saying ﴿Go on﴾, that is, saying to one another: "Carry on as you were, and do not enter his religion." ﴿And be steadfast in the worship of your gods﴾, that is, persist in worshipping them. It was also said: the meaning is that the nobles among them went off and said to the common people: "Go on and be steadfast in the worship of your gods." The *an* in His saying ﴿anil-shū﴾ (that go on) is either the explanatory *an* for an implied saying, or for His saying "and went off," since it contains the meaning of saying. It may also be the verbal *an* governed by the implied or the mentioned verb, that is, "with 'go on'."

It was also said: the meaning of "went off" is the rushing into speech, and *imshū* is from *mashat al-mar'atu* when a woman bears many children, that is, they gathered together and multiplied. This is very far-fetched, and contrary to what the going off and walking indicate in their literal sense, and contrary to what has preceded concerning the occasion of revelation.

His saying ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is desired﴾ is a reason for what preceded it, the command to patience. That is: Muhammad desires it against us and against our gods, and wishes to complete it so that he may prevail over us and have followers, and so he will rule over us as he wishes. Thus this speech comes out as a warning against him and a repelling from him.

It was also said: the meaning is: this matter is desired by Allah, glorified is He, and whatever He desires will certainly come to pass. So be steadfast in the worship of your gods.

Some said the meaning is: "Indeed, this religion of yours is something sought," i.e., it is sought in order to be taken from you and for you to be overcome by it. But the first view is preferable.

﴿We have not heard of this in the latest religion﴾ i.e., we have not heard of this which Muhammad says of tawhid (monotheism) in the latest religion.

This is the religion of Christianity, for it is the last of the religions before the religion of Islam. So said Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Qatadah, Muqatil, al-Kalbi and al-Suddi.

Mujahid said: "They mean the religion of Quraysh," and the same was narrated from Qatadah as well.

al-Hasan said: The meaning of "we have not heard" is that this would happen at the end of time.

Some said: The meaning is: we have not heard from the Jews and Christians that Muhammad is a messenger. ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾ i.e., this is nothing but a lie which Muhammad invented and forged.

Then they denied that Allah would single out His Messenger with the distinction of prophethood over them, saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ The interrogative is for denial, i.e., how could that be, when we are the leaders and nobles?

al-Zajjaj said: They said, "How is the Qur'an sent down upon Muhammad from among us, when we are greater in age and more honoured than him?" This is like their saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two towns?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], so they denied that Allah - glorified is He - would bestow His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants with whatever He wills.

When He mentioned their denial that the Qur'an was sent down upon the Messenger of Allah - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace - instead of them, He explained the cause for which they abandoned believing in the Messenger of Allah - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace - in what he brought, so He said: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾ i.e., about the Qur'an or the revelation, because of their turning away from the reflection that necessitates believing in it and their neglect of the proofs indicating that it is the truth sent down from Allah. ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ i.e., rather the cause is that they have not tasted My punishment, so they were deceived by the long respite. Had they tasted My punishment for what they are upon of polytheism and doubt, they would have believed what you brought of the Qur'an and would not have doubted it.

﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ i.e., the keys to the bounties of your Lord, which are prophethood and what is less than it of blessings, so that they could give them to whomever they wish. What business do they have denying what Allah has graciously bestowed upon this Prophet, chosen for him and preferred him for His message?

The meaning: "Rather, do they have them?" because ʾam here is the disjunctive ʾam, presumed to be equivalent to bal and the hamzah. al-ʿAziz is the Victorious, the Overpowering; al-Wahhab is the One who gives without reckoning.

﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them?﴾ i.e., rather, do they possess these things, so that they give to whomever they wish and withhold from whomever they wish, and object to Allah - glorified is He - giving what He wills to whomever He wills? His saying: ﴿then let them ascend by the means﴾ is the answer to an omitted condition, i.e., if they have that, then let them climb up by the means that reach the sky and the Throne, so that they may decide by what they desire of giving and withholding and manage the affairs of the world as they please; or let them ascend and prevent the angels from descending with revelation upon Muhammad - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace.

al-Asbab (the means) are the gates of the heavens through which the angels descend. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*"Even if he sought the means to the sky by a ladder."*

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: The means are finer than hair and stronger than iron, but they are not seen. al-Suddi said: "in the means" means in virtue and religion. It was also said: Let them work at means of strength if they think that they prevent it; this is the view of Abu ʿUbaydah. It was also said: al-asbab are ropes, meaning if they find ropes by which they can climb to the sky, they should do so. In the usage of the linguists, al-asbab is everything by which one reaches the desired goal, whatever it may be. In this statement there is mockery of them and a challenge to them.

﴿A host there, routed, of the factions﴾ This is a promise from Allah - glorified is He - to His Prophet - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace - of victory over them and triumph against them. "Jund" is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., they are a host, meaning the disbelievers. "Mahzum" means broken, soon to be defeated. So do not be concerned with them, and do not think that they will reach anything of the plotting they conceal against you. The "ma" in His saying "ma hunalika" is a descriptor of "jund" to convey magnification and belittlement, i.e., a host, what a host!

It was also said it is redundant: one says "hazamta al-jaysh" (you broke the army), meaning you shattered it, and "tahazzamat al-qaryah" (the village crumbled) when it broke apart. This statement is connected to what preceded, namely His saying: ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in pride and opposition﴾, and they are a routed host of the factions. So do not grieve over their might and opposition, for I will strip them of their might and defeat their gathering, and this has occurred, praise be to Allah, at Badr and in what followed of the occasions of Allah.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Abu Salih, who said: Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah and Ibn ʿAbbas were asked about "Sad," and he said: "We do not know what it is." Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Sad" is Muhammad - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace.

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding "wal-Qur'ani dhi'l-dhikr" that he said: "dhi'l-sharaf" (possessor of honour).

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) related from al-Tamimi, who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbas about Allah's saying, ﴿then they called out, but it was no time for escape﴾, and he said: "It is not the time for leaping or fleeing."

Ibn Abi Hatim related through ʿIkrimah from him regarding the verse, who said: "They called out the call when it would no longer benefit them," and recited:

*"I remembered Layla, but too late for remembering, and I have been separated from her, and escape is far."*

He also related from him regarding the verse: "This is not the time of withdrawal."

Ibn al-Mundhir related through ʿAtiyyah from him as well, who said: "No time for flight."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿The chiefs among them went forth﴾ up to the end of the verse: "It was revealed when the nobles of Quraysh went to Abu Talib and spoke to him about the Prophet - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace."

Ibn Mardawayh related from him regarding ﴿The chiefs among them went forth﴾: "Abu Jahl."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him as well regarding His saying ﴿We have not heard of this in the latest religion﴾: "Christianity."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him as well regarding His saying ﴿so let them ascend by the means﴾: "In the sky."

It was also said: the answer is *ṣād*, because its meaning is "true," so it is an answer to the phrase "by the Qur'an," just as you say "truly, by Allah" or "it is necessary, by Allah." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari, and it is also related from Tha'lab and al-Farra'. This is based on the view that the answer of an oath may precede it, and this is weak.

It was also said: the answer is omitted, and the estimate is: "By the Qur'an, full of reminder, you will surely be raised," and the like.

Ibn Atiyya said: its estimate is: "The matter is not as the disbelievers claim." The view that it is omitted is preferable.

It was also said: His saying *ṣād* is itself sworn by, and according to this view the *wa* in ﴿and the Qur'an﴾ is for conjunction with it. Since swearing by the Qur'an indicates its truthfulness, that it is true, and that it is not a place for doubt—

He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾. So He turned away from that, as if He said: there is no doubt in it at all, and the disbelieving polytheists' refusal to accept it was not due to any doubt about it.

Rather, they are in arrogance, that is, in refusing to accept the truth: pride and tyranny.

And *shiqaq* means opposition, that is, refusal to accept the truth. In the language of the Arabs, *'izza* means dominance and overpowering. It is said: "Whoever is mighty plunders," that is, whoever dominates takes spoil. From this comes His saying ﴿and he overpowered me in the discourse﴾ [Sad 38:23], that is, he dominated me. From it is the saying of the poet:

*He overpowers on the road with his two shoulders, as the gambler crouches over the arrows.*

*Shiqaq* is derived from *shiqq* (split, side), and its explanation has already preceded.

Then He, glorified is He, warned them and threatened them with what He did to the disbelievers before them, saying: ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them﴾, meaning the earlier nations destroyed for denying the messengers. That is: how many of the bygone nations did We destroy, who were stronger than these in defence, more powerful and richer in wealth. *Kam* here is the informative *kam* that indicates multiplicity; it is in the position of the accusative governed by *ahlaknā* (We destroyed), as its object. *Min qarn* is the specification. The *min* in ﴿min qablihim﴾ is for the starting point of the limit.

﴿Then they called out, but there was no time for escape﴾. The calling here is the calling for help from them at the descent of punishment upon them, and the time is not a time of escape.

Al-Hasan said: they called out for repentance, but it was not the time of repentance, nor a time when deeds benefit.

*Manas* is the verbal noun of *nāṣa yanūṣu*, meaning escape and withdrawal. *Lāta* in the sense of *laysa* is in the dialect of the people of Yemen.

The grammarians said: it is *lā* in the sense of *laysa*, to which the *tā'* has been added, as in their saying *rubba* and *rubbat*, and *thamma* and *thammat*. Al-Farra' said: *al-nawṣ* is withdrawal, and he recited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*Because of the memory of Layla, when she moved away from you withdrawing?*

He said: it is said: "He withdrew from his opponent, *yanūṣu nawṣan*," that is, fled and swerved.

Al-Farra' also said: it is said: *nāṣa yanūṣu* when he advanced.

It was also said: the meaning is that some of them said to others: "*Manas*!" that is, "Flee and be defeated!" Then when punishment came upon them they said "*manas*," and Allah said: ﴿but there was no time for escape﴾. Sibawayh said: *lāta* is made similar to *laysa*, and its subject is pronoun-implied, that is: "Our time is not a time for escape."

Al-Zajjaj said: the estimate is: "and it is not our time."

Ibn Kaysan said: the view is as Sibawayh said. Its pausal form, according to al-Kisa'i, is with a *hā'*, and al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash held the same.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Akhfash said: the *tā'* is written separated from *ḥīna*, and so it is in the codices.

Abu Ubayd said: it is written joined to *ḥīna*, so it is said *wa-lā taḥīnu*. From this is the saying of Abu Wajza al-Sa'di:

*The ones who bestow, at a time when no one bestows, and the ones who feed, at a time when no one feeds.*

*Ḥīn* may be used without its genitive complement, as the poet said:

*He remembered his love for Layla, a while too late, and grey hair had already cut off the companion.*

Abu Ubayd said: we have not found the Arabs adding this *tā'* except with *ḥīn*, *awān* and *al-ān*.

I say: rather they add it in other than that too, as in the saying of the poet:

*Then you will surely recognise dispositions held in common, and you will surely regret, and there is no time for regret.*

Al-Farra' cited this verse as evidence that some Arabs use it in the genitive. The clause ﴿but there was no time for escape﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *nādaw* (they called out).

The majority read *lāta* with a fatha on the *tā'*. It was also read *lāti* with a kasra, like *jayr*.

﴿And they wondered that a warner from among themselves came to them﴾. That is: the disbelievers, whom Allah described as being in arrogance and opposition, wondered that a warner from among themselves came to them, that is, a messenger from their own selves, warning them of punishment if they persisted in disbelief. *Anna* and what follows it is in the accusative position by removal of the preposition, that is, *min anna jā'ahum* (at the fact that he came to them). This is a new sentence including mention of one kind of their disbelief.

﴿And the disbelievers said: This is a magician, a liar﴾. They said this when they witnessed the miracles he brought, which lie beyond human power. That is: this one who claims prophethood is a magician in what he displays of miracles, and a liar in what he claims, that Allah sent him.

It was said: the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to show anger against them, and that what they said is not dared except by those who plunge deep into disbelief.

Then they denied what he (ﷺ) brought of monotheism, and of his negation of partners with Allah. They said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾, that is, has he turned them into one god and restricted them to Allah, glorified is He? ﴿Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾, that is, a matter utterly astonishing to the utmost degree. Al-Jawhari said: *ʿajīb* is a matter that is wondered at, and likewise *ʿujāb* with a damma and *ʿujjāb* with a shadda is more intense than it. The majority read *ʿujābun* with light pronunciation. Ali, al-Sulami, Isa ibn Umar and Ibn Miqsam read it with the *jīm* doubled.

Muqatil said: *ʿujābun* with light pronunciation is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a. It was said: both *ʿujāb* (light) and *ʿujjāb* (heavy) indicate that he has exceeded the limit in wonder, just as it is said: "the tall one" (*ṭawīl*) is one who has height, and "the very tall" (*ṭiwāl*) is one who has exceeded the limit of height. Al-Jawhari's statement implies that intensification is specific to *ʿujjāb* with the doubled *jīm*, not to the light form. We have already mentioned at the beginning of this surah the reason for the revelation of these verses.

﴿And the chiefs among them went off﴾. What is meant by *al-mala'* (the chiefs) is the nobles, as is established in many places in the commentary on the Mighty Book. That is: they went away from their gathering in which they were with Abu Talib, as has preceded, saying ﴿Go on﴾, that is, saying to one another: "Carry on as you were, and do not enter his religion." ﴿And be steadfast in the worship of your gods﴾, that is, persist in worshipping them. It was also said: the meaning is that the nobles among them went off and said to the common people: "Go on and be steadfast in the worship of your gods." The *an* in His saying ﴿anil-shū﴾ (that go on) is either the explanatory *an* for an implied saying, or for His saying "and went off," since it contains the meaning of saying. It may also be the verbal *an* governed by the implied or the mentioned verb, that is, "with 'go on'."

It was also said: the meaning of "went off" is the rushing into speech, and *imshū* is from *mashat al-mar'atu* when a woman bears many children, that is, they gathered together and multiplied. This is very far-fetched, and contrary to what the going off and walking indicate in their literal sense, and contrary to what has preceded concerning the occasion of revelation.

His saying ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is desired﴾ is a reason for what preceded it, the command to patience. That is: Muhammad desires it against us and against our gods, and wishes to complete it so that he may prevail over us and have followers, and so he will rule over us as he wishes. Thus this speech comes out as a warning against him and a repelling from him.

It was also said: the meaning is: this matter is desired by Allah, glorified is He, and whatever He desires will certainly come to pass. So be steadfast in the worship of your gods.

Some said the meaning is: "Indeed, this religion of yours is something sought," i.e., it is sought in order to be taken from you and for you to be overcome by it. But the first view is preferable.

﴿We have not heard of this in the latest religion﴾ i.e., we have not heard of this which Muhammad says of tawhid (monotheism) in the latest religion.

This is the religion of Christianity, for it is the last of the religions before the religion of Islam. So said Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Qatadah, Muqatil, al-Kalbi and al-Suddi.

Mujahid said: "They mean the religion of Quraysh," and the same was narrated from Qatadah as well.

al-Hasan said: The meaning of "we have not heard" is that this would happen at the end of time.

Some said: The meaning is: we have not heard from the Jews and Christians that Muhammad is a messenger. ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾ i.e., this is nothing but a lie which Muhammad invented and forged.

Then they denied that Allah would single out His Messenger with the distinction of prophethood over them, saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ The interrogative is for denial, i.e., how could that be, when we are the leaders and nobles?

al-Zajjaj said: They said, "How is the Qur'an sent down upon Muhammad from among us, when we are greater in age and more honoured than him?" This is like their saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two towns?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], so they denied that Allah - glorified is He - would bestow His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants with whatever He wills.

When He mentioned their denial that the Qur'an was sent down upon the Messenger of Allah - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace - instead of them, He explained the cause for which they abandoned believing in the Messenger of Allah - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace - in what he brought, so He said: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾ i.e., about the Qur'an or the revelation, because of their turning away from the reflection that necessitates believing in it and their neglect of the proofs indicating that it is the truth sent down from Allah. ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ i.e., rather the cause is that they have not tasted My punishment, so they were deceived by the long respite. Had they tasted My punishment for what they are upon of polytheism and doubt, they would have believed what you brought of the Qur'an and would not have doubted it.

﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ i.e., the keys to the bounties of your Lord, which are prophethood and what is less than it of blessings, so that they could give them to whomever they wish. What business do they have denying what Allah has graciously bestowed upon this Prophet, chosen for him and preferred him for His message?

The meaning: "Rather, do they have them?" because ʾam here is the disjunctive ʾam, presumed to be equivalent to bal and the hamzah. al-ʿAziz is the Victorious, the Overpowering; al-Wahhab is the One who gives without reckoning.

﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them?﴾ i.e., rather, do they possess these things, so that they give to whomever they wish and withhold from whomever they wish, and object to Allah - glorified is He - giving what He wills to whomever He wills? His saying: ﴿then let them ascend by the means﴾ is the answer to an omitted condition, i.e., if they have that, then let them climb up by the means that reach the sky and the Throne, so that they may decide by what they desire of giving and withholding and manage the affairs of the world as they please; or let them ascend and prevent the angels from descending with revelation upon Muhammad - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace.

al-Asbab (the means) are the gates of the heavens through which the angels descend. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*"Even if he sought the means to the sky by a ladder."*

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: The means are finer than hair and stronger than iron, but they are not seen. al-Suddi said: "in the means" means in virtue and religion. It was also said: Let them work at means of strength if they think that they prevent it; this is the view of Abu ʿUbaydah. It was also said: al-asbab are ropes, meaning if they find ropes by which they can climb to the sky, they should do so. In the usage of the linguists, al-asbab is everything by which one reaches the desired goal, whatever it may be. In this statement there is mockery of them and a challenge to them.

﴿A host there, routed, of the factions﴾ This is a promise from Allah - glorified is He - to His Prophet - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace - of victory over them and triumph against them. "Jund" is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., they are a host, meaning the disbelievers. "Mahzum" means broken, soon to be defeated. So do not be concerned with them, and do not think that they will reach anything of the plotting they conceal against you. The "ma" in His saying "ma hunalika" is a descriptor of "jund" to convey magnification and belittlement, i.e., a host, what a host!

It was also said it is redundant: one says "hazamta al-jaysh" (you broke the army), meaning you shattered it, and "tahazzamat al-qaryah" (the village crumbled) when it broke apart. This statement is connected to what preceded, namely His saying: ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in pride and opposition﴾, and they are a routed host of the factions. So do not grieve over their might and opposition, for I will strip them of their might and defeat their gathering, and this has occurred, praise be to Allah, at Badr and in what followed of the occasions of Allah.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Abu Salih, who said: Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah and Ibn ʿAbbas were asked about "Sad," and he said: "We do not know what it is." Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Sad" is Muhammad - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace.

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding "wal-Qur'ani dhi'l-dhikr" that he said: "dhi'l-sharaf" (possessor of honour).

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) related from al-Tamimi, who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbas about Allah's saying, ﴿then they called out, but it was no time for escape﴾, and he said: "It is not the time for leaping or fleeing."

Ibn Abi Hatim related through ʿIkrimah from him regarding the verse, who said: "They called out the call when it would no longer benefit them," and recited:

*"I remembered Layla, but too late for remembering, and I have been separated from her, and escape is far."*

He also related from him regarding the verse: "This is not the time of withdrawal."

Ibn al-Mundhir related through ʿAtiyyah from him as well, who said: "No time for flight."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿The chiefs among them went forth﴾ up to the end of the verse: "It was revealed when the nobles of Quraysh went to Abu Talib and spoke to him about the Prophet - may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace."

Ibn Mardawayh related from him regarding ﴿The chiefs among them went forth﴾: "Abu Jahl."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him as well regarding His saying ﴿We have not heard of this in the latest religion﴾: "Christianity."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him as well regarding His saying ﴿so let them ascend by the means﴾: "In the sky."

**Commentary on Surah Sad (38), by al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir)**

Surah Sad is Meccan. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the consensus. Ibn al-Duraysh, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in the *Dala'il* related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Surah Sad was revealed in Mecca." Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in the *Dala'il* related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "When Abu Talib fell ill, a group of the Quraysh, among them Abu Jahl, entered upon him and said: 'Your nephew insults our gods, and does this and that, and says this and that. Would you send for him and forbid him?' So he sent for him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) came and entered the house. Between them and Abu Talib there was the space of one man's seat. Abu Jahl feared that he would sit beside Abu Talib and be above him, so he leapt up and sat in that place. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) found no place near his uncle, so he sat by the door. Abu Talib said to him: 'O my nephew, what is the matter with your people? They complain about you, claiming that you insult their gods and say this and that.' He said: They pressed him with many words. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke and said: 'O uncle, I want them to adopt one word, by which the Arabs will submit to them and the non-Arabs will pay them the jizya.' They were startled by his words and his statement. The people said: 'One word? Yes, by your father, ten!' They said: 'What is it?' He said: 'There is no god but Allah.' They rose in alarm, shaking their garments, saying: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ [Sad 38:5]. Then there was revealed concerning them: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾" [Sad 38:1–8].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Sad﴾. The majority read it with a sukun on the dal, like all the disjoined letters at the beginnings of surahs, since they are pausal forms (ending in sukun when stopped upon).

Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Nasr ibn Asim, Ibn Abi Ablah and Abu al-Simak read it with a kasra on the dal without tanwin. The reason for the kasra is the meeting of two sukuns. It was also said that the reason for the kasra is that it derives from *sada yusadi* (to confront, to oppose), and the meaning is: confront the Qur'an with your deeds, that is, oppose it with your conduct and face it by acting upon it. Al-Nahhas related this from al-Hasan al-Basri and said that he interpreted his recitation this way. And it is related from him that the meaning is: recite it and present yourself to its recitation.

Isa ibn Umar read *ṣāda* with a fatha on the dal. The fatha is due to the meeting of two sukuns. It was also said that it is in the accusative by way of incitement (*al-igra'*).

It was also said that its meaning is: Muhammad has attracted the hearts of creation and won them over until they believed in him. This reading is related from Abu Amr. It is also related from Ibn Abi Ishaq that he read *ṣādi* with a kasra and tanwin, likening this letter to what is not fully declinable among sounds.

Harun al-A'war and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *ṣādu* with a damma without tanwin, in the manner of indeclinable forms such as *mundhu* and *haythu*.

The meaning of *ṣād* has been disputed. Al-Dahhak said: its meaning is "Allah has spoken truly." Ata' said: "Muhammad has spoken truly." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is a sea by which Allah will bring the dead to life between the two blasts. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it is the key to the name of Allah. Qatada said: it is one of the names of Allah. It is related from him that he said: it is one of the names of the Most Gracious. Mujahid said: it is the opening of the surah. It was also said: it is among the things Allah has kept to Himself in knowledge, and this is the truth, as we have mentioned at the opening of Surah al-Baqara.

It was said: it is either a name for the letters enumerated in a fixed pattern for worship, or a name for the surah, or the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative by the implied verb *udhkur* (mention) or *iqra'* (recite). The *wa* in His saying ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ is the *wa* of oath, and swearing by the Qur'an indicates the exaltedness of its rank and the loftiness of its station. The meaning of ﴿full of reminder﴾ is that it contains the reminder in which is the explanation of everything.

Muqatil said: the meaning of ﴿full of reminder﴾ is full of explanation.

Al-Dahhak said: full of honour, as in His saying: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:10], that is, your honour. It was also said: that is, full of admonition.
