Allah, glorified is He, has said: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord and erred﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121], and he was the father of mankind and the first of the prophets; and other prophets experienced what Allah has related to us in His Book.

Then He, glorified is He, informed us that He accepted his plea for forgiveness and his repentance. He said: ﴿So We forgave him that﴾, that is, that sin for which he sought forgiveness.

'Ata' al-Khurasani and others said: Dawud remained prostrate for forty days, until the grass grew around his face and covered his head.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The pause at His words ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ is complete, and then the speech begins with His words ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is nearness and a good return﴾. *Al-zulfa* is closeness and honor after the forgiveness of his sin.

Mujahid said: *al-zulfa* is drawing near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection, and by "a good return" is meant a good place of return, which is Paradise.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿it has no respite﴾, that he said: "no return."

﴿And they say, "Our Lord, hasten for us our portion"﴾: he said: they asked Allah to hasten for them [their portion].

Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-Zubayr ibn 'Adi from him: ﴿Hasten for us our portion﴾, he said: our share of Paradise.

Ibn Jarir also reported from him, concerning His words *dhu al-ayd*, that he said: "strength." Ibn Jarir also reported from him: "*al-awwab*" is the one who glorifies (Allah).

al-Daylami reported from Mujahid who said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar about *al-awwab*, and he said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'It is the one who mentions his sins in privacy, then seeks forgiveness from Allah.'"

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "*al-awwab* is the one who is certain (*al-muqin*)."

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from 'Ata' al-Khurasani from him, who said: "The matter of the forenoon prayer (*salat al-duha*) remained in my mind until I recited this verse: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him, at evening and sunrise﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him as well, who said: "A time came upon me when I did not know the meaning of this verse: ﴿They glorified with him at evening and sunrise﴾, until I saw people praying the forenoon prayer."

al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, who said: "I used to pass by this verse, ﴿They glorified [Allah] at evening and sunrise﴾, and I did not know what it was, until Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib related to me that the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon her on the day of the Conquest, asked for water for ablution, performed ablution, then prayed the forenoon prayer, and then said: 'O Umm Hani', this is the prayer of sunrise (*salat al-ishraq*).'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from another route from him, similarly.

The traditions on the forenoon prayer are very numerous, and we have mentioned them in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa*.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A man from the Children of Israel sought redress before Dawud against a man of their notables, saying: 'This man has seized my cow from me.' Dawud asked the man about that, and he denied it. He asked the other for evidence, and he had no evidence. Dawud said to them both: 'Stand up until I consider your matter.' So they rose from his presence. Then Dawud was visited in his dream and it was said to him: 'Kill the man who sought redress.' He said: 'This is a vision, and I will not hasten until I verify it.' Then on the second night he was visited in his dream and was commanded to kill the man, but he did not do it. Then he was visited on the third night and it was said to him: 'Kill the man, or the punishment from Allah will come to you.' So Dawud sent for the man and said: 'Allah has commanded me to kill you.' He said: 'Will you kill me without evidence or verification?' He said: 'Yes, by Allah, I will carry out the command of Allah concerning you.' The man said: 'Do not hasten against me until I tell you. By Allah, I was not seized for this sin, but I had secretly killed the father of this man, and for that I was seized.' So Dawud gave orders concerning him, and he was killed. His awe grew among the Children of Israel and his kingdom was strengthened by it. This is the meaning of Allah's words ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾, that he said: "He was given understanding."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daylami reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari who said: "The first to say *amma ba'du* ('now then') was Dawud (peace be upon him), and it is ﴿and decisive speech﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Sa'd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Sha'bi that he heard Ziyad ibn Abihi say: "The decisive speech that was given to Dawud is: *amma ba'du*."

(p-1262)

Ibn Abi Shaybah reported in *al-Musannaf*, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, that David (Dawud) (peace be upon him) would say to himself that when he was tested he would hold fast to his protection. It was said to him: "You will indeed be tested, and you will know the day on which you will be tested, so take your precaution." It was then said to him: "This is the day on which you will be tested." So he took the Psalms (*al-Zabur*) and entered the sanctuary (*al-mihrab*), closed the door of the sanctuary, placed the Psalms in his lap, and seated a *munsif* (meaning a servant) at the door, saying: "Do not admit anyone to me today." While he was reading the Psalms, a golden bird came, the most beautiful of birds, with every color in it, and it began to fly around before him. It came close to him, and he was able to take it. He reached out his hand to seize it, but it moved away from behind him. He closed the Psalms and rose to take it, but it flew and alighted on the window (*kuwwat*) of the sanctuary. He approached it to take it, but it flew off and landed on a *khusss* (a small enclosure). He looked over it to see where it had fallen, and behold, there was a woman at her pool, bathing from menstruation. When she saw his shadow, she moved her head and covered her entire body with her hair. Her husband was away fighting in the way of Allah. David wrote to the commander of the fighters: "Place Uriya (Uriah) at the front of the bearers of the Ark (*al-tabut*)," and the bearers of the Ark were either to be granted victory or to be killed. So he sent him forward among the bearers of the Ark, and he was killed. When her waiting period (*ʿiddah*) ended, David proposed to her. She stipulated that if she bore a son, he would be the successor after him, and she called fifty of the Children of Israel as witnesses against him, and a document was written to that effect. He did not realize that he had been tested until she bore Sulayman (Solomon). When he grew up, two angels climbed over the sanctuary wall to him, and their affair was as Allah related in His Book. David fell down prostrating, and Allah forgave him and accepted his repentance.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported that he said: "Nothing befell David after what had happened to him, except as a result of self-admiration (*ʿujb*) with which he was impressed. That was because he said: 'O Lord, there is not an hour of night or day but that a worshipper from the family of David worships You, prays to You, glorifies You, or exalts You,' and he mentioned other things. Allah disliked that and said: 'O David, that was not possible except through Me. Had it not been for My help, you would not have been able to do it. By My might and My majesty, I will leave you to yourself for one day.' He said: 'O Lord, inform me of it.' So he was informed of it, and the trial befell him on that day."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported the origin of the story in *Nawadir al-Usul*, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported it from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), with a weak chain of narration.

Ibn Jarir reported it through another route from Ibn ʿAbbas, in a longer version. A group reported it from a group of the Successors (*tabiʿun*).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Masʿud, regarding the words of Allah ﴿Indeed, this is my brother﴾, that he said: "(He is) upon my religion."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, and Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani reported from him, who said: "David did no more than say ﴿Entrust it to me﴾."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding the words ﴿and few are they﴾, that he said: "Few are those who are in it (the state they are in)." And regarding the words ﴿And David thought that We had tested him﴾, he said: "We had tested him."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* also reported from him, that he said regarding the prostration in Surah Sad: "It is not among the obligatory prostrations (*ʿaza'im al-sujud*), though I have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrate in it."

Al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh reported with a good chain from him as well that "the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in Sad and said: 'David prostrated it, and we prostrate it in thanks.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in Sad. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas the like of it, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Darimi, Abu Dawud, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* reported from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited Sad while on the pulpit. When he reached the prostration, he came down and prostrated, and the people prostrated with him. On another day he recited it, and when he reached the prostration, the people prepared themselves to prostrate. He said: 'It is only a repentance, but I saw that you were preparing yourselves to prostrate,' so he came down and prostrated."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, "from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he mentioned the Day of Resurrection and magnified its matter and its severity. He said: 'The Most Merciful will say to David (peace be upon him): Pass before Me.' David will say: 'O Lord, I fear that my sin will cause me to slip.' He will say: 'Take hold of My foot.' So he will take hold of His foot, and he will pass by.' He said: 'That is the nearness (*zulfa*) of which Allah said ﴿Indeed, for him with Us is a near station and a good return﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verses 12–25 (part 1 of 3):

When He, glorified be He, mentioned the conditions of the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), He mentioned their like among those who came before them and did the same deeds of disbelief and denial. He said: ﴿Before them the people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Pharaoh of the stakes denied.﴾ The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: He had stakes with which he tortured people. This is because whenever he became angry with someone, he would stake his hands, his feet and his head to the ground.

It was also said: the meaning of "the stakes" is the many hosts and armies, meaning that they strengthened his affair and reinforced his authority, just as stakes strengthen whatever they are driven into. On this interpretation the expression is a metaphor (isti'arah).

Ibn Qutaybah said: The Arabs say, "They are in a glory with firm stakes, and a kingdom with firm stakes," meaning a lasting, strong kingdom. The origin of this is that a tent of poetry (bayt al-sha'r) is only fixed and erected by means of stakes.

It was also said: the meaning of "the stakes" here is solid construction, i.e., "Pharaoh of the solid buildings."

al-Dahhak said: Buildings are also called stakes (awtad). The plural of watad is awtad, and its most eloquent form is with a fatha on the waw and a kasra on the ta'. It is also said watad with a fatha, and wadd with the ta' assimilated into the dal, and wadat.

al-Asma'i said: It is also said watid and watid, like shughl and shaghil. He recited:

"She met on the water a firm, stake-like stalk,
and it did not fail the promises it made."

﴿And Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the Thicket.﴾ "Al-Aykah" is the thicket, and its explanation and the variation of the readers in its recitation have already been discussed in surah al-Shu'ara'. The meaning of ﴿Those are the factions﴾ is that they are the ones described by strength and numbers, like the saying, "So-and-so is the man."

Although Quraysh are a faction, as Allah, glorified be He, said earlier: ﴿A host of factions, defeated there.﴾ [Sad: 11], yet those whom Allah has related to us from the earlier nations are more numerous than them, stronger in body, and greater in wealth and lifespans. This sentence may be a new statement (mustan'afah), or it may be a predicate (khabar). The subject would be His words "and 'Ad," so said Abu al-Baqa', but this is weak. Rather, the apparent sense is that "'Ad" and what follows it are conjoined to "the people of Noah." It is best that this sentence be a predicate of an omitted subject, or an apposition (badal) to the nations previously mentioned.

﴿There was none but denied the Messengers.﴾ The particle ("in") is negating. The meaning is: each one of these factions was not but a denier of the Messengers, because the denial by a faction of its messenger sent to it is a denial of all the Messengers; or it is an instance of matching the plural with the plural. What is meant is that each faction denied its messenger. The exception (istithna') is a "truncated" exception from the most general of states, meaning: every one of the factions, in all its states, did nothing but deny the Messengers. ﴿So My punishment was deserved.﴾ That is: My punishment became due upon them because of their denial. The meaning of "haqqa" is established and obligatory. Even though it is delayed, it is as if it has already befallen them, and everything that is coming is near.

Ya'qub read the yā' in ("'iqab") with its pronunciation, while the rest omitted it, in agreement with the endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayy).

﴿These people await only a single blast.﴾ That is: they do not await but a blast, which is the trumpet blast occurring at the establishment of the Hour.

It was also said: it is the second blast. On the first view, what is meant is the disbelievers contemporary with our Prophet (ﷺ). On the second view, what is meant is the disbelievers of the nations mentioned, meaning: there is nothing between them and the arrival of what Allah has prepared for them of the punishment of the Fire except that the second blast be blown into the Trumpet.

It was also said: what is meant by "the blast" is a punishment that will seize them in this world, as the poet said:

"The time cried out upon the house of Barmak with a cry,
and they fell upon their chins from its severity."

The clause ﴿There is no pause (fawaq) for it﴾ is in the position of an accusative qualifier (sifah) of "blast." al-Zajjaj said: "fawaq" and "fuwaq," with a fatha or a damma on the fa', mean: there is no return for it. "Al-fawaq" is the interval between the two milkings of a she-camel, and it is derived from the meaning of return as well, because the milk returns to the udder between the two milkings. Also "afaqa" from his illness means he returned to health. For this reason Mujahid and Muqatil said: "al-fawaq" is return.

Qatadah said: "There is no reprieve for it."

al-Suddi said: "There is no recovery for it." It was also said: "There is no turning back for it."

al-Jawhari said: "There is no respite, rest, or recovery for it." The meaning of the verse is that this blast is the appointed time of their punishment. When it comes, it does not return, nor is it turned back from them, nor averted from them, nor delayed even the measure of the fawaq of a she-camel, which is the interval between the two milkings by the milker. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Until, when a little milk gathered in her udder,
she came to suckle the half of the soul, had it suckled."

"Al-fiqah" is the name of the milk that gathers between the two milkings, and its plural is fiq and afwaq.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "mā lahā min fawāq" with a damma on the fa', while the rest read it with a fatha.

al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Al-fawaq" with a fatha on the fa' means rest, i.e., they will not recover in it as the sick or the unconscious person recovers. With a damma it means waiting.

﴿And they said: "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ When they heard what Allah had threatened them with of punishment, they said this statement in mockery and derision. "Al-qitt" in the language means the portion, derived from "al-qatt," which is cutting. This is what Qatadah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said.

al-Farra' said: "Al-qitt" in the speech of the Arabs means the lot and the portion. From it, a written document (sakk) is called "qitt."

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Kisa'i said: "Al-qitt" is the written document of gifts, and its plural is qutut. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Nor the king al-Nu'man, on the day I met him,
gave the qutut in his prosperity, and he set things right."

The meaning of "yafiq" is "yuslih" (sets right). The meaning of the verse is that they asked their Lord to hasten to them their share and portion of the punishment. This is like His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment.﴾ [al-Hajj: 47; al-'Ankabut: 53].

al-Suddi said: They asked their Lord to show them their dwellings in Paradise, so that they might know the reality of what they were promised.

Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid said: The meaning is "hasten to us our provisions." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi also said this.

Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: When the verse ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 19; al-Inshiqaq: 7] and ﴿But as for him who is given his record in his left hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 25] was revealed, Quraysh said: "You claim, O Muhammad, that we will be given our records in our left hands. So hasten to us our share before the Day of Reckoning."

Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Prophet to be patient over what he hears of their sayings, and said: ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, of their false sayings, of which this statement reported from them is part. This verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿And mention Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength.﴾ When He finished mentioning the generations of error and the nations of disbelief and denial, and commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient over what he hears, He increased his consolation by mentioning the story of Dawud and what follows it.

The meaning of ﴿And mention Our servant Dawud﴾ is: mention his story, for you will find in it what you may be consoled by. "Al-ayd" is strength, and from it comes "rajul ayyid," meaning a strong man, and "ta'ayyada al-shay'" means it became strong. What is meant is the strength he (peace be upon him) had in worship.

al-Zajjaj said: Dawud's strength in worship was the most complete strength. Among his strength is what our Prophet (ﷺ) informed us of: that he used to fast one day and break his fast the next day, used to pray half the night, and did not flee when he met the enemy.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he was constantly returning (awwab)﴾ is a justification for his being "the possessor of strength." "Al-awwab" is one who returns from everything that Allah, glorified be He, dislikes to what He loves. Only one who is strong in his religion can do that.

It was also said: its meaning is that whenever he remembered his sin, he asked forgiveness for it and repented of it. This is included in the first meaning. It is said "aba yaubu" when someone returns.

﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify Him with him at evening and sunrise.﴾ That is: they sanctify Allah, glorified be He, and exalt Him above what is not befitting to Him.

The clause "yusabbihna" is in the position of an accusative circumstantial (hal). In this is a clarification of what Allah gave him of proof and miracle, which is the mountains glorifying Allah with him.

Muqatil said: Whenever Dawud remembered Allah, the mountains would remember with him, and he would understand the glorification of the mountains.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Dawud was given such a beautiful voice that the mountains would echo with a lovely resonance. This is the meaning of the glorification of the mountains, and the first is better.

It was also said: the meaning of "yusabbihna" is "yuṣallina" (they pray). "Ma'ahu" is connected to "sakhkharna" (We subjected).

As for the meaning of ﴿at evening and sunrise﴾, al-Kalbi said: in the morning and the evening. It is said "ashraqat al-shams" when it shines, and that is the time of forenoon. As for its "shuruq," that is its rising. al-Zajjaj said: "Sharaqat al-shams" means it rose, and "ashraqat" means it shone.

﴿And the birds, gathered (mahshurah)﴾ is conjoined to "the mountains." The accusative of "mahshurah" is a circumstantial (hal) from "the birds," meaning: and We subjected the birds, in a state of being gathered, that is, assembled to him, glorifying Allah with him.

It was said: the angels used to gather them to him. It was also said: the wind used to gather them.

﴿Each one of them was constantly returning to Him.﴾ That is: each one of Dawud, the mountains and the birds was returning to the obedience of Allah and His command. The pronoun in "lahu" refers to Allah, mighty and majestic.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to Dawud, meaning: for the sake of Dawud's glorification, a glorifier. So "awwab" is placed in the position of "musabbih" (glorifier). The first is better.

We have already stated that "awwab" means one who returns much to Allah, glorified be He.

﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾: We strengthened and established it by victory on the battlefields over his enemies, and by casting terror of him into their hearts.

It was also said: by the multitude of soldiers.

﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech (fasl al-khitab).﴾ What is meant by "wisdom" is prophethood and knowledge of everything by which one judges.

Muqatil said: understanding and knowledge. Mujahid said: justice. Abu al-'Aliyah said: knowledge of the Book of Allah. Shurayh said: the Sunnah.

What is meant by "fasl al-khitab" is the decisive judgment in legal disputes, and this was said by al-Hasan, al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

al-Wahidi related from the majority that "fasl al-khitab" is testimony (shuhud) and the oath (iman), because the dispute is only ended by these.

It was also said: it is concision, by placing a great meaning in few words.

﴿And has there come to you the news of the litigants, when they climbed over the sanctuary wall (al-mihrab)?﴾ When Allah, glorified be He, praised him with what has been mentioned, He followed that with the mention of this story, because of the wondrous reports it contains.

Muqatil said: Allah sent to Dawud two angels, Jibril and Mika'il, to alert him to repentance. They came to him while he was in his sanctuary.

al-Nahhas said: There is no disagreement among the people of tafsir that what is meant by "the litigants" here are the two angels, and "khasm" is a verbal noun that applies to the singular, the dual and the plural.

The meaning of ﴿they climbed over the sanctuary wall﴾ is that they came to him from the top of his wall and descended to him. "Al-sur" is a high wall. The plural form was used in "tasawwaru" although they were two, looking at what the word "khasm" allows of plurality.

From this is the poet's saying:

"And adversaries, angry, I have shaken their beards
like the shaking of noble, saddled horses."

"Al-mihrab" is the upper chamber, because they climbed over the wall onto him while he was in it, so said Yahya ibn Salam.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the front of the assembly, and from it comes the "mihrab" of the mosque.

It was also said: they were two humans, not two angels.

The governing element (al-'amil) of "idh" in His saying ﴿when they entered upon Dawud﴾ is "al-naba'" (the news), meaning: has the news reached you that occurred at the time of their climbing over? This is what Ibn 'Atiyyah, Makki and Abu al-Baqa' said. It was said: the governing element is "atak" (has come to you). It was said: it is governed by "khasm." It was said: it is governed by an omitted element, meaning: "and has the news of the litigation of the adversaries reached you?" It was said: it is governed by "tasawwaru." It was said: it is a substitute (badal) for what precedes it.

al-Farra' said: one of the two mentioned temporal adverbs has the sense of "lamma" (when). ﴿So he was frightened of them﴾, because they came to him at night at a time other than the time for litigants to enter, and they entered upon him without his permission, and they did not enter by the door through which people enter.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: The *mihrab* (the upper chamber) of Dawud was so high that no human could climb to it by any stratagem. The clause ﴿They said, "Fear not"﴾ is a new sentence (*isti'naf*), an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did they say to Dawud when he was startled by them?" The word *khasmani* ("two adversaries") is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "we are two adversaries." In what preceded, the verb was in the plural, and here it is in the dual, because the word *khasm* ("adversary") may be singular, dual, or plural, so all of these are permissible.

Al-Khalil said: It is like your saying "we did such-and-such" when you are two. Al-Kisa'i said: "[p. 1260] They used the plural because it was a report; when the report ended and direct address came, the two spoke about themselves in the dual and said 'two adversaries.'" His words ﴿One of us has wronged the other﴾ are said by way of supposition and hypothesis, and also by way of allusion, since it is known that the two angels do not wrong anyone.

Then they asked him to judge between them justly and forbade him from injustice, saying: ﴿So judge between us with truth, and do not exceed [the bounds]﴾, that is, do not be unjust in your judgment. It is said: *shatta al-rajulu* and *ashatta shatatan wa-ishatatan* ("the man went beyond bounds") when he acted unjustly in his judgment. Abu 'Ubayd said: "I *shatatu* against him and *ashatatu*," meaning "I acted unjustly." Al-Akhfash said its meaning is "do not be excessive"; it was also said "do not be negligent," and "do not incline." The meanings are close, and its root sense is distance, from *shatta al-dar*, "the house became distant." Abu 'Amr said: *al-shatat* is exceeding the proper measure in anything. ﴿And guide us to the even path﴾: *sawa' al-sirat* is its middle.

The meaning is: guide us to the truth and keep us upon it. Then, after they had informed him of the dispute in summary, they began to explain it in detail and to clarify it, saying: ﴿Indeed, this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe﴾. The "brotherhood" here means brotherhood in religion, or companionship. *Al-na'jah* is the female of sheep, though it may be said of wild cattle as well. Al-Wahidi said: *al-na'jah* is the wild cow, and the Arabs use it as a metaphor for a woman, comparing women to the cows among the herd.

The majority read ﴿tis'un wa-tis'una﴾ with a kasra on the *ta'* (*tis'un*, *tis'una*, as written). Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a fatha on the *ta'*. Al-Nahhas said: "This is an anomalous dialect." By "this" he meant Dawud, because he had ninety-nine wives, and by his words ﴿I have one ewe﴾ he meant [Uriya], the husband of the woman whom Dawud wished to marry, as will be explained later.

﴿So he said, "Entrust her to me"﴾, that is: join her to me and give her over to me, so that I may take charge of her and become her husband (*ba'l*).

Ibn Kaysan said: "Make her my portion and my share." ﴿And he overpowered me in speech﴾, that is, he overcame me. It is said: *'azzahu ya'uzzuhu 'izzan*, when he overcame him. There is a proverb: "Whoever overpowers, plunders," meaning whoever overcomes, takes spoil. The noun *al-'izzah* is strength. 'Ata' said: the meaning is that if he speaks, he is more eloquent than I.

Ibn Mas'ud and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read *wa-'azzani fi al-khitab* ("and he was stronger than me in argument"), meaning he prevailed over me, from *al-mu'azzah*, which is contest or overpowering.

﴿He said, "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes."﴾ That is: by his demanding your ewe to add it to his ninety-nine ewes, if the matter is as you say. The *lam* is the preparatory *lam* of an oath, and it together with what follows is the answer to an implied oath. He introduced the oath into his speech for emphasis, in denying what he heard of the request of the owner of the ninety-nine that the one ewe belonging to his companion be added to his own, when he had no other.

It is possible that he said this only after he had heard the admission from the other. Al-Nahhas said: "It is said that Dawud's error was his saying ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾, because he said that before he had verified the matter." ﴿And indeed, many of the partners﴾, that is the associates (*al-khulata'*), singular *khalit*, the one who mixes with another in property, ﴿do wrong one another﴾, that is, some of them transgress against others and oppress them, not respecting their rights, ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, for they avoid that and do not wrong an associate or anyone else. ﴿And few are they﴾, that is, and few are they; *ma* is superfluous, for emphasis and for wonder.

It was also said that *ma* is a relative pronoun, *hum* is the subject, and *qalil* is its predicate.

﴿And Dawud thought that We had only tested him﴾. Abu 'Amr and al-Farra' said: *zanna* here means *ayqana*, "was certain." The meaning of *fatannahu* is "We tested him." The meaning is that when they came to him in dispute and said what they said, he then knew what was intended, and that their true aim was to allude to him and to his companion, whom he wished to let go of his wife.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: When Dawud had judged between them, one of them looked at his companion and laughed, and at that Dawud knew what was meant.

The majority read *fatannahu* with the *ta'* lightened and the *nun* doubled. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja' read it with both the *ta'* and the *nun* doubled, which is an intensification of the testing. Al-Dahhak read *iftannahu*. Qatada, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *fatanahu*, with both lightened and the verb attributed to the two angels. This reading is reported from Abu 'Amr.

﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord﴾ for his sin, ﴿and fell down prostrate, and turned in repentance﴾, that is, he fell prostrate, and he expressed prostration by the word *raki'an* ("bowing").

Ibn al-'Arabi said: There is no disagreement among the scholars that what is meant here by *ruku'* is prostration, for prostration is inclination and bowing is bending, and each of them may enter into the other, though each may be specific to a particular posture. Thereafter this usage came in naming one by the other. It was also said: the meaning is "prostrating, bowing," that is, praying. It was also said: rather their bowing was prostration, and it was said: rather their prostration was bowing. ﴿And he turned in repentance﴾, that is, he returned to Allah in repentance from his sin.

The exegetes differed concerning the sin of Dawud for which he sought forgiveness and repented, in several views. The first: he looked at the wife of the man whom he wished to take as his wife; so said Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others. Al-Zajjaj said: Dawud did not deliberately look at the woman, but he repeated his looking at her, and the first look was his, but the second was against him.

The second view: he sent her husband among those sent out to war.

The third: he intended that, if her husband died, he would marry her.

The fourth: Uriya had proposed to that woman, and when he was absent, Dawud proposed to her, and she was married to him because of his high rank; Uriya was grieved by this, and so Allah rebuked him for not leaving her to her suitor.

The fifth: he did not grieve over the killing of Uriya as he would grieve over anyone of the soldiers who perished; then he married his wife, and Allah rebuked him for that, because the sins of prophets, though small, are great.

The sixth: he judged for one of the two adversaries before hearing from the other, as we have mentioned.

I say: the apparent meaning of the dispute that took place between the two angels, as an allusion to Dawud (peace be upon him), is that he asked the husband of the one woman to give her up to him and to join her to his wives. This does not contradict the infallibility (*'isma*) that belongs to the prophets. Allah drew attention to this and alluded to it by sending His angels to him to dispute over a matter like his story, until he would seek forgiveness for his sin and repent of it. So he sought forgiveness and repented.

Allah, glorified is He, has said: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord and erred﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121], and he was the father of mankind and the first of the prophets; and other prophets experienced what Allah has related to us in His Book.

Then He, glorified is He, informed us that He accepted his plea for forgiveness and his repentance. He said: ﴿So We forgave him that﴾, that is, that sin for which he sought forgiveness.

'Ata' al-Khurasani and others said: Dawud remained prostrate for forty days, until the grass grew around his face and covered his head.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The pause at His words ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ is complete, and then the speech begins with His words ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is nearness and a good return﴾. *Al-zulfa* is closeness and honor after the forgiveness of his sin.

Mujahid said: *al-zulfa* is drawing near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection, and by "a good return" is meant a good place of return, which is Paradise.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿it has no respite﴾, that he said: "no return."

﴿And they say, "Our Lord, hasten for us our portion"﴾: he said: they asked Allah to hasten for them [their portion].

Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-Zubayr ibn 'Adi from him: ﴿Hasten for us our portion﴾, he said: our share of Paradise.

Ibn Jarir also reported from him, concerning His words *dhu al-ayd*, that he said: "strength." Ibn Jarir also reported from him: "*al-awwab*" is the one who glorifies (Allah).

al-Daylami reported from Mujahid who said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar about *al-awwab*, and he said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'It is the one who mentions his sins in privacy, then seeks forgiveness from Allah.'"

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "*al-awwab* is the one who is certain (*al-muqin*)."

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from 'Ata' al-Khurasani from him, who said: "The matter of the forenoon prayer (*salat al-duha*) remained in my mind until I recited this verse: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him, at evening and sunrise﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him as well, who said: "A time came upon me when I did not know the meaning of this verse: ﴿They glorified with him at evening and sunrise﴾, until I saw people praying the forenoon prayer."

al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, who said: "I used to pass by this verse, ﴿They glorified [Allah] at evening and sunrise﴾, and I did not know what it was, until Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib related to me that the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon her on the day of the Conquest, asked for water for ablution, performed ablution, then prayed the forenoon prayer, and then said: 'O Umm Hani', this is the prayer of sunrise (*salat al-ishraq*).'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from another route from him, similarly.

The traditions on the forenoon prayer are very numerous, and we have mentioned them in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa*.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A man from the Children of Israel sought redress before Dawud against a man of their notables, saying: 'This man has seized my cow from me.' Dawud asked the man about that, and he denied it. He asked the other for evidence, and he had no evidence. Dawud said to them both: 'Stand up until I consider your matter.' So they rose from his presence. Then Dawud was visited in his dream and it was said to him: 'Kill the man who sought redress.' He said: 'This is a vision, and I will not hasten until I verify it.' Then on the second night he was visited in his dream and was commanded to kill the man, but he did not do it. Then he was visited on the third night and it was said to him: 'Kill the man, or the punishment from Allah will come to you.' So Dawud sent for the man and said: 'Allah has commanded me to kill you.' He said: 'Will you kill me without evidence or verification?' He said: 'Yes, by Allah, I will carry out the command of Allah concerning you.' The man said: 'Do not hasten against me until I tell you. By Allah, I was not seized for this sin, but I had secretly killed the father of this man, and for that I was seized.' So Dawud gave orders concerning him, and he was killed. His awe grew among the Children of Israel and his kingdom was strengthened by it. This is the meaning of Allah's words ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾, that he said: "He was given understanding."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daylami reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari who said: "The first to say *amma ba'du* ('now then') was Dawud (peace be upon him), and it is ﴿and decisive speech﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Sa'd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Sha'bi that he heard Ziyad ibn Abihi say: "The decisive speech that was given to Dawud is: *amma ba'du*."

(p-1262)

Ibn Abi Shaybah reported in *al-Musannaf*, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, that David (Dawud) (peace be upon him) would say to himself that when he was tested he would hold fast to his protection. It was said to him: "You will indeed be tested, and you will know the day on which you will be tested, so take your precaution." It was then said to him: "This is the day on which you will be tested." So he took the Psalms (*al-Zabur*) and entered the sanctuary (*al-mihrab*), closed the door of the sanctuary, placed the Psalms in his lap, and seated a *munsif* (meaning a servant) at the door, saying: "Do not admit anyone to me today." While he was reading the Psalms, a golden bird came, the most beautiful of birds, with every color in it, and it began to fly around before him. It came close to him, and he was able to take it. He reached out his hand to seize it, but it moved away from behind him. He closed the Psalms and rose to take it, but it flew and alighted on the window (*kuwwat*) of the sanctuary. He approached it to take it, but it flew off and landed on a *khusss* (a small enclosure). He looked over it to see where it had fallen, and behold, there was a woman at her pool, bathing from menstruation. When she saw his shadow, she moved her head and covered her entire body with her hair. Her husband was away fighting in the way of Allah. David wrote to the commander of the fighters: "Place Uriya (Uriah) at the front of the bearers of the Ark (*al-tabut*)," and the bearers of the Ark were either to be granted victory or to be killed. So he sent him forward among the bearers of the Ark, and he was killed. When her waiting period (*ʿiddah*) ended, David proposed to her. She stipulated that if she bore a son, he would be the successor after him, and she called fifty of the Children of Israel as witnesses against him, and a document was written to that effect. He did not realize that he had been tested until she bore Sulayman (Solomon). When he grew up, two angels climbed over the sanctuary wall to him, and their affair was as Allah related in His Book. David fell down prostrating, and Allah forgave him and accepted his repentance.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported that he said: "Nothing befell David after what had happened to him, except as a result of self-admiration (*ʿujb*) with which he was impressed. That was because he said: 'O Lord, there is not an hour of night or day but that a worshipper from the family of David worships You, prays to You, glorifies You, or exalts You,' and he mentioned other things. Allah disliked that and said: 'O David, that was not possible except through Me. Had it not been for My help, you would not have been able to do it. By My might and My majesty, I will leave you to yourself for one day.' He said: 'O Lord, inform me of it.' So he was informed of it, and the trial befell him on that day."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported the origin of the story in *Nawadir al-Usul*, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported it from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), with a weak chain of narration.

Ibn Jarir reported it through another route from Ibn ʿAbbas, in a longer version. A group reported it from a group of the Successors (*tabiʿun*).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Masʿud, regarding the words of Allah ﴿Indeed, this is my brother﴾, that he said: "(He is) upon my religion."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, and Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani reported from him, who said: "David did no more than say ﴿Entrust it to me﴾."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding the words ﴿and few are they﴾, that he said: "Few are those who are in it (the state they are in)." And regarding the words ﴿And David thought that We had tested him﴾, he said: "We had tested him."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* also reported from him, that he said regarding the prostration in Surah Sad: "It is not among the obligatory prostrations (*ʿaza'im al-sujud*), though I have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrate in it."

Al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh reported with a good chain from him as well that "the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in Sad and said: 'David prostrated it, and we prostrate it in thanks.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in Sad. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas the like of it, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Darimi, Abu Dawud, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* reported from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited Sad while on the pulpit. When he reached the prostration, he came down and prostrated, and the people prostrated with him. On another day he recited it, and when he reached the prostration, the people prepared themselves to prostrate. He said: 'It is only a repentance, but I saw that you were preparing yourselves to prostrate,' so he came down and prostrated."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, "from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he mentioned the Day of Resurrection and magnified its matter and its severity. He said: 'The Most Merciful will say to David (peace be upon him): Pass before Me.' David will say: 'O Lord, I fear that my sin will cause me to slip.' He will say: 'Take hold of My foot.' So he will take hold of His foot, and he will pass by.' He said: 'That is the nearness (*zulfa*) of which Allah said ﴿Indeed, for him with Us is a near station and a good return﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verses 12–25 (part 1 of 3):

When He, glorified be He, mentioned the conditions of the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), He mentioned their like among those who came before them and did the same deeds of disbelief and denial. He said: ﴿Before them the people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Pharaoh of the stakes denied.﴾ The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: He had stakes with which he tortured people. This is because whenever he became angry with someone, he would stake his hands, his feet and his head to the ground.

It was also said: the meaning of "the stakes" is the many hosts and armies, meaning that they strengthened his affair and reinforced his authority, just as stakes strengthen whatever they are driven into. On this interpretation the expression is a metaphor (isti'arah).

Ibn Qutaybah said: The Arabs say, "They are in a glory with firm stakes, and a kingdom with firm stakes," meaning a lasting, strong kingdom. The origin of this is that a tent of poetry (bayt al-sha'r) is only fixed and erected by means of stakes.

It was also said: the meaning of "the stakes" here is solid construction, i.e., "Pharaoh of the solid buildings."

al-Dahhak said: Buildings are also called stakes (awtad). The plural of watad is awtad, and its most eloquent form is with a fatha on the waw and a kasra on the ta'. It is also said watad with a fatha, and wadd with the ta' assimilated into the dal, and wadat.

al-Asma'i said: It is also said watid and watid, like shughl and shaghil. He recited:

"She met on the water a firm, stake-like stalk,
and it did not fail the promises it made."

﴿And Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the Thicket.﴾ "Al-Aykah" is the thicket, and its explanation and the variation of the readers in its recitation have already been discussed in surah al-Shu'ara'. The meaning of ﴿Those are the factions﴾ is that they are the ones described by strength and numbers, like the saying, "So-and-so is the man."

Although Quraysh are a faction, as Allah, glorified be He, said earlier: ﴿A host of factions, defeated there.﴾ [Sad: 11], yet those whom Allah has related to us from the earlier nations are more numerous than them, stronger in body, and greater in wealth and lifespans. This sentence may be a new statement (mustan'afah), or it may be a predicate (khabar). The subject would be His words "and 'Ad," so said Abu al-Baqa', but this is weak. Rather, the apparent sense is that "'Ad" and what follows it are conjoined to "the people of Noah." It is best that this sentence be a predicate of an omitted subject, or an apposition (badal) to the nations previously mentioned.

﴿There was none but denied the Messengers.﴾ The particle ("in") is negating. The meaning is: each one of these factions was not but a denier of the Messengers, because the denial by a faction of its messenger sent to it is a denial of all the Messengers; or it is an instance of matching the plural with the plural. What is meant is that each faction denied its messenger. The exception (istithna') is a "truncated" exception from the most general of states, meaning: every one of the factions, in all its states, did nothing but deny the Messengers. ﴿So My punishment was deserved.﴾ That is: My punishment became due upon them because of their denial. The meaning of "haqqa" is established and obligatory. Even though it is delayed, it is as if it has already befallen them, and everything that is coming is near.

Ya'qub read the yā' in ("'iqab") with its pronunciation, while the rest omitted it, in agreement with the endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayy).

﴿These people await only a single blast.﴾ That is: they do not await but a blast, which is the trumpet blast occurring at the establishment of the Hour.

It was also said: it is the second blast. On the first view, what is meant is the disbelievers contemporary with our Prophet (ﷺ). On the second view, what is meant is the disbelievers of the nations mentioned, meaning: there is nothing between them and the arrival of what Allah has prepared for them of the punishment of the Fire except that the second blast be blown into the Trumpet.

It was also said: what is meant by "the blast" is a punishment that will seize them in this world, as the poet said:

"The time cried out upon the house of Barmak with a cry,
and they fell upon their chins from its severity."

The clause ﴿There is no pause (fawaq) for it﴾ is in the position of an accusative qualifier (sifah) of "blast." al-Zajjaj said: "fawaq" and "fuwaq," with a fatha or a damma on the fa', mean: there is no return for it. "Al-fawaq" is the interval between the two milkings of a she-camel, and it is derived from the meaning of return as well, because the milk returns to the udder between the two milkings. Also "afaqa" from his illness means he returned to health. For this reason Mujahid and Muqatil said: "al-fawaq" is return.

Qatadah said: "There is no reprieve for it."

al-Suddi said: "There is no recovery for it." It was also said: "There is no turning back for it."

al-Jawhari said: "There is no respite, rest, or recovery for it." The meaning of the verse is that this blast is the appointed time of their punishment. When it comes, it does not return, nor is it turned back from them, nor averted from them, nor delayed even the measure of the fawaq of a she-camel, which is the interval between the two milkings by the milker. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Until, when a little milk gathered in her udder,
she came to suckle the half of the soul, had it suckled."

"Al-fiqah" is the name of the milk that gathers between the two milkings, and its plural is fiq and afwaq.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "mā lahā min fawāq" with a damma on the fa', while the rest read it with a fatha.

al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Al-fawaq" with a fatha on the fa' means rest, i.e., they will not recover in it as the sick or the unconscious person recovers. With a damma it means waiting.

﴿And they said: "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ When they heard what Allah had threatened them with of punishment, they said this statement in mockery and derision. "Al-qitt" in the language means the portion, derived from "al-qatt," which is cutting. This is what Qatadah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said.

al-Farra' said: "Al-qitt" in the speech of the Arabs means the lot and the portion. From it, a written document (sakk) is called "qitt."

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Kisa'i said: "Al-qitt" is the written document of gifts, and its plural is qutut. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Nor the king al-Nu'man, on the day I met him,
gave the qutut in his prosperity, and he set things right."

The meaning of "yafiq" is "yuslih" (sets right). The meaning of the verse is that they asked their Lord to hasten to them their share and portion of the punishment. This is like His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment.﴾ [al-Hajj: 47; al-'Ankabut: 53].

al-Suddi said: They asked their Lord to show them their dwellings in Paradise, so that they might know the reality of what they were promised.

Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid said: The meaning is "hasten to us our provisions." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi also said this.

Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: When the verse ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 19; al-Inshiqaq: 7] and ﴿But as for him who is given his record in his left hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 25] was revealed, Quraysh said: "You claim, O Muhammad, that we will be given our records in our left hands. So hasten to us our share before the Day of Reckoning."

Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Prophet to be patient over what he hears of their sayings, and said: ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, of their false sayings, of which this statement reported from them is part. This verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿And mention Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength.﴾ When He finished mentioning the generations of error and the nations of disbelief and denial, and commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient over what he hears, He increased his consolation by mentioning the story of Dawud and what follows it.

The meaning of ﴿And mention Our servant Dawud﴾ is: mention his story, for you will find in it what you may be consoled by. "Al-ayd" is strength, and from it comes "rajul ayyid," meaning a strong man, and "ta'ayyada al-shay'" means it became strong. What is meant is the strength he (peace be upon him) had in worship.

al-Zajjaj said: Dawud's strength in worship was the most complete strength. Among his strength is what our Prophet (ﷺ) informed us of: that he used to fast one day and break his fast the next day, used to pray half the night, and did not flee when he met the enemy.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he was constantly returning (awwab)﴾ is a justification for his being "the possessor of strength." "Al-awwab" is one who returns from everything that Allah, glorified be He, dislikes to what He loves. Only one who is strong in his religion can do that.

It was also said: its meaning is that whenever he remembered his sin, he asked forgiveness for it and repented of it. This is included in the first meaning. It is said "aba yaubu" when someone returns.

﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify Him with him at evening and sunrise.﴾ That is: they sanctify Allah, glorified be He, and exalt Him above what is not befitting to Him.

The clause "yusabbihna" is in the position of an accusative circumstantial (hal). In this is a clarification of what Allah gave him of proof and miracle, which is the mountains glorifying Allah with him.

Muqatil said: Whenever Dawud remembered Allah, the mountains would remember with him, and he would understand the glorification of the mountains.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Dawud was given such a beautiful voice that the mountains would echo with a lovely resonance. This is the meaning of the glorification of the mountains, and the first is better.

It was also said: the meaning of "yusabbihna" is "yuṣallina" (they pray). "Ma'ahu" is connected to "sakhkharna" (We subjected).

As for the meaning of ﴿at evening and sunrise﴾, al-Kalbi said: in the morning and the evening. It is said "ashraqat al-shams" when it shines, and that is the time of forenoon. As for its "shuruq," that is its rising. al-Zajjaj said: "Sharaqat al-shams" means it rose, and "ashraqat" means it shone.

﴿And the birds, gathered (mahshurah)﴾ is conjoined to "the mountains." The accusative of "mahshurah" is a circumstantial (hal) from "the birds," meaning: and We subjected the birds, in a state of being gathered, that is, assembled to him, glorifying Allah with him.

It was said: the angels used to gather them to him. It was also said: the wind used to gather them.

﴿Each one of them was constantly returning to Him.﴾ That is: each one of Dawud, the mountains and the birds was returning to the obedience of Allah and His command. The pronoun in "lahu" refers to Allah, mighty and majestic.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to Dawud, meaning: for the sake of Dawud's glorification, a glorifier. So "awwab" is placed in the position of "musabbih" (glorifier). The first is better.

We have already stated that "awwab" means one who returns much to Allah, glorified be He.

﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾: We strengthened and established it by victory on the battlefields over his enemies, and by casting terror of him into their hearts.

It was also said: by the multitude of soldiers.

﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech (fasl al-khitab).﴾ What is meant by "wisdom" is prophethood and knowledge of everything by which one judges.

Muqatil said: understanding and knowledge. Mujahid said: justice. Abu al-'Aliyah said: knowledge of the Book of Allah. Shurayh said: the Sunnah.

What is meant by "fasl al-khitab" is the decisive judgment in legal disputes, and this was said by al-Hasan, al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

al-Wahidi related from the majority that "fasl al-khitab" is testimony (shuhud) and the oath (iman), because the dispute is only ended by these.

It was also said: it is concision, by placing a great meaning in few words.

﴿And has there come to you the news of the litigants, when they climbed over the sanctuary wall (al-mihrab)?﴾ When Allah, glorified be He, praised him with what has been mentioned, He followed that with the mention of this story, because of the wondrous reports it contains.

Muqatil said: Allah sent to Dawud two angels, Jibril and Mika'il, to alert him to repentance. They came to him while he was in his sanctuary.

al-Nahhas said: There is no disagreement among the people of tafsir that what is meant by "the litigants" here are the two angels, and "khasm" is a verbal noun that applies to the singular, the dual and the plural.

The meaning of ﴿they climbed over the sanctuary wall﴾ is that they came to him from the top of his wall and descended to him. "Al-sur" is a high wall. The plural form was used in "tasawwaru" although they were two, looking at what the word "khasm" allows of plurality.

From this is the poet's saying:

"And adversaries, angry, I have shaken their beards
like the shaking of noble, saddled horses."

"Al-mihrab" is the upper chamber, because they climbed over the wall onto him while he was in it, so said Yahya ibn Salam.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the front of the assembly, and from it comes the "mihrab" of the mosque.

It was also said: they were two humans, not two angels.

The governing element (al-'amil) of "idh" in His saying ﴿when they entered upon Dawud﴾ is "al-naba'" (the news), meaning: has the news reached you that occurred at the time of their climbing over? This is what Ibn 'Atiyyah, Makki and Abu al-Baqa' said. It was said: the governing element is "atak" (has come to you). It was said: it is governed by "khasm." It was said: it is governed by an omitted element, meaning: "and has the news of the litigation of the adversaries reached you?" It was said: it is governed by "tasawwaru." It was said: it is a substitute (badal) for what precedes it.

al-Farra' said: one of the two mentioned temporal adverbs has the sense of "lamma" (when). ﴿So he was frightened of them﴾, because they came to him at night at a time other than the time for litigants to enter, and they entered upon him without his permission, and they did not enter by the door through which people enter.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: The *mihrab* (the upper chamber) of Dawud was so high that no human could climb to it by any stratagem. The clause ﴿They said, "Fear not"﴾ is a new sentence (*isti'naf*), an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did they say to Dawud when he was startled by them?" The word *khasmani* ("two adversaries") is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "we are two adversaries." In what preceded, the verb was in the plural, and here it is in the dual, because the word *khasm* ("adversary") may be singular, dual, or plural, so all of these are permissible.

Al-Khalil said: It is like your saying "we did such-and-such" when you are two. Al-Kisa'i said: "[p. 1260] They used the plural because it was a report; when the report ended and direct address came, the two spoke about themselves in the dual and said 'two adversaries.'" His words ﴿One of us has wronged the other﴾ are said by way of supposition and hypothesis, and also by way of allusion, since it is known that the two angels do not wrong anyone.

Then they asked him to judge between them justly and forbade him from injustice, saying: ﴿So judge between us with truth, and do not exceed [the bounds]﴾, that is, do not be unjust in your judgment. It is said: *shatta al-rajulu* and *ashatta shatatan wa-ishatatan* ("the man went beyond bounds") when he acted unjustly in his judgment. Abu 'Ubayd said: "I *shatatu* against him and *ashatatu*," meaning "I acted unjustly." Al-Akhfash said its meaning is "do not be excessive"; it was also said "do not be negligent," and "do not incline." The meanings are close, and its root sense is distance, from *shatta al-dar*, "the house became distant." Abu 'Amr said: *al-shatat* is exceeding the proper measure in anything. ﴿And guide us to the even path﴾: *sawa' al-sirat* is its middle.

The meaning is: guide us to the truth and keep us upon it. Then, after they had informed him of the dispute in summary, they began to explain it in detail and to clarify it, saying: ﴿Indeed, this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe﴾. The "brotherhood" here means brotherhood in religion, or companionship. *Al-na'jah* is the female of sheep, though it may be said of wild cattle as well. Al-Wahidi said: *al-na'jah* is the wild cow, and the Arabs use it as a metaphor for a woman, comparing women to the cows among the herd.

The majority read ﴿tis'un wa-tis'una﴾ with a kasra on the *ta'* (*tis'un*, *tis'una*, as written). Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a fatha on the *ta'*. Al-Nahhas said: "This is an anomalous dialect." By "this" he meant Dawud, because he had ninety-nine wives, and by his words ﴿I have one ewe﴾ he meant [Uriya], the husband of the woman whom Dawud wished to marry, as will be explained later.

﴿So he said, "Entrust her to me"﴾, that is: join her to me and give her over to me, so that I may take charge of her and become her husband (*ba'l*).

Ibn Kaysan said: "Make her my portion and my share." ﴿And he overpowered me in speech﴾, that is, he overcame me. It is said: *'azzahu ya'uzzuhu 'izzan*, when he overcame him. There is a proverb: "Whoever overpowers, plunders," meaning whoever overcomes, takes spoil. The noun *al-'izzah* is strength. 'Ata' said: the meaning is that if he speaks, he is more eloquent than I.

Ibn Mas'ud and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read *wa-'azzani fi al-khitab* ("and he was stronger than me in argument"), meaning he prevailed over me, from *al-mu'azzah*, which is contest or overpowering.

﴿He said, "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes."﴾ That is: by his demanding your ewe to add it to his ninety-nine ewes, if the matter is as you say. The *lam* is the preparatory *lam* of an oath, and it together with what follows is the answer to an implied oath. He introduced the oath into his speech for emphasis, in denying what he heard of the request of the owner of the ninety-nine that the one ewe belonging to his companion be added to his own, when he had no other.

It is possible that he said this only after he had heard the admission from the other. Al-Nahhas said: "It is said that Dawud's error was his saying ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾, because he said that before he had verified the matter." ﴿And indeed, many of the partners﴾, that is the associates (*al-khulata'*), singular *khalit*, the one who mixes with another in property, ﴿do wrong one another﴾, that is, some of them transgress against others and oppress them, not respecting their rights, ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, for they avoid that and do not wrong an associate or anyone else. ﴿And few are they﴾, that is, and few are they; *ma* is superfluous, for emphasis and for wonder.

It was also said that *ma* is a relative pronoun, *hum* is the subject, and *qalil* is its predicate.

﴿And Dawud thought that We had only tested him﴾. Abu 'Amr and al-Farra' said: *zanna* here means *ayqana*, "was certain." The meaning of *fatannahu* is "We tested him." The meaning is that when they came to him in dispute and said what they said, he then knew what was intended, and that their true aim was to allude to him and to his companion, whom he wished to let go of his wife.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: When Dawud had judged between them, one of them looked at his companion and laughed, and at that Dawud knew what was meant.

The majority read *fatannahu* with the *ta'* lightened and the *nun* doubled. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja' read it with both the *ta'* and the *nun* doubled, which is an intensification of the testing. Al-Dahhak read *iftannahu*. Qatada, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *fatanahu*, with both lightened and the verb attributed to the two angels. This reading is reported from Abu 'Amr.

﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord﴾ for his sin, ﴿and fell down prostrate, and turned in repentance﴾, that is, he fell prostrate, and he expressed prostration by the word *raki'an* ("bowing").

Ibn al-'Arabi said: There is no disagreement among the scholars that what is meant here by *ruku'* is prostration, for prostration is inclination and bowing is bending, and each of them may enter into the other, though each may be specific to a particular posture. Thereafter this usage came in naming one by the other. It was also said: the meaning is "prostrating, bowing," that is, praying. It was also said: rather their bowing was prostration, and it was said: rather their prostration was bowing. ﴿And he turned in repentance﴾, that is, he returned to Allah in repentance from his sin.

The exegetes differed concerning the sin of Dawud for which he sought forgiveness and repented, in several views. The first: he looked at the wife of the man whom he wished to take as his wife; so said Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others. Al-Zajjaj said: Dawud did not deliberately look at the woman, but he repeated his looking at her, and the first look was his, but the second was against him.

The second view: he sent her husband among those sent out to war.

The third: he intended that, if her husband died, he would marry her.

The fourth: Uriya had proposed to that woman, and when he was absent, Dawud proposed to her, and she was married to him because of his high rank; Uriya was grieved by this, and so Allah rebuked him for not leaving her to her suitor.

The fifth: he did not grieve over the killing of Uriya as he would grieve over anyone of the soldiers who perished; then he married his wife, and Allah rebuked him for that, because the sins of prophets, though small, are great.

The sixth: he judged for one of the two adversaries before hearing from the other, as we have mentioned.

I say: the apparent meaning of the dispute that took place between the two angels, as an allusion to Dawud (peace be upon him), is that he asked the husband of the one woman to give her up to him and to join her to his wives. This does not contradict the infallibility (*'isma*) that belongs to the prophets. Allah drew attention to this and alluded to it by sending His angels to him to dispute over a matter like his story, until he would seek forgiveness for his sin and repent of it. So he sought forgiveness and repented.

Allah, glorified is He, has said: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord and erred﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121], and he was the father of mankind and the first of the prophets; and other prophets experienced what Allah has related to us in His Book.

Then He, glorified is He, informed us that He accepted his plea for forgiveness and his repentance. He said: ﴿So We forgave him that﴾, that is, that sin for which he sought forgiveness.

'Ata' al-Khurasani and others said: Dawud remained prostrate for forty days, until the grass grew around his face and covered his head.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The pause at His words ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ is complete, and then the speech begins with His words ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is nearness and a good return﴾. *Al-zulfa* is closeness and honor after the forgiveness of his sin.

Mujahid said: *al-zulfa* is drawing near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection, and by "a good return" is meant a good place of return, which is Paradise.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿it has no respite﴾, that he said: "no return."

﴿And they say, "Our Lord, hasten for us our portion"﴾: he said: they asked Allah to hasten for them [their portion].

Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-Zubayr ibn 'Adi from him: ﴿Hasten for us our portion﴾, he said: our share of Paradise.

Ibn Jarir also reported from him, concerning His words *dhu al-ayd*, that he said: "strength." Ibn Jarir also reported from him: "*al-awwab*" is the one who glorifies (Allah).

al-Daylami reported from Mujahid who said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar about *al-awwab*, and he said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'It is the one who mentions his sins in privacy, then seeks forgiveness from Allah.'"

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "*al-awwab* is the one who is certain (*al-muqin*)."

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from 'Ata' al-Khurasani from him, who said: "The matter of the forenoon prayer (*salat al-duha*) remained in my mind until I recited this verse: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him, at evening and sunrise﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him as well, who said: "A time came upon me when I did not know the meaning of this verse: ﴿They glorified with him at evening and sunrise﴾, until I saw people praying the forenoon prayer."

al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, who said: "I used to pass by this verse, ﴿They glorified [Allah] at evening and sunrise﴾, and I did not know what it was, until Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib related to me that the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon her on the day of the Conquest, asked for water for ablution, performed ablution, then prayed the forenoon prayer, and then said: 'O Umm Hani', this is the prayer of sunrise (*salat al-ishraq*).'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from another route from him, similarly.

The traditions on the forenoon prayer are very numerous, and we have mentioned them in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa*.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A man from the Children of Israel sought redress before Dawud against a man of their notables, saying: 'This man has seized my cow from me.' Dawud asked the man about that, and he denied it. He asked the other for evidence, and he had no evidence. Dawud said to them both: 'Stand up until I consider your matter.' So they rose from his presence. Then Dawud was visited in his dream and it was said to him: 'Kill the man who sought redress.' He said: 'This is a vision, and I will not hasten until I verify it.' Then on the second night he was visited in his dream and was commanded to kill the man, but he did not do it. Then he was visited on the third night and it was said to him: 'Kill the man, or the punishment from Allah will come to you.' So Dawud sent for the man and said: 'Allah has commanded me to kill you.' He said: 'Will you kill me without evidence or verification?' He said: 'Yes, by Allah, I will carry out the command of Allah concerning you.' The man said: 'Do not hasten against me until I tell you. By Allah, I was not seized for this sin, but I had secretly killed the father of this man, and for that I was seized.' So Dawud gave orders concerning him, and he was killed. His awe grew among the Children of Israel and his kingdom was strengthened by it. This is the meaning of Allah's words ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, concerning ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾, that he said: "He was given understanding."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daylami reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari who said: "The first to say *amma ba'du* ('now then') was Dawud (peace be upon him), and it is ﴿and decisive speech﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Sa'd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Sha'bi that he heard Ziyad ibn Abihi say: "The decisive speech that was given to Dawud is: *amma ba'du*."

(p-1262)

Ibn Abi Shaybah reported in *al-Musannaf*, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, that David (Dawud) (peace be upon him) would say to himself that when he was tested he would hold fast to his protection. It was said to him: "You will indeed be tested, and you will know the day on which you will be tested, so take your precaution." It was then said to him: "This is the day on which you will be tested." So he took the Psalms (*al-Zabur*) and entered the sanctuary (*al-mihrab*), closed the door of the sanctuary, placed the Psalms in his lap, and seated a *munsif* (meaning a servant) at the door, saying: "Do not admit anyone to me today." While he was reading the Psalms, a golden bird came, the most beautiful of birds, with every color in it, and it began to fly around before him. It came close to him, and he was able to take it. He reached out his hand to seize it, but it moved away from behind him. He closed the Psalms and rose to take it, but it flew and alighted on the window (*kuwwat*) of the sanctuary. He approached it to take it, but it flew off and landed on a *khusss* (a small enclosure). He looked over it to see where it had fallen, and behold, there was a woman at her pool, bathing from menstruation. When she saw his shadow, she moved her head and covered her entire body with her hair. Her husband was away fighting in the way of Allah. David wrote to the commander of the fighters: "Place Uriya (Uriah) at the front of the bearers of the Ark (*al-tabut*)," and the bearers of the Ark were either to be granted victory or to be killed. So he sent him forward among the bearers of the Ark, and he was killed. When her waiting period (*ʿiddah*) ended, David proposed to her. She stipulated that if she bore a son, he would be the successor after him, and she called fifty of the Children of Israel as witnesses against him, and a document was written to that effect. He did not realize that he had been tested until she bore Sulayman (Solomon). When he grew up, two angels climbed over the sanctuary wall to him, and their affair was as Allah related in His Book. David fell down prostrating, and Allah forgave him and accepted his repentance.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported that he said: "Nothing befell David after what had happened to him, except as a result of self-admiration (*ʿujb*) with which he was impressed. That was because he said: 'O Lord, there is not an hour of night or day but that a worshipper from the family of David worships You, prays to You, glorifies You, or exalts You,' and he mentioned other things. Allah disliked that and said: 'O David, that was not possible except through Me. Had it not been for My help, you would not have been able to do it. By My might and My majesty, I will leave you to yourself for one day.' He said: 'O Lord, inform me of it.' So he was informed of it, and the trial befell him on that day."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported the origin of the story in *Nawadir al-Usul*, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported it from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), with a weak chain of narration.

Ibn Jarir reported it through another route from Ibn ʿAbbas, in a longer version. A group reported it from a group of the Successors (*tabiʿun*).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Masʿud, regarding the words of Allah ﴿Indeed, this is my brother﴾, that he said: "(He is) upon my religion."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, and Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani reported from him, who said: "David did no more than say ﴿Entrust it to me﴾."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding the words ﴿and few are they﴾, that he said: "Few are those who are in it (the state they are in)." And regarding the words ﴿And David thought that We had tested him﴾, he said: "We had tested him."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* also reported from him, that he said regarding the prostration in Surah Sad: "It is not among the obligatory prostrations (*ʿaza'im al-sujud*), though I have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrate in it."

Al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh reported with a good chain from him as well that "the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in Sad and said: 'David prostrated it, and we prostrate it in thanks.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in Sad. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas the like of it, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Darimi, Abu Dawud, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* reported from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited Sad while on the pulpit. When he reached the prostration, he came down and prostrated, and the people prostrated with him. On another day he recited it, and when he reached the prostration, the people prepared themselves to prostrate. He said: 'It is only a repentance, but I saw that you were preparing yourselves to prostrate,' so he came down and prostrated."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, "from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he mentioned the Day of Resurrection and magnified its matter and its severity. He said: 'The Most Merciful will say to David (peace be upon him): Pass before Me.' David will say: 'O Lord, I fear that my sin will cause me to slip.' He will say: 'Take hold of My foot.' So he will take hold of His foot, and he will pass by.' He said: 'That is the nearness (*zulfa*) of which Allah said ﴿Indeed, for him with Us is a near station and a good return﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verses 12–25 (part 1 of 3):

When He, glorified be He, mentioned the conditions of the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), He mentioned their like among those who came before them and did the same deeds of disbelief and denial. He said: ﴿Before them the people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Pharaoh of the stakes denied.﴾ The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: He had stakes with which he tortured people. This is because whenever he became angry with someone, he would stake his hands, his feet and his head to the ground.

It was also said: the meaning of "the stakes" is the many hosts and armies, meaning that they strengthened his affair and reinforced his authority, just as stakes strengthen whatever they are driven into. On this interpretation the expression is a metaphor (isti'arah).

Ibn Qutaybah said: The Arabs say, "They are in a glory with firm stakes, and a kingdom with firm stakes," meaning a lasting, strong kingdom. The origin of this is that a tent of poetry (bayt al-sha'r) is only fixed and erected by means of stakes.

It was also said: the meaning of "the stakes" here is solid construction, i.e., "Pharaoh of the solid buildings."

al-Dahhak said: Buildings are also called stakes (awtad). The plural of watad is awtad, and its most eloquent form is with a fatha on the waw and a kasra on the ta'. It is also said watad with a fatha, and wadd with the ta' assimilated into the dal, and wadat.

al-Asma'i said: It is also said watid and watid, like shughl and shaghil. He recited:

"She met on the water a firm, stake-like stalk,
and it did not fail the promises it made."

﴿And Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the Thicket.﴾ "Al-Aykah" is the thicket, and its explanation and the variation of the readers in its recitation have already been discussed in surah al-Shu'ara'. The meaning of ﴿Those are the factions﴾ is that they are the ones described by strength and numbers, like the saying, "So-and-so is the man."

Although Quraysh are a faction, as Allah, glorified be He, said earlier: ﴿A host of factions, defeated there.﴾ [Sad: 11], yet those whom Allah has related to us from the earlier nations are more numerous than them, stronger in body, and greater in wealth and lifespans. This sentence may be a new statement (mustan'afah), or it may be a predicate (khabar). The subject would be His words "and 'Ad," so said Abu al-Baqa', but this is weak. Rather, the apparent sense is that "'Ad" and what follows it are conjoined to "the people of Noah." It is best that this sentence be a predicate of an omitted subject, or an apposition (badal) to the nations previously mentioned.
