So he sent him forward among the bearers of the Ark, and he was killed. When her waiting period (*ʿiddah*) ended, David proposed to her. She stipulated that if she bore a son, he would be the successor after him, and she called fifty of the Children of Israel as witnesses against him, and a document was written to that effect. He did not realize that he had been tested until she bore Sulayman (Solomon). When he grew up, two angels climbed over the sanctuary wall to him, and their affair was as Allah related in His Book. David fell down prostrating, and Allah forgave him and accepted his repentance.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported that he said: "Nothing befell David after what had happened to him, except as a result of self-admiration (*ʿujb*) with which he was impressed. That was because he said: 'O Lord, there is not an hour of night or day but that a worshipper from the family of David worships You, prays to You, glorifies You, or exalts You,' and he mentioned other things. Allah disliked that and said: 'O David, that was not possible except through Me. Had it not been for My help, you would not have been able to do it. By My might and My majesty, I will leave you to yourself for one day.' He said: 'O Lord, inform me of it.' So he was informed of it, and the trial befell him on that day."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported the origin of the story in *Nawadir al-Usul*, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported it from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), with a weak chain of narration.

Ibn Jarir reported it through another route from Ibn ʿAbbas, in a longer version. A group reported it from a group of the Successors (*tabiʿun*).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Masʿud, regarding the words of Allah ﴿Indeed, this is my brother﴾, that he said: "(He is) upon my religion."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, and Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani reported from him, who said: "David did no more than say ﴿Entrust it to me﴾."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding the words ﴿and few are they﴾, that he said: "Few are those who are in it (the state they are in)." And regarding the words ﴿And David thought that We had tested him﴾, he said: "We had tested him."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* also reported from him, that he said regarding the prostration in Surah Sad: "It is not among the obligatory prostrations (*ʿaza'im al-sujud*), though I have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrate in it."

Al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh reported with a good chain from him as well that "the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in Sad and said: 'David prostrated it, and we prostrate it in thanks.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in Sad. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas the like of it, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Darimi, Abu Dawud, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* reported from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited Sad while on the pulpit. When he reached the prostration, he came down and prostrated, and the people prostrated with him. On another day he recited it, and when he reached the prostration, the people prepared themselves to prostrate. He said: 'It is only a repentance, but I saw that you were preparing yourselves to prostrate,' so he came down and prostrated."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, "from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he mentioned the Day of Resurrection and magnified its matter and its severity. He said: 'The Most Merciful will say to David (peace be upon him): Pass before Me.' David will say: 'O Lord, I fear that my sin will cause me to slip.' He will say: 'Take hold of My foot.' So he will take hold of His foot, and he will pass by.' He said: 'That is the nearness (*zulfa*) of which Allah said ﴿Indeed, for him with Us is a near station and a good return﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verses 26–33 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glorified is He, completed the story of Dawud (ﷺ)... [sic: Dawud (عليه السلام)], He followed it with an explanation of the delegation of the affair of the caliphate over the earth to him. The sentence is a *maqulah* (a direct speech) for an implied *qawl* (saying), coordinated with "*ghafarna*" (We forgave). That is: and We said to him, ﴿O Dawud, indeed We﴾ have appointed you over the earth, or ﴿have made you a successor﴾ to those prophets who came before you, so that you may enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. ﴿So judge between the people with truth﴾, that is, with justice, which is the judgment of God among His servants. ﴿And do not follow desire﴾, that is, the desire of the self in judging between the servants.

In this there is a warning to Dawud, upon him be peace, that what he was rebuked for was not just, and that there was in it a trace of following the desire of the self. ﴿Lest it lead you astray from the path of God﴾. It is in the accusative (*nasb*) on the basis that it is a response (*jawab*) to the prohibition (*nahy*), and the subject of "*yudillaka*" (lead you astray) is "*al-hawa*" (desire). It is permissible for the verb to be in the jussive (*majzum*) by coordination with the prohibition, and it was vowelled only because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. On the first reading, what is prohibited is the combination of the two (following desire and going astray), and on the second reading, the prohibition is against each of them separately.

"*Sabil Allah*" (the path of God) is the path of truth, or the path of Paradise. The sentence ﴿Indeed, those who go astray from the path of God have a severe punishment﴾ is a reason for the prohibition against following desire and falling into error. The *ba'* in ﴿for what they forgot of the Day of Reckoning﴾ denotes causation. The meaning of "*al-nisyan*" (forgetting) is abandonment. That is: because of their abandonment of action for that Day. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, by their abandonment of action for that Day, they became like those who forget, even though they are warned and reminded.

ʿIkrimah and al-Suddi said: in the verse there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*), and the implied meaning is: "And for them is the punishment of the Day of Reckoning, because they forgot," that is, they abandoned judging with justice. The first is more appropriate.

The sentence ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ is a new (*mustanafah*) sentence confirming what precedes it concerning the matter of resurrection and reckoning. That is: We did not create these things as a vain creation, outside of a manifest wisdom, but We created them as evidence of Our power. The accusative of "*batilan*" (in vain) is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), or a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*), or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). The demonstrative in His words "*dhalika*" (that) refers to the negated thing before it, and it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾, that is, their supposition, for they suppose that these things were created without purpose, and they say that there is no Resurrection, no raising, and no reckoning. And that entails that the creation of these creatures is in vain. ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾. The *fa'* indicates the consequence of the establishment of woe for them upon their false supposition. That is: so woe to them because of the Fire that follows from their supposition and their disbelief.

Then He rebuked them and reproached them, saying: ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth?﴾ Muqatil said: the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the believers: "We will be given in the Hereafter as you are given," so this was revealed. The "*am*" is the disjunctive one implicitly equivalent to "*bal*" (rather) and the interrogative hamza, that is: Do We make those who believe in God, affirm His messengers, and act upon His obligations like the corrupters in the earth through sins?

Then He, glorified is He, made another turn (*idrab*) and moved from the first to what is more evidently impossible than it, saying: ﴿Shall We make the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ That is: rather, We make the God-fearing among the believers like the wretched among the disbelievers, the hypocrites, and those among the Muslims who are immersed in the disobedience of God, glorified is He. It was said: the "*fujjar*" (wicked) here is specific to the disbelievers. It was said: the intended "*muttaqin*" (God-fearing) are the Companions. There is no basis for specification without a specifying indicator, and the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not with the specificity of the cause.

﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed﴾. "*Kitab*" (a Book) is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, and "*anzalnahu ilayka*" (We have sent it down to you) is a description of it, and "*mubarak*" (blessed) is a second predicate of the subject. It is not permissible for it to be another adjective of "*kitab*," because it is established that a clear (*sarih*) adjective may not be placed after a non-clear one; some grammarians nevertheless permitted it. The estimate is: The Qur'an is a Book We have sent down to you, O Muhammad, abundant in good and blessing.

"*Mubarakan*" (blessed) has been read as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*). His words ﴿that they may ponder﴾: its original form is "*liyatadabbaru*," and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal*. It is connected to "*anzalnahu*" (We have sent it down).

In the verse there is evidence that God, glorified is He, sent down the Qur'an only for pondering and reflecting upon its meanings, not for mere recitation without contemplation.

The majority read "*liyaddabbaru*" with assimilation (*idgham*). Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "*litadabbaru*" with the second-person *ta'* (addressing them), and this reading is narrated from ʿAsim and al-Kisa'i, and it is the reading of ʿAli, may God be pleased with him. The original is "*litatadabbaru*" with two *ta's*, and one was omitted for lightness. ﴿And that those of understanding may be reminded﴾, that is: that those possessed of minds may take heed. "*Al-albab*" is the plural of "*lubb*," which is intellect.

﴿And We gave to Dawud Sulayman, an excellent servant; indeed, he was one who turned often (to God)﴾. He, glorified is He, informed that among the blessings upon Dawud was that He gave him Sulayman as a son. Then He praised Sulayman, saying: ﴿an excellent servant﴾. The one specified for praise is omitted, that is: an excellent servant is Sulayman. It was said: the praise here with "*ni'ma al-'abd*" is for Dawud. The first is more appropriate. The sentence ﴿indeed, he was one who turned often﴾ is a reason for the praise before it. "*Al-awwab*" is one who returns to God in repentance, as has been explained earlier.

The adverbial in His words ﴿when there were displayed before him﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, which is "*udhkur*" (remember), that is: remember what proceeded from him at the time when the swift, noble horses were displayed before him in the evening. It was said: it is connected to "*ni'ma*," but despite its being non-inflected (*ghayr mutasarrif*), there is no basis for restricting it to that time. It was said: it is connected to "*awwab*," but there is no basis for restricting his being one who turns often to that time. "*Al-ashiyy*" (the evening) is from midday or afternoon until the end of the day.

"*Al-safinat*" is the plural of "*safin*." The lexicographers differed about its meaning. Al-Qutaybi and al-Farra' said: "*al-safin*" in the speech of the Arabs is standing still, of horses or others, and Qatadah said likewise. From this is the hadith: "Whoever wishes that people stand for him in rows, let him take his seat in the Fire," that is, they continually stand for him. They cited the words of al-Nabigha:

*Ours is a tent pitched in its courtyard, with noble camels and swift horses standing still.*

There is no proof for them in this, for it is an argument based on the very point of dispute, which is a begging of the question (*musadarah*), since the dispute concerns what "*safin*" actually is. Al-Zajjaj said it is the one that stands on one of its two forelegs, raising the other and placing the tip of its hoof on the ground, so that it appears to stand on three legs, which are the two hind legs and one foreleg. It may also do this with one of its hind legs, and this is a sign of excellence. Al-Zajjaj cited the poet's verse:

*He has become accustomed to standing still, so that it seems that it stands on three legs like a lame one.*

From this is the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

*We left the horses clustered around it, their reins hung, standing still.*

For his words "*sufunan*" (standing still) must be understood as having a meaning other than mere standing, since mere standing has already been conveyed by his words "clustered around it."

Abu ʿUbayd said: "*al-safin*" is the one who gathers its two forelegs and makes them even. As for the one that stands on the tip of its hoof, its name is "*al-mutakhayyim*." "*Al-jiyad*" is the plural of "*jawad*," said of a horse when it is very swift in running.

It was said: they are long-necked, derived from "*al-jid*," which is the neck. It was said: they were one hundred horses. It was said: they were twenty thousand. It was said: they were twenty horses. It was said: they came out to him from the sea and had wings.

﴿So he said, "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord."﴾ The accusative of "*hubba al-khayr*" is the object of "*ahbabtu*" (I loved) after it has been made to imply the sense of "*athartu*" (I preferred). Al-Farra' said: he means "I preferred the love of good," and whoever loves something has preferred it.

It was said: its accusative is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) by omission of the extra elements, and the governing verb is "*ahbabtu*." It was said: it is an analogous verbal noun (*maṣdar tashbihi*), that is: a love like the love of good. The first is more appropriate.

The intended "*khayr*" here is horses. Al-Zajjaj said: "*al-khayr*" here means horses. Al-Farra' said: "*al-khayr*" and "*al-khayl*" are one in the speech of the Arabs.

Al-Nahhas said: in a hadith: "Good is tied to the forelocks of horses," so it may have been called "good" for this reason. It was said: it was called "good" because of the benefits in it.

The "*ʿan*" in ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾ means "*ʿala*" (upon). The meaning: I preferred the love of horses over the remembrance of my Lord, that is, the afternoon prayer. ﴿Until they went out of sight behind the veil﴾, that is, the sun, though it has not been previously mentioned, but the context indicates it.

Al-Zajjaj said: a pronoun is permissible only when the thing has been mentioned or there is an indication of the mention, and here the indication has occurred, which is His words "in the evening."

"*Al-tawari*" is being concealed from sight, and "*al-hijab*" is what veils them from sight.

Qatadah and Kaʿb said: the veil is a green mountain surrounding the creation, and it is the Mountain of Qaf. The night is called a veil because it conceals what is in it. It was said: the pronoun in His words "until they went out of sight" refers to the horses, that is, until they went out of sight in the race away from the eyes. The first is more appropriate.

His words ﴿"Bring them back to me"﴾ are part of Sulayman's speech, that is: restore their display to me once more. Al-Hasan said: when the displaying of the horses preoccupied Sulayman until the afternoon prayer was missed, he became angry for God's sake and said, "Bring them back to me," that is, restore them.

It was said: the pronoun in "*rudduha*" (bring them back) refers to the sun, and this would be a miracle for him. He was ordered to return it after its setting so that he could pray the afternoon prayer. The first is more appropriate. The *fa'* in His words ﴿then he began to pass his hand over their shins and necks﴾ is the explanatory *fa'* (*fa' al-fasiha*), which indicates an omitted element in the speech; the estimate here is: "So they were brought back to him."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "*tafiqa yaf'alu*" is like "*ma zala yaf'alu*" (he continued to do), and it is like "*zalla*" and "*bata*." The accusative of "*mashan*" is a verbal noun by an implied verb: that is, he wiped with wiping, since the predicate of "*tafiqa*" can only be an imperfect verb. It was said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative. The first is more appropriate.

"*Al-suq*" is the plural of "*saq*" (shin), and "*al-a'naq*" is the plural of "*unuq*" (neck). The meaning is that he began to strike their necks and shins. It is said: "*masaha ʿilawatahu*," that is, he struck his neck.

Al-Farra' said: "*al-mash*" here means cutting. He said: the meaning is that he came to strike their shins and necks, because they had been the cause of missing his prayer. Abu ʿUbayda said likewise.

Al-Zajjaj said: he did not do that except that God had permitted it to him, and it is possible that this was permitted to Sulayman and that it occurred at this time.

The commentators differed in interpreting this verse. A group said: the intended "*mash*" is what has preceded. Others, among them al-Zuhri and Qatadah, said: the intended meaning is passing the hand over their shins and necks to remove dust from them out of love for them. The first view is more appropriate to the context of the speech, for He mentioned that he postponed them because of the remembrance of his Lord until the afternoon prayer was missed, and then he ordered them to be brought back to him, in order to punish himself by destroying what had distracted him from that and what had prevented him from worshipping his Lord and had occupied him from carrying out what God had obligated upon him. It is not consistent with this that the purpose of returning them to him was to remove dust from their shins and necks by wiping them with his hand or his garment. Nor does the one who says that squandering property does not proceed from a prophet have any support, for this is merely a judgment based on what is established in our law, while it is possible that in the law of Sulayman such a thing was permitted. Moreover, the squandering of property prohibited in our law is only its wasting without a valid purpose, whereas for a valid purpose the like of it has been permitted in our law, as when the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, overturned the pots of food cooked from the spoils before distribution. There are many similar examples in the Shariah, and among them is what the Companions did in burning the food of a hoarder.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: ﴿the swift, noble horses﴾ are horses created as He willed.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verse 26–33 (part 2 of 2):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿al-ṣāfināt﴾ (those standing on three legs, with the foreleg raised), that he said: "Ṣufūn (standing on three legs) of the horse is raising one of its forelegs until it rests on the tips of the hoof." And regarding His words ﴿al-jiyād﴾ (the swift, noble horses), he said: "They are the swift ones."

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿ḥubb al-khayr﴾ (love of good), that he said: "It is the water." And regarding His words ﴿Return them to me﴾, he said: "The horses." ﴿Then he began to pass his hand over them (maskan)﴾, he said: "Cutting their legs with the sword."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "The prayer which Sulayman neglected was the ʿAṣr prayer."

al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibrahim al-Taymi, regarding His words ﴿When there were displayed before him in the evening the standing, noble horses﴾, that he said: "They were twenty thousand horses, having wings, and he slaughtered them."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Masud regarding His words ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾, that he said: "They were hidden behind a green emerald, and the greenness of the sky is from it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Sulayman was not spoken to out of reverence for him, so the ʿAṣr prayer passed him by, and no one was able to speak to him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾, that he said: "From the remembrance of my Lord." ﴿Then he began to pass his hand over the shanks and necks﴾, he said: "He cut off their shanks and necks with the sword."

That is: and We said to him, ﴿O Dawud, indeed We﴾ have appointed you over the earth, or ﴿have made you a successor﴾ to those prophets who came before you, so that you may enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. ﴿So judge between the people with truth﴾, that is, with justice, which is the judgment of God among His servants. ﴿And do not follow desire﴾, that is, the desire of the self in judging between the servants.

In this there is a warning to Dawud, upon him be peace, that what he was rebuked for was not just, and that there was in it a trace of following the desire of the self. ﴿Lest it lead you astray from the path of God﴾. It is in the accusative (*nasb*) on the basis that it is a response (*jawab*) to the prohibition (*nahy*), and the subject of "*yudillaka*" (lead you astray) is "*al-hawa*" (desire). It is permissible for the verb to be in the jussive (*majzum*) by coordination with the prohibition, and it was vowelled only because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. On the first reading, what is prohibited is the combination of the two (following desire and going astray), and on the second reading, the prohibition is against each of them separately.

"*Sabil Allah*" (the path of God) is the path of truth, or the path of Paradise. The sentence ﴿Indeed, those who go astray from the path of God have a severe punishment﴾ is a reason for the prohibition against following desire and falling into error. The *ba'* in ﴿for what they forgot of the Day of Reckoning﴾ denotes causation. The meaning of "*al-nisyan*" (forgetting) is abandonment. That is: because of their abandonment of action for that Day. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, by their abandonment of action for that Day, they became like those who forget, even though they are warned and reminded.

ʿIkrimah and al-Suddi said: in the verse there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*), and the implied meaning is: "And for them is the punishment of the Day of Reckoning, because they forgot," that is, they abandoned judging with justice. The first is more appropriate.

The sentence ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ is a new (*mustanafah*) sentence confirming what precedes it concerning the matter of resurrection and reckoning. That is: We did not create these things as a vain creation, outside of a manifest wisdom, but We created them as evidence of Our power. The accusative of "*batilan*" (in vain) is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), or a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*), or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). The demonstrative in His words "*dhalika*" (that) refers to the negated thing before it, and it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾, that is, their supposition, for they suppose that these things were created without purpose, and they say that there is no Resurrection, no raising, and no reckoning. And that entails that the creation of these creatures is in vain. ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾. The *fa'* indicates the consequence of the establishment of woe for them upon their false supposition. That is: so woe to them because of the Fire that follows from their supposition and their disbelief.

Then He rebuked them and reproached them, saying: ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth?﴾ Muqatil said: the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the believers: "We will be given in the Hereafter as you are given," so this was revealed. The "*am*" is the disjunctive one implicitly equivalent to "*bal*" (rather) and the interrogative hamza, that is: Do We make those who believe in God, affirm His messengers, and act upon His obligations like the corrupters in the earth through sins?

Then He, glorified is He, made another turn (*idrab*) and moved from the first to what is more evidently impossible than it, saying: ﴿Shall We make the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ That is: rather, We make the God-fearing among the believers like the wretched among the disbelievers, the hypocrites, and those among the Muslims who are immersed in the disobedience of God, glorified is He. It was said: the "*fujjar*" (wicked) here is specific to the disbelievers. It was said: the intended "*muttaqin*" (God-fearing) are the Companions. There is no basis for specification without a specifying indicator, and the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not with the specificity of the cause.

﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed﴾. "*Kitab*" (a Book) is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, and "*anzalnahu ilayka*" (We have sent it down to you) is a description of it, and "*mubarak*" (blessed) is a second predicate of the subject. It is not permissible for it to be another adjective of "*kitab*," because it is established that a clear (*sarih*) adjective may not be placed after a non-clear one; some grammarians nevertheless permitted it. The estimate is: The Qur'an is a Book We have sent down to you, O Muhammad, abundant in good and blessing.

"*Mubarakan*" (blessed) has been read as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*). His words ﴿that they may ponder﴾: its original form is "*liyatadabbaru*," and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal*. It is connected to "*anzalnahu*" (We have sent it down).

In the verse there is evidence that God, glorified is He, sent down the Qur'an only for pondering and reflecting upon its meanings, not for mere recitation without contemplation.

The majority read "*liyaddabbaru*" with assimilation (*idgham*). Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "*litadabbaru*" with the second-person *ta'* (addressing them), and this reading is narrated from ʿAsim and al-Kisa'i, and it is the reading of ʿAli, may God be pleased with him. The original is "*litatadabbaru*" with two *ta's*, and one was omitted for lightness. ﴿And that those of understanding may be reminded﴾, that is: that those possessed of minds may take heed. "*Al-albab*" is the plural of "*lubb*," which is intellect.

﴿And We gave to Dawud Sulayman, an excellent servant; indeed, he was one who turned often (to God)﴾. He, glorified is He, informed that among the blessings upon Dawud was that He gave him Sulayman as a son. Then He praised Sulayman, saying: ﴿an excellent servant﴾. The one specified for praise is omitted, that is: an excellent servant is Sulayman. It was said: the praise here with "*ni'ma al-'abd*" is for Dawud. The first is more appropriate. The sentence ﴿indeed, he was one who turned often﴾ is a reason for the praise before it. "*Al-awwab*" is one who returns to God in repentance, as has been explained earlier.

The adverbial in His words ﴿when there were displayed before him﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, which is "*udhkur*" (remember), that is: remember what proceeded from him at the time when the swift, noble horses were displayed before him in the evening. It was said: it is connected to "*ni'ma*," but despite its being non-inflected (*ghayr mutasarrif*), there is no basis for restricting it to that time. It was said: it is connected to "*awwab*," but there is no basis for restricting his being one who turns often to that time. "*Al-ashiyy*" (the evening) is from midday or afternoon until the end of the day.

The *ba'* in ﴿for what they forgot of the Day of Reckoning﴾ denotes causation. The meaning of "*al-nisyan*" (forgetting) is abandonment. That is: because of their abandonment of action for that Day. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, by their abandonment of action for that Day, they became like those who forget, even though they are warned and reminded.

ʿIkrimah and al-Suddi said: in the verse there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*), and the implied meaning is: "And for them is the punishment of the Day of Reckoning, because they forgot," that is, they abandoned judging with justice. The first is more appropriate.

The sentence ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ is a new (*mustanafah*) sentence confirming what precedes it concerning the matter of resurrection and reckoning. That is: We did not create these things as a vain creation, outside of a manifest wisdom, but We created them as evidence of Our power. The accusative of "*batilan*" (in vain) is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), or a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*), or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). The demonstrative in His words "*dhalika*" (that) refers to the negated thing before it, and it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾, that is, their supposition, for they suppose that these things were created without purpose, and they say that there is no Resurrection, no raising, and no reckoning. And that entails that the creation of these creatures is in vain. ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾. The *fa'* indicates the consequence of the establishment of woe for them upon their false supposition. That is: so woe to them because of the Fire that follows from their supposition and their disbelief.

Then He rebuked them and reproached them, saying: ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth?﴾ Muqatil said: the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the believers: "We will be given in the Hereafter as you are given," so this was revealed. The "*am*" is the disjunctive one implicitly equivalent to "*bal*" (rather) and the interrogative hamza, that is: Do We make those who believe in God, affirm His messengers, and act upon His obligations like the corrupters in the earth through sins?

Then He, glorified is He, made another turn (*idrab*) and moved from the first to what is more evidently impossible than it, saying: ﴿Shall We make the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ That is: rather, We make the God-fearing among the believers like the wretched among the disbelievers, the hypocrites, and those among the Muslims who are immersed in the disobedience of God, glorified is He. It was said: the "*fujjar*" (wicked) here is specific to the disbelievers. It was said: the intended "*muttaqin*" (God-fearing) are the Companions. There is no basis for specification without a specifying indicator, and the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not with the specificity of the cause.

﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed﴾. "*Kitab*" (a Book) is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, and "*anzalnahu ilayka*" (We have sent it down to you) is a description of it, and "*mubarak*" (blessed) is a second predicate of the subject. It is not permissible for it to be another adjective of "*kitab*," because it is established that a clear (*sarih*) adjective may not be placed after a non-clear one; some grammarians nevertheless permitted it. The estimate is: The Qur'an is a Book We have sent down to you, O Muhammad, abundant in good and blessing.

"*Mubarakan*" (blessed) has been read as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*). His words ﴿that they may ponder﴾: its original form is "*liyatadabbaru*," and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal*. It is connected to "*anzalnahu*" (We have sent it down).

In the verse there is evidence that God, glorified is He, sent down the Qur'an only for pondering and reflecting upon its meanings, not for mere recitation without contemplation.

The majority read "*liyaddabbaru*" with assimilation (*idgham*). Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "*litadabbaru*" with the second-person *ta'* (addressing them), and this reading is narrated from ʿAsim and al-Kisa'i, and it is the reading of ʿAli, may God be pleased with him. The original is "*litatadabbaru*" with two *ta's*, and one was omitted for lightness. ﴿And that those of understanding may be reminded﴾, that is: that those possessed of minds may take heed. "*Al-albab*" is the plural of "*lubb*," which is intellect.

﴿And We gave to Dawud Sulayman, an excellent servant; indeed, he was one who turned often (to God)﴾. He, glorified is He, informed that among the blessings upon Dawud was that He gave him Sulayman as a son. Then He praised Sulayman, saying: ﴿an excellent servant﴾. The one specified for praise is omitted, that is: an excellent servant is Sulayman. It was said: the praise here with "*ni'ma al-'abd*" is for Dawud. The first is more appropriate. The sentence ﴿indeed, he was one who turned often﴾ is a reason for the praise before it. "*Al-awwab*" is one who returns to God in repentance, as has been explained earlier.

The adverbial in His words ﴿when there were displayed before him﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, which is "*udhkur*" (remember), that is: remember what proceeded from him at the time when the swift, noble horses were displayed before him in the evening. It was said: it is connected to "*ni'ma*," but despite its being non-inflected (*ghayr mutasarrif*), there is no basis for restricting it to that time. It was said: it is connected to "*awwab*," but there is no basis for restricting his being one who turns often to that time. "*Al-ashiyy*" (the evening) is from midday or afternoon until the end of the day.

"*Al-safinat*" is the plural of "*safin*." The lexicographers differed about its meaning. Al-Qutaybi and al-Farra' said: "*al-safin*" in the speech of the Arabs is standing still, of horses or others, and Qatadah said likewise. From this is the hadith: "Whoever wishes that people stand for him in rows, let him take his seat in the Fire," that is, they continually stand for him. They cited the words of al-Nabigha:

*Ours is a tent pitched in its courtyard, with noble camels and swift horses standing still.*

There is no proof for them in this, for it is an argument based on the very point of dispute, which is a begging of the question (*musadarah*), since the dispute concerns what "*safin*" actually is. Al-Zajjaj said it is the one that stands on one of its two forelegs, raising the other and placing the tip of its hoof on the ground, so that it appears to stand on three legs, which are the two hind legs and one foreleg. It may also do this with one of its hind legs, and this is a sign of excellence. Al-Zajjaj cited the poet's verse:

*He has become accustomed to standing still, so that it seems that it stands on three legs like a lame one.*

From this is the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

*We left the horses clustered around it, their reins hung, standing still.*

For his words "*sufunan*" (standing still) must be understood as having a meaning other than mere standing, since mere standing has already been conveyed by his words "clustered around it."

Abu ʿUbayd said: "*al-safin*" is the one who gathers its two forelegs and makes them even. As for the one that stands on the tip of its hoof, its name is "*al-mutakhayyim*." "*Al-jiyad*" is the plural of "*jawad*," said of a horse when it is very swift in running.

It was said: they are long-necked, derived from "*al-jid*," which is the neck. It was said: they were one hundred horses. It was said: they were twenty thousand. It was said: they were twenty horses. It was said: they came out to him from the sea and had wings.

﴿So he said, "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord."﴾ The accusative of "*hubba al-khayr*" is the object of "*ahbabtu*" (I loved) after it has been made to imply the sense of "*athartu*" (I preferred). Al-Farra' said: he means "I preferred the love of good," and whoever loves something has preferred it.

It was said: its accusative is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) by omission of the extra elements, and the governing verb is "*ahbabtu*." It was said: it is an analogous verbal noun (*maṣdar tashbihi*), that is: a love like the love of good. The first is more appropriate.

The intended "*khayr*" here is horses. Al-Zajjaj said: "*al-khayr*" here means horses. Al-Farra' said: "*al-khayr*" and "*al-khayl*" are one in the speech of the Arabs.

Al-Nahhas said: in a hadith: "Good is tied to the forelocks of horses," so it may have been called "good" for this reason. It was said: it was called "good" because of the benefits in it.

The "*ʿan*" in ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾ means "*ʿala*" (upon). The meaning: I preferred the love of horses over the remembrance of my Lord, that is, the afternoon prayer. ﴿Until they went out of sight behind the veil﴾, that is, the sun, though it has not been previously mentioned, but the context indicates it.

Al-Zajjaj said: a pronoun is permissible only when the thing has been mentioned or there is an indication of the mention, and here the indication has occurred, which is His words "in the evening."

"*Al-tawari*" is being concealed from sight, and "*al-hijab*" is what veils them from sight.

Qatadah and Kaʿb said: the veil is a green mountain surrounding the creation, and it is the Mountain of Qaf. The night is called a veil because it conceals what is in it. It was said: the pronoun in His words "until they went out of sight" refers to the horses, that is, until they went out of sight in the race away from the eyes. The first is more appropriate.

His words ﴿"Bring them back to me"﴾ are part of Sulayman's speech, that is: restore their display to me once more. Al-Hasan said: when the displaying of the horses preoccupied Sulayman until the afternoon prayer was missed, he became angry for God's sake and said, "Bring them back to me," that is, restore them.

It was said: the pronoun in "*rudduha*" (bring them back) refers to the sun, and this would be a miracle for him. He was ordered to return it after its setting so that he could pray the afternoon prayer. The first is more appropriate. The *fa'* in His words ﴿then he began to pass his hand over their shins and necks﴾ is the explanatory *fa'* (*fa' al-fasiha*), which indicates an omitted element in the speech; the estimate here is: "So they were brought back to him."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "*tafiqa yaf'alu*" is like "*ma zala yaf'alu*" (he continued to do), and it is like "*zalla*" and "*bata*." The accusative of "*mashan*" is a verbal noun by an implied verb: that is, he wiped with wiping, since the predicate of "*tafiqa*" can only be an imperfect verb. It was said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative. The first is more appropriate.

"*Al-suq*" is the plural of "*saq*" (shin), and "*al-a'naq*" is the plural of "*unuq*" (neck). The meaning is that he began to strike their necks and shins. It is said: "*masaha ʿilawatahu*," that is, he struck his neck.

Al-Farra' said: "*al-mash*" here means cutting. He said: the meaning is that he came to strike their shins and necks, because they had been the cause of missing his prayer. Abu ʿUbayda said likewise.

Al-Zajjaj said: he did not do that except that God had permitted it to him, and it is possible that this was permitted to Sulayman and that it occurred at this time.

The commentators differed in interpreting this verse. A group said: the intended "*mash*" is what has preceded. Others, among them al-Zuhri and Qatadah, said: the intended meaning is passing the hand over their shins and necks to remove dust from them out of love for them. The first view is more appropriate to the context of the speech, for He mentioned that he postponed them because of the remembrance of his Lord until the afternoon prayer was missed, and then he ordered them to be brought back to him, in order to punish himself by destroying what had distracted him from that and what had prevented him from worshipping his Lord and had occupied him from carrying out what God had obligated upon him. It is not consistent with this that the purpose of returning them to him was to remove dust from their shins and necks by wiping them with his hand or his garment. Nor does the one who says that squandering property does not proceed from a prophet have any support, for this is merely a judgment based on what is established in our law, while it is possible that in the law of Sulayman such a thing was permitted. Moreover, the squandering of property prohibited in our law is only its wasting without a valid purpose, whereas for a valid purpose the like of it has been permitted in our law, as when the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, overturned the pots of food cooked from the spoils before distribution. There are many similar examples in the Shariah, and among them is what the Companions did in burning the food of a hoarder.

Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth?﴾, that he said: "Those who believed" are ʿAli, Hamzah, and ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, and "the corrupters in the earth" are ʿUtbah, Shaybah, and al-Walid.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: ﴿the swift, noble horses﴾ are horses created as He willed.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verse 26–33 (part 2 of 2):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿al-ṣāfināt﴾ (those standing on three legs, with the foreleg raised), that he said: "Ṣufūn (standing on three legs) of the horse is raising one of its forelegs until it rests on the tips of the hoof." And regarding His words ﴿al-jiyād﴾ (the swift, noble horses), he said: "They are the swift ones."

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿ḥubb al-khayr﴾ (love of good), that he said: "It is the water." And regarding His words ﴿Return them to me﴾, he said: "The horses." ﴿Then he began to pass his hand over them (maskan)﴾, he said: "Cutting their legs with the sword."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "The prayer which Sulayman neglected was the ʿAṣr prayer."

al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibrahim al-Taymi, regarding His words ﴿When there were displayed before him in the evening the standing, noble horses﴾, that he said: "They were twenty thousand horses, having wings, and he slaughtered them."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Masud regarding His words ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾, that he said: "They were hidden behind a green emerald, and the greenness of the sky is from it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Sulayman was not spoken to out of reverence for him, so the ʿAṣr prayer passed him by, and no one was able to speak to him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾, that he said: "From the remembrance of my Lord." ﴿Then he began to pass his hand over the shanks and necks﴾, he said: "He cut off their shanks and necks with the sword."

It is permissible for the verb to be in the jussive (*majzum*) by coordination with the prohibition, and it was vowelled only because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Al-Zajjaj said: he did not do that except that God had permitted it to him, and it is possible that this was permitted to Sulayman and that it occurred at this time.

The commentators differed in interpreting this verse. A group said: the intended "*mash*" is what has preceded. Others, among them al-Zuhri and Qatadah, said: the intended meaning is passing the hand over their shins and necks to remove dust from them out of love for them. The first view is more appropriate to the context of the speech, for He mentioned that he postponed them because of the remembrance of his Lord until the afternoon prayer was missed, and then he ordered them to be brought back to him, in order to punish himself by destroying what had distracted him from that and what had prevented him from worshipping his Lord and had occupied him from carrying out what God had obligated upon him. It is not consistent with this that the purpose of returning them to him was to remove dust from their shins and necks by wiping them with his hand or his garment. Nor does the one who says that squandering property does not proceed from a prophet have any support, for this is merely a judgment based on what is established in our law, while it is possible that in the law of Sulayman such a thing was permitted. Moreover, the squandering of property prohibited in our law is only its wasting without a valid purpose, whereas for a valid purpose the like of it has been permitted in our law, as when the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, overturned the pots of food cooked from the spoils before distribution. There are many similar examples in the Shariah, and among them is what the Companions did in burning the food of a hoarder.

Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth?﴾, that he said: "Those who believed" are ʿAli, Hamzah, and ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, and "the corrupters in the earth" are ʿUtbah, Shaybah, and al-Walid.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: ﴿the swift, noble horses﴾ are horses created as He willed.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verse 26–33 (part 2 of 2):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿al-ṣāfināt﴾ (those standing on three legs, with the foreleg raised), that he said: "Ṣufūn (standing on three legs) of the horse is raising one of its forelegs until it rests on the tips of the hoof." And regarding His words ﴿al-jiyād﴾ (the swift, noble horses), he said: "They are the swift ones."

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿ḥubb al-khayr﴾ (love of good), that he said: "It is the water." And regarding His words ﴿Return them to me﴾, he said: "The horses." ﴿Then he began to pass his hand over them (maskan)﴾, he said: "Cutting their legs with the sword."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "The prayer which Sulayman neglected was the ʿAṣr prayer."

al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibrahim al-Taymi, regarding His words ﴿When there were displayed before him in the evening the standing, noble horses﴾, that he said: "They were twenty thousand horses, having wings, and he slaughtered them."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Masud regarding His words ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾, that he said: "They were hidden behind a green emerald, and the greenness of the sky is from it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Sulayman was not spoken to out of reverence for him, so the ʿAṣr prayer passed him by, and no one was able to speak to him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾, that he said: "From the remembrance of my Lord." ﴿Then he began to pass his hand over the shanks and necks﴾, he said: "He cut off their shanks and necks with the sword."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verses 26–33 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glorified is He, completed the story of Dawud (ﷺ)... [sic: Dawud (عليه السلام)], He followed it with an explanation of the delegation of the affair of the caliphate over the earth to him. The sentence is a *maqulah* (a direct speech) for an implied *qawl* (saying), coordinated with "*ghafarna*" (We forgave). That is: and We said to him, ﴿O Dawud, indeed We﴾ have appointed you over the earth, or ﴿have made you a successor﴾ to those prophets who came before you, so that you may enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. ﴿So judge between the people with truth﴾, that is, with justice, which is the judgment of God among His servants. ﴿And do not follow desire﴾, that is, the desire of the self in judging between the servants.

In this there is a warning to Dawud, upon him be peace, that what he was rebuked for was not just, and that there was in it a trace of following the desire of the self. ﴿Lest it lead you astray from the path of God﴾. It is in the accusative (*nasb*) on the basis that it is a response (*jawab*) to the prohibition (*nahy*), and the subject of "*yudillaka*" (lead you astray) is "*al-hawa*" (desire). It is permissible for the verb to be in the jussive (*majzum*) by coordination with the prohibition, and it was vowelled only because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. On the first reading, what is prohibited is the combination of the two (following desire and going astray), and on the second reading, the prohibition is against each of them separately.

"*Sabil Allah*" (the path of God) is the path of truth, or the path of Paradise. The sentence ﴿Indeed, those who go astray from the path of God have a severe punishment﴾ is a reason for the prohibition against following desire and falling into error. The *ba'* in ﴿for what they forgot of the Day of Reckoning﴾ denotes causation. The meaning of "*al-nisyan*" (forgetting) is abandonment. That is: because of their abandonment of action for that Day. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, by their abandonment of action for that Day, they became like those who forget, even though they are warned and reminded.

ʿIkrimah and al-Suddi said: in the verse there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*), and the implied meaning is: "And for them is the punishment of the Day of Reckoning, because they forgot," that is, they abandoned judging with justice. The first is more appropriate.

The sentence ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ is a new (*mustanafah*) sentence confirming what precedes it concerning the matter of resurrection and reckoning. That is: We did not create these things as a vain creation, outside of a manifest wisdom, but We created them as evidence of Our power. The accusative of "*batilan*" (in vain) is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), or a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*), or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). The demonstrative in His words "*dhalika*" (that) refers to the negated thing before it, and it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾, that is, their supposition, for they suppose that these things were created without purpose, and they say that there is no Resurrection, no raising, and no reckoning. And that entails that the creation of these creatures is in vain. ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾. The *fa'* indicates the consequence of the establishment of woe for them upon their false supposition. That is: so woe to them because of the Fire that follows from their supposition and their disbelief.

Then He rebuked them and reproached them, saying: ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth?﴾ Muqatil said: the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the believers: "We will be given in the Hereafter as you are given," so this was revealed. The "*am*" is the disjunctive one implicitly equivalent to "*bal*" (rather) and the interrogative hamza, that is: Do We make those who believe in God, affirm His messengers, and act upon His obligations like the corrupters in the earth through sins?

Then He, glorified is He, made another turn (*idrab*) and moved from the first to what is more evidently impossible than it, saying: ﴿Shall We make the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ That is: rather, We make the God-fearing among the believers like the wretched among the disbelievers, the hypocrites, and those among the Muslims who are immersed in the disobedience of God, glorified is He. It was said: the "*fujjar*" (wicked) here is specific to the disbelievers. It was said: the intended "*muttaqin*" (God-fearing) are the Companions. There is no basis for specification without a specifying indicator, and the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not with the specificity of the cause.

﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed﴾. "*Kitab*" (a Book) is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, and "*anzalnahu ilayka*" (We have sent it down to you) is a description of it, and "*mubarak*" (blessed) is a second predicate of the subject. It is not permissible for it to be another adjective of "*kitab*," because it is established that a clear (*sarih*) adjective may not be placed after a non-clear one; some grammarians nevertheless permitted it. The estimate is: The Qur'an is a Book We have sent down to you, O Muhammad, abundant in good and blessing.

"*Mubarakan*" (blessed) has been read as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*). His words ﴿that they may ponder﴾: its original form is "*liyatadabbaru*," and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal*. It is connected to "*anzalnahu*" (We have sent it down).

In the verse there is evidence that God, glorified is He, sent down the Qur'an only for pondering and reflecting upon its meanings, not for mere recitation without contemplation.

The majority read "*liyaddabbaru*" with assimilation (*idgham*). Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "*litadabbaru*" with the second-person *ta'* (addressing them), and this reading is narrated from ʿAsim and al-Kisa'i, and it is the reading of ʿAli, may God be pleased with him. The original is "*litatadabbaru*" with two *ta's*, and one was omitted for lightness. ﴿And that those of understanding may be reminded﴾, that is: that those possessed of minds may take heed. "*Al-albab*" is the plural of "*lubb*," which is intellect.

﴿And We gave to Dawud Sulayman, an excellent servant; indeed, he was one who turned often (to God)﴾. He, glorified is He, informed that among the blessings upon Dawud was that He gave him Sulayman as a son. Then He praised Sulayman, saying: ﴿an excellent servant﴾. The one specified for praise is omitted, that is: an excellent servant is Sulayman. It was said: the praise here with "*ni'ma al-'abd*" is for Dawud. The first is more appropriate. The sentence ﴿indeed, he was one who turned often﴾ is a reason for the praise before it. "*Al-awwab*" is one who returns to God in repentance, as has been explained earlier.

The adverbial in His words ﴿when there were displayed before him﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, which is "*udhkur*" (remember), that is: remember what proceeded from him at the time when the swift, noble horses were displayed before him in the evening. It was said: it is connected to "*ni'ma*," but despite its being non-inflected (*ghayr mutasarrif*), there is no basis for restricting it to that time. It was said: it is connected to "*awwab*," but there is no basis for restricting his being one who turns often to that time. "*Al-ashiyy*" (the evening) is from midday or afternoon until the end of the day.

"*Al-safinat*" is the plural of "*safin*." The lexicographers differed about its meaning. Al-Qutaybi and al-Farra' said: "*al-safin*" in the speech of the Arabs is standing still, of horses or others, and Qatadah said likewise. From this is the hadith: "Whoever wishes that people stand for him in rows, let him take his seat in the Fire," that is, they continually stand for him. They cited the words of al-Nabigha:

*Ours is a tent pitched in its courtyard, with noble camels and swift horses standing still.*

There is no proof for them in this, for it is an argument based on the very point of dispute, which is a begging of the question (*musadarah*), since the dispute concerns what "*safin*" actually is. Al-Zajjaj said it is the one that stands on one of its two forelegs, raising the other and placing the tip of its hoof on the ground, so that it appears to stand on three legs, which are the two hind legs and one foreleg. It may also do this with one of its hind legs, and this is a sign of excellence. Al-Zajjaj cited the poet's verse:

*He has become accustomed to standing still, so that it seems that it stands on three legs like a lame one.*

From this is the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

*We left the horses clustered around it, their reins hung, standing still.*

For his words "*sufunan*" (standing still) must be understood as having a meaning other than mere standing, since mere standing has already been conveyed by his words "clustered around it."

Abu ʿUbayd said: "*al-safin*" is the one who gathers its two forelegs and makes them even. As for the one that stands on the tip of its hoof, its name is "*al-mutakhayyim*." "*Al-jiyad*" is the plural of "*jawad*," said of a horse when it is very swift in running.

It was said: they are long-necked, derived from "*al-jid*," which is the neck. It was said: they were one hundred horses. It was said: they were twenty thousand. It was said: they were twenty horses. It was said: they came out to him from the sea and had wings.

﴿So he said, "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord."﴾ The accusative of "*hubba al-khayr*" is the object of "*ahbabtu*" (I loved) after it has been made to imply the sense of "*athartu*" (I preferred). Al-Farra' said: he means "I preferred the love of good," and whoever loves something has preferred it.

It was said: its accusative is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) by omission of the extra elements, and the governing verb is "*ahbabtu*." It was said: it is an analogous verbal noun (*maṣdar tashbihi*), that is: a love like the love of good. The first is more appropriate.

The intended "*khayr*" here is horses. Al-Zajjaj said: "*al-khayr*" here means horses. Al-Farra' said: "*al-khayr*" and "*al-khayl*" are one in the speech of the Arabs.

Al-Nahhas said: in a hadith: "Good is tied to the forelocks of horses," so it may have been called "good" for this reason. It was said: it was called "good" because of the benefits in it.

The "*ʿan*" in ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾ means "*ʿala*" (upon). The meaning: I preferred the love of horses over the remembrance of my Lord, that is, the afternoon prayer. ﴿Until they went out of sight behind the veil﴾, that is, the sun, though it has not been previously mentioned, but the context indicates it.

Al-Zajjaj said: a pronoun is permissible only when the thing has been mentioned or there is an indication of the mention, and here the indication has occurred, which is His words "in the evening."

"*Al-tawari*" is being concealed from sight, and "*al-hijab*" is what veils them from sight.

Qatadah and Kaʿb said: the veil is a green mountain surrounding the creation, and it is the Mountain of Qaf. The night is called a veil because it conceals what is in it. It was said: the pronoun in His words "until they went out of sight" refers to the horses, that is, until they went out of sight in the race away from the eyes. The first is more appropriate.

His words ﴿"Bring them back to me"﴾ are part of Sulayman's speech, that is: restore their display to me once more. Al-Hasan said: when the displaying of the horses preoccupied Sulayman until the afternoon prayer was missed, he became angry for God's sake and said, "Bring them back to me," that is, restore them.

It was said: the pronoun in "*rudduha*" (bring them back) refers to the sun, and this would be a miracle for him. He was ordered to return it after its setting so that he could pray the afternoon prayer. The first is more appropriate. The *fa'* in His words ﴿then he began to pass his hand over their shins and necks﴾ is the explanatory *fa'* (*fa' al-fasiha*), which indicates an omitted element in the speech; the estimate here is: "So they were brought back to him."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "*tafiqa yaf'alu*" is like "*ma zala yaf'alu*" (he continued to do), and it is like "*zalla*" and "*bata*." The accusative of "*mashan*" is a verbal noun by an implied verb: that is, he wiped with wiping, since the predicate of "*tafiqa*" can only be an imperfect verb. It was said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative. The first is more appropriate.

"*Al-suq*" is the plural of "*saq*" (shin), and "*al-a'naq*" is the plural of "*unuq*" (neck). The meaning is that he began to strike their necks and shins. It is said: "*masaha ʿilawatahu*," that is, he struck his neck.

Al-Farra' said: "*al-mash*" here means cutting. He said: the meaning is that he came to strike their shins and necks, because they had been the cause of missing his prayer. Abu ʿUbayda said likewise.

Al-Zajjaj said: he did not do that except that God had permitted it to him, and it is possible that this was permitted to Sulayman and that it occurred at this time.

The commentators differed in interpreting this verse. A group said: the intended "*mash*" is what has preceded. Others, among them al-Zuhri and Qatadah, said: the intended meaning is passing the hand over their shins and necks to remove dust from them out of love for them. The adverbial in His words ﴿when there were displayed before him﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, which is "*udhkur*" (remember), that is: remember what proceeded from him at the time when the swift, noble horses were displayed before him in the evening. It was said: it is connected to "*ni'ma*," but despite its being non-inflected (*ghayr mutasarrif*), there is no basis for restricting it to that time. It was said: it is connected to "*awwab*," but there is no basis for restricting his being one who turns often to that time. "*Al-ashiyy*" (the evening) is from midday or afternoon until the end of the day.

"*Al-safinat*" is the plural of "*safin*." The lexicographers differed about its meaning. Al-Qutaybi and al-Farra' said: "*al-safin*" in the speech of the Arabs is standing still, of horses or others, and Qatadah said likewise. From this is the hadith: "Whoever wishes that people stand for him in rows, let him take his seat in the Fire," that is, they continually stand for him. They cited the words of al-Nabigha:

*Ours is a tent pitched in its courtyard, with noble camels and swift horses standing still.*

There is no proof for them in this, for it is an argument based on the very point of dispute, which is a begging of the question (*musadarah*), since the dispute concerns what "*safin*" actually is. Al-Zajjaj said it is the one that stands on one of its two forelegs, raising the other and placing the tip of its hoof on the ground, so that it appears to stand on three legs, which are the two hind legs and one foreleg. It may also do this with one of its hind legs, and this is a sign of excellence. Al-Zajjaj cited the poet's verse:

*He has become accustomed to standing still, so that it seems that it stands on three legs like a lame one.*

From this is the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

*We left the horses clustered around it, their reins hung, standing still.*

For his words "*sufunan*" (standing still) must be understood as having a meaning other than mere standing, since mere standing has already been conveyed by his words "clustered around it."

Abu ʿUbayd said: "*al-safin*" is the one who gathers its two forelegs and makes them even. As for the one that stands on the tip of its hoof, its name is "*al-mutakhayyim*." "*Al-jiyad*" is the plural of "*jawad*," said of a horse when it is very swift in running.

It was said: they are long-necked, derived from "*al-jid*," which is the neck. It was said: they were one hundred horses. It was said: they were twenty thousand. It was said: they were twenty horses. It was said: they came out to him from the sea and had wings.

﴿So he said, "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord."﴾ The accusative of "*hubba al-khayr*" is the object of "*ahbabtu*" (I loved) after it has been made to imply the sense of "*athartu*" (I preferred). Al-Farra' said: he means "I preferred the love of good," and whoever loves something has preferred it.

It was said: its accusative is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) by omission of the extra elements, and the governing verb is "*ahbabtu*." It was said: it is an analogous verbal noun (*maṣdar tashbihi*), that is: a love like the love of good. The first is more appropriate.

The intended "*khayr*" here is horses. Al-Zajjaj said: "*al-khayr*" here means horses. Al-Farra' said: "*al-khayr*" and "*al-khayl*" are one in the speech of the Arabs.

Al-Nahhas said: in a hadith: "Good is tied to the forelocks of horses," so it may have been called "good" for this reason. It was said: it was called "good" because of the benefits in it.

The "*ʿan*" in ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾ means "*ʿala*" (upon). The meaning: I preferred the love of horses over the remembrance of my Lord, that is, the afternoon prayer. ﴿Until they went out of sight behind the veil﴾, that is, the sun, though it has not been previously mentioned, but the context indicates it.

Al-Zajjaj said: a pronoun is permissible only when the thing has been mentioned or there is an indication of the mention, and here the indication has occurred, which is His words "in the evening."

"*Al-tawari*" is being concealed from sight, and "*al-hijab*" is what veils them from sight.

Qatadah and Kaʿb said: the veil is a green mountain surrounding the creation, and it is the Mountain of Qaf. The night is called a veil because it conceals what is in it. It was said: the pronoun in His words "until they went out of sight" refers to the horses, that is, until they went out of sight in the race away from the eyes. The first is more appropriate.

His words ﴿"Bring them back to me"﴾ are part of Sulayman's speech, that is: restore their display to me once more. Al-Hasan said: when the displaying of the horses preoccupied Sulayman until the afternoon prayer was missed, he became angry for God's sake and said, "Bring them back to me," that is, restore them.

It was said: the pronoun in "*rudduha*" (bring them back) refers to the sun, and this would be a miracle for him. He was ordered to return it after its setting so that he could pray the afternoon prayer. The first is more appropriate. The *fa'* in His words ﴿then he began to pass his hand over their shins and necks﴾ is the explanatory *fa'* (*fa' al-fasiha*), which indicates an omitted element in the speech; the estimate here is: "So they were brought back to him."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "*tafiqa yaf'alu*" is like "*ma zala yaf'alu*" (he continued to do), and it is like "*zalla*" and "*bata*." The accusative of "*mashan*" is a verbal noun by an implied verb: that is, he wiped with wiping, since the predicate of "*tafiqa*" can only be an imperfect verb. It was said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative. The first is more appropriate.

"*Al-suq*" is the plural of "*saq*" (shin), and "*al-a'naq*" is the plural of "*unuq*" (neck). The meaning is that he began to strike their necks and shins. It is said: "*masaha ʿilawatahu*," that is, he struck his neck.

Al-Farra' said: "*al-mash*" here means cutting. He said: the meaning is that he came to strike their shins and necks, because they had been the cause of missing his prayer. Abu ʿUbayda said likewise.

Al-Zajjaj said: he did not do that except that God had permitted it to him, and it is possible that this was permitted to Sulayman and that it occurred at this time.

The commentators differed in interpreting this verse. A group said: the intended "*mash*" is what has preceded. Others, among them al-Zuhri and Qatadah, said: the intended meaning is passing the hand over their shins and necks to remove dust from them out of love for them. The first view is more appropriate to the context of the speech, for He mentioned that he postponed them because of the remembrance of his Lord until the afternoon prayer was missed, and then he ordered them to be brought back to him, in order to punish himself by destroying what had distracted him from that and what had prevented him from worshipping his Lord and had occupied him from carrying out what God had obligated upon him. It is not consistent with this that the purpose of returning them to him was to remove dust from their shins and necks by wiping them with his hand or his garment. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: ﴿the swift, noble horses﴾ are horses created as He willed.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verse 26–33 (part 2 of 2):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿al-ṣāfināt﴾ (those standing on three legs, with the foreleg raised), that he said: "Ṣufūn (standing on three legs) of the horse is raising one of its forelegs until it rests on the tips of the hoof." And regarding His words ﴿al-jiyād﴾ (the swift, noble horses), he said: "They are the swift ones."

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿ḥubb al-khayr﴾ (love of good), that he said: "It is the water." And regarding His words ﴿Return them to me﴾, he said: "The horses." ﴿Then he began to pass his hand over them (maskan)﴾, he said: "Cutting their legs with the sword."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "The prayer which Sulayman neglected was the ʿAṣr prayer."

al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibrahim al-Taymi, regarding His words ﴿When there were displayed before him in the evening the standing, noble horses﴾, that he said: "They were twenty thousand horses, having wings, and he slaughtered them."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Masud regarding His words ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾, that he said: "They were hidden behind a green emerald, and the greenness of the sky is from it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Sulayman was not spoken to out of reverence for him, so the ʿAṣr prayer passed him by, and no one was able to speak to him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾, that he said: "From the remembrance of my Lord." ﴿Then he began to pass his hand over the shanks and necks﴾, he said: "He cut off their shanks and necks with the sword."

The sentence is a *maqulah* (a direct speech) for an implied *qawl* (saying), coordinated with "*ghafarna*" (We forgave). That is: and We said to him, ﴿O Dawud, indeed We﴾ have appointed you over the earth, or ﴿have made you a successor﴾ to those prophets who came before you, so that you may enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. ﴿So judge between the people with truth﴾, that is, with justice, which is the judgment of God among His servants. ﴿And do not follow desire﴾, that is, the desire of the self in judging between the servants.

In this there is a warning to Dawud, upon him be peace, that what he was rebuked for was not just, and that there was in it a trace of following the desire of the self. ﴿Lest it lead you astray from the path of God﴾. It is in the accusative (*nasb*) on the basis that it is a response (*jawab*) to the prohibition (*nahy*), and the subject of "*yudillaka*" (lead you astray) is "*al-hawa*" (desire). It is permissible for the verb to be in the jussive (*majzum*) by coordination with the prohibition, and it was vowelled only because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. On the first reading, what is prohibited is the combination of the two (following desire and going astray), and on the second reading, the prohibition is against each of them separately.

"*Sabil Allah*" (the path of God) is the path of truth, or the path of Paradise. The sentence ﴿Indeed, those who go astray from the path of God have a severe punishment﴾ is a reason for the prohibition against following desire and falling into error. The *ba'* in ﴿for what they forgot of the Day of Reckoning﴾ denotes causation. The meaning of "*al-nisyan*" (forgetting) is abandonment. That is: because of their abandonment of action for that Day. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, by their abandonment of action for that Day, they became like those who forget, even though they are warned and reminded.

ʿIkrimah and al-Suddi said: in the verse there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*), and the implied meaning is: "And for them is the punishment of the Day of Reckoning, because they forgot," that is, they abandoned judging with justice. The first is more appropriate.

The sentence ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ is a new (*mustanafah*) sentence confirming what precedes it concerning the matter of resurrection and reckoning. That is: We did not create these things as a vain creation, outside of a manifest wisdom, but We created them as evidence of Our power. The accusative of "*batilan*" (in vain) is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), or a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*), or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). The demonstrative in His words "*dhalika*" (that) refers to the negated thing before it, and it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾, that is, their supposition, for they suppose that these things were created without purpose, and they say that there is no Resurrection, no raising, and no reckoning. And that entails that the creation of these creatures is in vain. ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾. The *fa'* indicates the consequence of the establishment of woe for them upon their false supposition. That is: so woe to them because of the Fire that follows from their supposition and their disbelief.

Then He rebuked them and reproached them, saying: ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth?﴾ Muqatil said: the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the believers: "We will be given in the Hereafter as you are given," so this was revealed. The "*am*" is the disjunctive one implicitly equivalent to "*bal*" (rather) and the interrogative hamza, that is: Do We make those who believe in God, affirm His messengers, and act upon His obligations like the corrupters in the earth through sins?

Then He, glorified is He, made another turn (*idrab*) and moved from the first to what is more evidently impossible than it, saying: ﴿Shall We make the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ That is: rather, We make the God-fearing among the believers like the wretched among the disbelievers, the hypocrites, and those among the Muslims who are immersed in the disobedience of God, glorified is He. It was said: the "*fujjar*" (wicked) here is specific to the disbelievers. It was said: the intended "*muttaqin*" (God-fearing) are the Companions. There is no basis for specification without a specifying indicator, and the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not with the specificity of the cause.

﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed﴾. "*Kitab*" (a Book) is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, and "*anzalnahu ilayka*" (We have sent it down to you) is a description of it, and "*mubarak*" (blessed) is a second predicate of the subject. It is not permissible for it to be another adjective of "*kitab*," because it is established that a clear (*sarih*) adjective may not be placed after a non-clear one; some grammarians nevertheless permitted it. The estimate is: The Qur'an is a Book We have sent down to you, O Muhammad, abundant in good and blessing.

"*Mubarakan*" (blessed) has been read as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*). His words ﴿that they may ponder﴾: its original form is "*liyatadabbaru*," and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal*. It is connected to "*anzalnahu*" (We have sent it down).

In the verse there is evidence that God, glorified is He, sent down the Qur'an only for pondering and reflecting upon its meanings, not for mere recitation without contemplation.

The majority read "*liyaddabbaru*" with assimilation (*idgham*). Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "*litadabbaru*" with the second-person *ta'* (addressing them), and this reading is narrated from ʿAsim and al-Kisa'i, and it is the reading of ʿAli, may God be pleased with him. The original is "*litatadabbaru*" with two *ta's*, and one was omitted for lightness. ﴿And that those of understanding may be reminded﴾, that is: that those possessed of minds may take heed. "*Al-albab*" is the plural of "*lubb*," which is intellect.

﴿And We gave to Dawud Sulayman, an excellent servant; indeed, he was one who turned often (to God)﴾. He, glorified is He, informed that among the blessings upon Dawud was that He gave him Sulayman as a son. Then He praised Sulayman, saying: ﴿an excellent servant﴾. The one specified for praise is omitted, that is: an excellent servant is Sulayman. It was said: the praise here with "*ni'ma al-'abd*" is for Dawud. The first is more appropriate.
