The sentence is a *maqulah* (a direct speech) for an implied *qawl* (saying), coordinated with "*ghafarna*" (We forgave). That is: and We said to him, ﴿O Dawud, indeed We﴾ have appointed you over the earth, or ﴿have made you a successor﴾ to those prophets who came before you, so that you may enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. ﴿So judge between the people with truth﴾, that is, with justice, which is the judgment of God among His servants. ﴿And do not follow desire﴾, that is, the desire of the self in judging between the servants.

In this there is a warning to Dawud, upon him be peace, that what he was rebuked for was not just, and that there was in it a trace of following the desire of the self. ﴿Lest it lead you astray from the path of God﴾. It is in the accusative (*nasb*) on the basis that it is a response (*jawab*) to the prohibition (*nahy*), and the subject of "*yudillaka*" (lead you astray) is "*al-hawa*" (desire). It is permissible for the verb to be in the jussive (*majzum*) by coordination with the prohibition, and it was vowelled only because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. On the first reading, what is prohibited is the combination of the two (following desire and going astray), and on the second reading, the prohibition is against each of them separately.

"*Sabil Allah*" (the path of God) is the path of truth, or the path of Paradise. The sentence ﴿Indeed, those who go astray from the path of God have a severe punishment﴾ is a reason for the prohibition against following desire and falling into error. The *ba'* in ﴿for what they forgot of the Day of Reckoning﴾ denotes causation. The meaning of "*al-nisyan*" (forgetting) is abandonment. That is: because of their abandonment of action for that Day. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, by their abandonment of action for that Day, they became like those who forget, even though they are warned and reminded.

ʿIkrimah and al-Suddi said: in the verse there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*), and the implied meaning is: "And for them is the punishment of the Day of Reckoning, because they forgot," that is, they abandoned judging with justice. The first is more appropriate.

The sentence ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ is a new (*mustanafah*) sentence confirming what precedes it concerning the matter of resurrection and reckoning. That is: We did not create these things as a vain creation, outside of a manifest wisdom, but We created them as evidence of Our power. The accusative of "*batilan*" (in vain) is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), or a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*), or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). The demonstrative in His words "*dhalika*" (that) refers to the negated thing before it, and it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾, that is, their supposition, for they suppose that these things were created without purpose, and they say that there is no Resurrection, no raising, and no reckoning. And that entails that the creation of these creatures is in vain. ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾. The *fa'* indicates the consequence of the establishment of woe for them upon their false supposition. That is: so woe to them because of the Fire that follows from their supposition and their disbelief.

Then He rebuked them and reproached them, saying: ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth?﴾ Muqatil said: the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the believers: "We will be given in the Hereafter as you are given," so this was revealed. The "*am*" is the disjunctive one implicitly equivalent to "*bal*" (rather) and the interrogative hamza, that is: Do We make those who believe in God, affirm His messengers, and act upon His obligations like the corrupters in the earth through sins?

Then He, glorified is He, made another turn (*idrab*) and moved from the first to what is more evidently impossible than it, saying: ﴿Shall We make the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ That is: rather, We make the God-fearing among the believers like the wretched among the disbelievers, the hypocrites, and those among the Muslims who are immersed in the disobedience of God, glorified is He. It was said: the "*fujjar*" (wicked) here is specific to the disbelievers. It was said: the intended "*muttaqin*" (God-fearing) are the Companions. There is no basis for specification without a specifying indicator, and the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not with the specificity of the cause.

﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed﴾. "*Kitab*" (a Book) is raised as the predicate of an omitted subject, and "*anzalnahu ilayka*" (We have sent it down to you) is a description of it, and "*mubarak*" (blessed) is a second predicate of the subject. It is not permissible for it to be another adjective of "*kitab*," because it is established that a clear (*sarih*) adjective may not be placed after a non-clear one; some grammarians nevertheless permitted it. The estimate is: The Qur'an is a Book We have sent down to you, O Muhammad, abundant in good and blessing.

"*Mubarakan*" (blessed) has been read as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥal*). His words ﴿that they may ponder﴾: its original form is "*liyatadabbaru*," and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal*. It is connected to "*anzalnahu*" (We have sent it down).

In the verse there is evidence that God, glorified is He, sent down the Qur'an only for pondering and reflecting upon its meanings, not for mere recitation without contemplation.

The majority read "*liyaddabbaru*" with assimilation (*idgham*). Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "*litadabbaru*" with the second-person *ta'* (addressing them), and this reading is narrated from ʿAsim and al-Kisa'i, and it is the reading of ʿAli, may God be pleased with him. The original is "*litatadabbaru*" with two *ta's*, and one was omitted for lightness. ﴿And that those of understanding may be reminded﴾, that is: that those possessed of minds may take heed. "*Al-albab*" is the plural of "*lubb*," which is intellect.

﴿And We gave to Dawud Sulayman, an excellent servant; indeed, he was one who turned often (to God)﴾. He, glorified is He, informed that among the blessings upon Dawud was that He gave him Sulayman as a son. Then He praised Sulayman, saying: ﴿an excellent servant﴾. The one specified for praise is omitted, that is: an excellent servant is Sulayman. It was said: the praise here with "*ni'ma al-'abd*" is for Dawud. The first is more appropriate. The sentence ﴿indeed, he was one who turned often﴾ is a reason for the praise before it. "*Al-awwab*" is one who returns to God in repentance, as has been explained earlier.

The adverbial in His words ﴿when there were displayed before him﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, which is "*udhkur*" (remember), that is: remember what proceeded from him at the time when the swift, noble horses were displayed before him in the evening. It was said: it is connected to "*ni'ma*," but despite its being non-inflected (*ghayr mutasarrif*), there is no basis for restricting it to that time. It was said: it is connected to "*awwab*," but there is no basis for restricting his being one who turns often to that time. "*Al-ashiyy*" (the evening) is from midday or afternoon until the end of the day.

"*Al-safinat*" is the plural of "*safin*." The lexicographers differed about its meaning. Al-Qutaybi and al-Farra' said: "*al-safin*" in the speech of the Arabs is standing still, of horses or others, and Qatadah said likewise. From this is the hadith: "Whoever wishes that people stand for him in rows, let him take his seat in the Fire," that is, they continually stand for him. They cited the words of al-Nabigha:

*Ours is a tent pitched in its courtyard, with noble camels and swift horses standing still.*

There is no proof for them in this, for it is an argument based on the very point of dispute, which is a begging of the question (*musadarah*), since the dispute concerns what "*safin*" actually is. Al-Zajjaj said it is the one that stands on one of its two forelegs, raising the other and placing the tip of its hoof on the ground, so that it appears to stand on three legs, which are the two hind legs and one foreleg. It may also do this with one of its hind legs, and this is a sign of excellence. Al-Zajjaj cited the poet's verse:

*He has become accustomed to standing still, so that it seems that it stands on three legs like a lame one.*

From this is the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

*We left the horses clustered around it, their reins hung, standing still.*

For his words "*sufunan*" (standing still) must be understood as having a meaning other than mere standing, since mere standing has already been conveyed by his words "clustered around it."

Abu ʿUbayd said: "*al-safin*" is the one who gathers its two forelegs and makes them even. As for the one that stands on the tip of its hoof, its name is "*al-mutakhayyim*." "*Al-jiyad*" is the plural of "*jawad*," said of a horse when it is very swift in running.

It was said: they are long-necked, derived from "*al-jid*," which is the neck. It was said: they were one hundred horses. It was said: they were twenty thousand. It was said: they were twenty horses. It was said: they came out to him from the sea and had wings.

﴿So he said, "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord."﴾ The accusative of "*hubba al-khayr*" is the object of "*ahbabtu*" (I loved) after it has been made to imply the sense of "*athartu*" (I preferred). Al-Farra' said: he means "I preferred the love of good," and whoever loves something has preferred it.

It was said: its accusative is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) by omission of the extra elements, and the governing verb is "*ahbabtu*." It was said: it is an analogous verbal noun (*maṣdar tashbihi*), that is: a love like the love of good. The first is more appropriate.

The intended "*khayr*" here is horses. Al-Zajjaj said: "*al-khayr*" here means horses. Al-Farra' said: "*al-khayr*" and "*al-khayl*" are one in the speech of the Arabs.

Al-Nahhas said: in a hadith: "Good is tied to the forelocks of horses," so it may have been called "good" for this reason. It was said: it was called "good" because of the benefits in it.

The "*ʿan*" in ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾ means "*ʿala*" (upon). The meaning: I preferred the love of horses over the remembrance of my Lord, that is, the afternoon prayer. ﴿Until they went out of sight behind the veil﴾, that is, the sun, though it has not been previously mentioned, but the context indicates it.

Al-Zajjaj said: a pronoun is permissible only when the thing has been mentioned or there is an indication of the mention, and here the indication has occurred, which is His words "in the evening."

"*Al-tawari*" is being concealed from sight, and "*al-hijab*" is what veils them from sight.

Qatadah and Kaʿb said: the veil is a green mountain surrounding the creation, and it is the Mountain of Qaf. The night is called a veil because it conceals what is in it. It was said: the pronoun in His words "until they went out of sight" refers to the horses, that is, until they went out of sight in the race away from the eyes. The first is more appropriate.

His words ﴿"Bring them back to me"﴾ are part of Sulayman's speech, that is: restore their display to me once more. Al-Hasan said: when the displaying of the horses preoccupied Sulayman until the afternoon prayer was missed, he became angry for God's sake and said, "Bring them back to me," that is, restore them.

It was said: the pronoun in "*rudduha*" (bring them back) refers to the sun, and this would be a miracle for him. He was ordered to return it after its setting so that he could pray the afternoon prayer. The first is more appropriate. The *fa'* in His words ﴿then he began to pass his hand over their shins and necks﴾ is the explanatory *fa'* (*fa' al-fasiha*), which indicates an omitted element in the speech; the estimate here is: "So they were brought back to him."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "*tafiqa yaf'alu*" is like "*ma zala yaf'alu*" (he continued to do), and it is like "*zalla*" and "*bata*." The accusative of "*mashan*" is a verbal noun by an implied verb: that is, he wiped with wiping, since the predicate of "*tafiqa*" can only be an imperfect verb. It was said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative. The first is more appropriate.

"*Al-suq*" is the plural of "*saq*" (shin), and "*al-a'naq*" is the plural of "*unuq*" (neck). The meaning is that he began to strike their necks and shins. It is said: "*masaha ʿilawatahu*," that is, he struck his neck.

Al-Farra' said: "*al-mash*" here means cutting. He said: the meaning is that he came to strike their shins and necks, because they had been the cause of missing his prayer. Abu ʿUbayda said likewise.

Al-Zajjaj said: he did not do that except that God had permitted it to him, and it is possible that this was permitted to Sulayman and that it occurred at this time.

The commentators differed in interpreting this verse. A group said: the intended "*mash*" is what has preceded. Others, among them al-Zuhri and Qatadah, said: the intended meaning is passing the hand over their shins and necks to remove dust from them out of love for them. The first view is more appropriate to the context of the speech, for He mentioned that he postponed them because of the remembrance of his Lord until the afternoon prayer was missed, and then he ordered them to be brought back to him, in order to punish himself by destroying what had distracted him from that and what had prevented him from worshipping his Lord and had occupied him from carrying out what God had obligated upon him. It is not consistent with this that the purpose of returning them to him was to remove dust from their shins and necks by wiping them with his hand or his garment. Nor does the one who says that squandering property does not proceed from a prophet have any support, for this is merely a judgment based on what is established in our law, while it is possible that in the law of Sulayman such a thing was permitted. Moreover, the squandering of property prohibited in our law is only its wasting without a valid purpose, whereas for a valid purpose the like of it has been permitted in our law, as when the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, overturned the pots of food cooked from the spoils before distribution. There are many similar examples in the Shariah, and among them is what the Companions did in burning the food of a hoarder.

Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth?﴾, that he said: "Those who believed" are ʿAli, Hamzah, and ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, and "the corrupters in the earth" are ʿUtbah, Shaybah, and al-Walid.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: ﴿the swift, noble horses﴾ are horses created as He willed.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verse 26–33 (part 2 of 2):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿al-ṣāfināt﴾ (those standing on three legs, with the foreleg raised), that he said: "Ṣufūn (standing on three legs) of the horse is raising one of its forelegs until it rests on the tips of the hoof." And regarding His words ﴿al-jiyād﴾ (the swift, noble horses), he said: "They are the swift ones."

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿ḥubb al-khayr﴾ (love of good), that he said: "It is the water." And regarding His words ﴿Return them to me﴾, he said: "The horses." ﴿Then he began to pass his hand over them (maskan)﴾, he said: "Cutting their legs with the sword."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "The prayer which Sulayman neglected was the ʿAṣr prayer."

al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibrahim al-Taymi, regarding His words ﴿When there were displayed before him in the evening the standing, noble horses﴾, that he said: "They were twenty thousand horses, having wings, and he slaughtered them."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Masud regarding His words ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾, that he said: "They were hidden behind a green emerald, and the greenness of the sky is from it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Sulayman was not spoken to out of reverence for him, so the ʿAṣr prayer passed him by, and no one was able to speak to him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾, that he said: "From the remembrance of my Lord." ﴿Then he began to pass his hand over the shanks and necks﴾, he said: "He cut off their shanks and necks with the sword."

God says: ﴿And We had certainly tested Solomon﴾, meaning: We tried him and put him to the test.

Al-Wahidi said: Most of the exegetes said: Solomon married a woman from the daughters of kings, and she worshipped an idol in his house, and Solomon did not know of this. He was tested because of his unawareness of it.

It was also said: The cause of the trial was that Solomon married a woman called Jaradah, whom he loved intensely. Two parties came to him for judgment, one of them from the people of Jaradah, and he wished that the judgment would go in their favour. Then he judged between them with the truth.

It was also said: The cause was that he secluded himself from the people for three days and did not judge between anyone.

It was also said: He married this Jaradah while she was a polytheist, because he offered her Islam and she said: "Kill me, and I will not become a Muslim."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: When he wronged the horses by killing them, his kingdom was taken from him. Al-Hasan said: He approached some of his wives during menstruation or something else. It was also said: He was commanded not to marry any woman except from the Children of Israel, but he married a woman from outside them.

It was also said: The cause of his trial is what is established in the sound hadith that he said: "Tonight I will go round ninety women, and each one will bear a horseman who will fight in the cause of Allah," and he did not say: "If Allah wills." It has also been said other than this.

Then He, glorified be He, explained what He punished him with, saying: ﴿And We cast upon his throne a body﴾. The accusative of (jasadan, "a body") is that it is the object of (alqayna, "We cast"). It was also said that it is in the accusative of circumstance, interpreted as a derived noun, meaning "weak" or "empty." The first is more preferable.

Most of the exegetes said: This body that Allah cast upon the throne of Solomon was a devil named Sakhr. He was rebellious against Solomon and did not enter into his obedience. Allah cast Solomon's likeness upon him, and he kept scheming until he obtained Solomon's ring. That happened when Solomon entered the privy, since he used to remove it when he entered the privy. Sakhr came in the form of Solomon and took the ring from one of Solomon's wives. He sat on Solomon's throne and remained for forty days in his kingdom, while Solomon was fleeing.

Mujahid said: A devil said to him: "Solomon, how do you subdue people?" He said: "Show me your ring and I will tell you." When Solomon gave it to him, he threw it into the sea. Thus his kingdom was lost, and the devil sat on his throne. Allah prevented him from his wives, so he did not approach them. Solomon used to beg for food, saying: "Do you know me? Feed me!" but they would deny him, until a woman gave him a fish one day. He split its belly and found his ring inside it, and so his kingdom returned to him. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Then he turned penitently﴾, that is, he returned to his kingdom after forty days. It was also said: The meaning of "turned penitently" is that he returned to Allah in repentance for his sin, and this is the correct view.

The clause ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me"﴾ may be a substitute for the clause "turned penitently" and an explanation of it, meaning: forgive me for the sin that proceeded from me, for which You tested me.

Then, having mentioned repentance and seeking forgiveness, he made them a means to the granting of his request, saying: ﴿And grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: The meaning of "that will not befit anyone after me" is: "that will not belong to anyone after me." It was also said: The meaning is: "No one should be able to strip it from me after this stripping," or: "It will not be fitting for anyone in the distant future because of its greatness." This is not a request of the Prophet of Allah Solomon (peace be upon him) for the world, its kingdom, or honour among its people. Rather, the intention of his request for kingship was that he might be empowered thereby to enforce the commands of Allah, glorified be He, and to restrain the rebellious among His servants, both jinn and humans. Even if the only reason for this request from him had been what he saw of the satanic judgments taking place among the servants of Allah when the devil sat on his throne, that would have been enough. The clause ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾ is a justification for what preceded it, of what he asked: forgiveness from Allah and the granting of a kingdom that will not befit anyone after him. That is, indeed You are abundant in gifts and great in what is given.

Then He, glorified be He, mentioned His answer to his supplication and His granting of his request, saying: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾, that is, We made it submissive to him and made it compliant with his command.

Then He explained the manner of its subjection by His saying: ﴿blowing gently by his command﴾, that is, mild in its blowing, not violent, derived from softness (rukhawah). The meaning is that it was a gentle wind that does not shake or storm, despite the strength of its blowing and the speed of its course. This does not contradict His saying in another verse: ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, blowing violently, running by his command﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 81], because the meaning is that it was of the strength of a storm, yet it did not storm.

It was also said: It was sometimes gentle and sometimes violent, according to what Solomon willed and desired. This is better for reconciling the two verses. ﴿Wherever he directed it﴾ (p-1265), that is, wherever he intended.

Al-Zajjaj said: The consensus of the linguists and exegetes is that the meaning of "wherever he directed it" is "wherever he intended," and its literal meaning is "wherever he sat."

Al-Asma'i and Ibn al-A'rabi said: The Arabs say: "He hit the right thing (asaba al-sawab) and erred in the answer (akhta' al-jawab)."

It was also said: The meaning of asaba in the language of Himyar is "intended," and it is not from the language of the Arabs. It was also said: It is in the dialect of Hajar. The first is preferable, and it is derived from an arrow hitting its target.

And "the devils" is coordinated with "the wind," meaning: We subjected to him the devils. His saying ﴿every builder and diver﴾ is an apposition to "the devils," meaning: every builder among them and every diver among them, who build for him whatever structures he wills and dive into the sea to extract pearls for him. From this is the saying of the poet:

Except Solomon, when the Majestic said to him:
"Stand in the wilderness and mark its boundaries against the desert."

And inform the jinn that I have permitted them
To build Tadmur with stone blocks and pillars.

﴿And others bound together in shackles﴾ is coordinated with "every" and falls under the same ruling as the apposition. They are the rebellious devils, who were subjected to him until he bound them together in shackles.

It is said: He bound them with ropes when they were a large group. The word "al-asfad" means fetters, and its singular is "safad."

Al-Zajjaj said: They are chains. Whatever you tie firmly with iron or other things, you have fettered (safadta).

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "I fettered the man (safadtu al-rajul), so he is maf'ud (fettered); and I shackled him heavily (saffadtahu), so he is musaffad (heavily shackled)." From this is the saying of 'Amr ibn Kulthum in his mu'allaqah:

They returned with plunder and captives,
And we returned with kings shackled.

Yahya ibn Salam said: He would not do this except to their unbelievers. When they believed, he released them and did not subject them.

The reference in His saying "this" is to what was mentioned before: the subjection of the wind and the devils to him.

It is by implication of a saying, meaning: And We said to him: ﴿This is Our gift﴾, which We have given you, of the great kingdom you asked for. ﴿So bestow or withhold﴾. Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and others said: That is, give to whom you wish and withhold from whom you wish. ﴿Without account﴾: there is no account upon you in that giving or withholding. Or: Our gift to you is without account, because of its abundance and greatness.

Qatadah said: His saying ﴿This is Our gift﴾ refers to what he was given of sexual potency. There is no justification for restricting the verse to this, even if we assume it was mentioned before among those things. How can one claim that the verse is specific to it when it is not mentioned?

﴿And indeed for him with Us is a nearness﴾, that is, a closeness in the Hereafter, ﴿and a good final return﴾, a good place of return, which is Paradise.

Al-Firyabi, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And We had certainly tested Solomon and We cast upon his throne a body﴾ that he said: It is the devil who was upon his throne judging between the people for forty days. Solomon had a wife called Jaradah, and there was a dispute between some of her people and a group of people. He judged between them with the truth, except that he wished the truth had been for her people. Allah revealed to him that a trial would befall him. He did not know whether it would come to him from the sky or from the earth.

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported, as al-Suyuti said with a strong chain, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Solomon wished to enter the lavatory, so he gave his ring to Jaradah, who was his wife and the most beloved of his wives to him. The devil came in the form of Solomon and said to her: "Give me my ring!" and she gave it to him. When he put it on, humans, jinn and devils submitted to him. When Solomon came out of the lavatory he said: "Give me my ring!" She said: "I have given it to Solomon." He said: "I am Solomon!" She said: "You lie, you are not Solomon!" So he began to go to anyone and say: "I am Solomon," and they would deny him, until the children began to pelt him with stones. When he saw this, he knew it was from the command of Allah. The devil stood judging among the people. When Allah wished to restore Solomon's authority, He cast into the hearts of the people the rejection of that devil. They sent to the wives of Solomon and said to them: "Do you notice anything strange about Solomon's conduct?" They said: "Yes, he comes to us while we are menstruating, and he did not used to come to us before that." When the devil saw that he had been detected, he thought his affair had come to an end. They wrote books containing sorcery and disbelief and buried them beneath Solomon's throne. Then they dug them up and read them to the people, saying: "With this Solomon used to dominate the people and overcome them." So the people declared Solomon an unbeliever and continued to call him an unbeliever. That devil sent the ring and threw it into the sea, and a fish swallowed it. Solomon used to work on the seashore for wages. A man came and bought fish, among which was that fish that had the ring in its belly. Solomon was called by him, who said: "Will you carry this fish for me?" He said: "Yes." He asked: "For how much?" He said: "For one fish from this fish." So Solomon carried the fish and then went with it to his home. When the man reached the door of his house, he gave him that fish which had the ring in its belly. Solomon took it, split its belly, and found the ring inside it. He took it and put it on. When he put it on, the jinn, humans and devils submitted to him, and he returned to his former state. The devil fled until he reached an island among the islands of the sea. Solomon sent for him. He was a rebellious devil, and they kept searching for him but could not find him, until one day they found him sleeping. They came and built over him a structure of lead. When he woke up and leapt, he could not leap in any place of the house without the lead moving with him. They seized him, bound him, and brought him to Solomon. He ordered that a chest of marble be hollowed out for him, placed him inside it, bound it with copper, and then ordered that it be thrown into the sea. That is His saying: ﴿And We had certainly tested Solomon and We cast upon his throne a body﴾, meaning the devil who had been empowered over him.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿and We cast upon his throne a body﴾ that he said: Sakhr the jinn appeared upon his throne in his form.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed an 'Ifrit from the jinn kept attacking me last night to cut off my prayer, but Allah gave me power over him. I was determined to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque until you all arise and look at him, but I remembered the saying of my brother Solomon: ﴿Grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me﴾, so Allah sent him back humiliated."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So bestow﴾ that he said: Free from the jinn whomever you wish and keep whomever you wish of them.

God says: ﴿And We had certainly tested Solomon﴾, meaning: We tried him and put him to the test.

It was also said: The cause of the trial was that Solomon married a woman called Jaradah, whom he loved intensely. Two parties came to him for judgment, one of them from the people of Jaradah, and he wished that the judgment would go in their favour. Then he judged between them with the truth.

It was also said: The cause was that he secluded himself from the people for three days and did not judge between anyone.

It was also said: He married this Jaradah while she was a polytheist, because he offered her Islam and she said: "Kill me, and I will not become a Muslim."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: When he wronged the horses by killing them, his kingdom was taken from him. Al-Hasan said: He approached some of his wives during menstruation or something else. It was also said: He was commanded not to marry any woman except from the Children of Israel, but he married a woman from outside them.

It was also said: The cause of his trial is what is established in the sound hadith that he said: "Tonight I will go round ninety women, and each one will bear a horseman who will fight in the cause of Allah," and he did not say: "If Allah wills." It has also been said other than this.

Then He, glorified be He, explained what He punished him with, saying: ﴿And We cast upon his throne a body﴾. The accusative of (jasadan, "a body") is that it is the object of (alqayna, "We cast"). It was also said that it is in the accusative of circumstance, interpreted as a derived noun, meaning "weak" or "empty." The first is more preferable.

Most of the exegetes said: This body that Allah cast upon the throne of Solomon was a devil named Sakhr. He was rebellious against Solomon and did not enter into his obedience. Allah cast Solomon's likeness upon him, and he kept scheming until he obtained Solomon's ring. That happened when Solomon entered the privy, since he used to remove it when he entered the privy. Sakhr came in the form of Solomon and took the ring from one of Solomon's wives. He sat on Solomon's throne and remained for forty days in his kingdom, while Solomon was fleeing.

Mujahid said: A devil said to him: "Solomon, how do you subdue people?" He said: "Show me your ring and I will tell you." When Solomon gave it to him, he threw it into the sea. Thus his kingdom was lost, and the devil sat on his throne. Allah prevented him from his wives, so he did not approach them. Solomon used to beg for food, saying: "Do you know me? Feed me!" but they would deny him, until a woman gave him a fish one day. He split its belly and found his ring inside it, and so his kingdom returned to him. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Then he turned penitently﴾, that is, he returned to his kingdom after forty days. It was also said: The meaning of "turned penitently" is that he returned to Allah in repentance for his sin, and this is the correct view.

The clause ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me"﴾ may be a substitute for the clause "turned penitently" and an explanation of it, meaning: forgive me for the sin that proceeded from me, for which You tested me.

Then, having mentioned repentance and seeking forgiveness, he made them a means to the granting of his request, saying: ﴿And grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: The meaning of "that will not befit anyone after me" is: "that will not belong to anyone after me." It was also said: The meaning is: "No one should be able to strip it from me after this stripping," or: "It will not be fitting for anyone in the distant future because of its greatness." This is not a request of the Prophet of Allah Solomon (peace be upon him) for the world, its kingdom, or honour among its people. Rather, the intention of his request for kingship was that he might be empowered thereby to enforce the commands of Allah, glorified be He, and to restrain the rebellious among His servants, both jinn and humans. Even if the only reason for this request from him had been what he saw of the satanic judgments taking place among the servants of Allah when the devil sat on his throne, that would have been enough. The clause ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾ is a justification for what preceded it, of what he asked: forgiveness from Allah and the granting of a kingdom that will not befit anyone after him. That is, indeed You are abundant in gifts and great in what is given.

Then He, glorified be He, mentioned His answer to his supplication and His granting of his request, saying: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾, that is, We made it submissive to him and made it compliant with his command.

Then He explained the manner of its subjection by His saying: ﴿blowing gently by his command﴾, that is, mild in its blowing, not violent, derived from softness (rukhawah). The meaning is that it was a gentle wind that does not shake or storm, despite the strength of its blowing and the speed of its course. And "the devils" is coordinated with "the wind," meaning: We subjected to him the devils. His saying ﴿every builder and diver﴾ is an apposition to "the devils," meaning: every builder among them and every diver among them, who build for him whatever structures he wills and dive into the sea to extract pearls for him. From this is the saying of the poet:

Except Solomon, when the Majestic said to him:
"Stand in the wilderness and mark its boundaries against the desert."

And inform the jinn that I have permitted them
To build Tadmur with stone blocks and pillars.

﴿And others bound together in shackles﴾ is coordinated with "every" and falls under the same ruling as the apposition. They are the rebellious devils, who were subjected to him until he bound them together in shackles.

It is said: He bound them with ropes when they were a large group. The word "al-asfad" means fetters, and its singular is "safad."

Al-Zajjaj said: They are chains. Whatever you tie firmly with iron or other things, you have fettered (safadta).

And we returned with kings shackled.

It is by implication of a saying, meaning: And We said to him: ﴿This is Our gift﴾, which We have given you, of the great kingdom you asked for. ﴿So bestow or withhold﴾. Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and others said: That is, give to whom you wish and withhold from whom you wish. ﴿Without account﴾: there is no account upon you in that giving or withholding. Or: Our gift to you is without account, because of its abundance and greatness.

Qatadah said: His saying ﴿This is Our gift﴾ refers to what he was given of sexual potency. There is no justification for restricting the verse to this, even if we assume it was mentioned before among those things. How can one claim that the verse is specific to it when it is not mentioned?

﴿And indeed for him with Us is a nearness﴾, that is, a closeness in the Hereafter, ﴿and a good final return﴾, a good place of return, which is Paradise.

Al-Firyabi, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And We had certainly tested Solomon and We cast upon his throne a body﴾ that he said: It is the devil who was upon his throne judging between the people for forty days. Solomon had a wife called Jaradah, and there was a dispute between some of her people and a group of people. He judged between them with the truth, except that he wished the truth had been for her people. Allah revealed to him that a trial would befall him. He did not know whether it would come to him from the sky or from the earth.

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported, as al-Suyuti said with a strong chain, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Solomon wished to enter the lavatory, so he gave his ring to Jaradah, who was his wife and the most beloved of his wives to him. The devil came in the form of Solomon and said to her: "Give me my ring!" and she gave it to him. When he put it on, humans, jinn and devils submitted to him. When Solomon came out of the lavatory he said: "Give me my ring!" She said: "I have given it to Solomon." He said: "I am Solomon!" She said: "You lie, you are not Solomon!" So he began to go to anyone and say: "I am Solomon," and they would deny him, until the children began to pelt him with stones. When he saw this, he knew it was from the command of Allah. The devil stood judging among the people. When Allah wished to restore Solomon's authority, He cast into the hearts of the people the rejection of that devil. They sent to the wives of Solomon and said to them: "Do you notice anything strange about Solomon's conduct?" They said: "Yes, he comes to us while we are menstruating, and he did not used to come to us before that." When the devil saw that he had been detected, he thought his affair had come to an end. They wrote books containing sorcery and disbelief and buried them beneath Solomon's throne. Then they dug them up and read them to the people, saying: "With this Solomon used to dominate the people and overcome them." So the people declared Solomon an unbeliever and continued to call him an unbeliever. That devil sent the ring and threw it into the sea, and a fish swallowed it. Solomon used to work on the seashore for wages. A man came and bought fish, among which was that fish that had the ring in its belly. Solomon was called by him, who said: "Will you carry this fish for me?" He said: "Yes." He asked: "For how much?" He said: "For one fish from this fish." So Solomon carried the fish and then went with it to his home. When the man reached the door of his house, he gave him that fish which had the ring in its belly. Solomon took it, split its belly, and found the ring inside it. He took it and put it on. When he put it on, the jinn, humans and devils submitted to him, and he returned to his former state. The devil fled until he reached an island among the islands of the sea. Solomon sent for him. He was a rebellious devil, and they kept searching for him but could not find him, until one day they found him sleeping. They came and built over him a structure of lead. When he woke up and leapt, he could not leap in any place of the house without the lead moving with him. They seized him, bound him, and brought him to Solomon. He ordered that a chest of marble be hollowed out for him, placed him inside it, bound it with copper, and then ordered that it be thrown into the sea. That is His saying: ﴿And We had certainly tested Solomon and We cast upon his throne a body﴾, meaning the devil who had been empowered over him.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿and We cast upon his throne a body﴾ that he said: Sakhr the jinn appeared upon his throne in his form.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed an 'Ifrit from the jinn kept attacking me last night to cut off my prayer, but Allah gave me power over him. I was determined to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque until you all arise and look at him, but I remembered the saying of my brother Solomon: ﴿Grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me﴾, so Allah sent him back humiliated."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So bestow﴾ that he said: Free from the jinn whomever you wish and keep whomever you wish of them.

God says: ﴿And We had certainly tested Solomon﴾, meaning: We tried him and put him to the test.

Al-Wahidi said: Most of the exegetes said: Solomon married a woman from the daughters of kings, and she worshipped an idol in his house, and Solomon did not know of this. He was tested because of his unawareness of it.

It was also said: The cause of the trial was that Solomon married a woman called Jaradah, whom he loved intensely. Two parties came to him for judgment, one of them from the people of Jaradah, and he wished that the judgment would go in their favour. Then he judged between them with the truth.

It was also said: The cause was that he secluded himself from the people for three days and did not judge between anyone.

It was also said: He married this Jaradah while she was a polytheist, because he offered her Islam and she said: "Kill me, and I will not become a Muslim."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: When he wronged the horses by killing them, his kingdom was taken from him. Al-Hasan said: He approached some of his wives during menstruation or something else. It was also said: He was commanded not to marry any woman except from the Children of Israel, but he married a woman from outside them.

It was also said: The cause of his trial is what is established in the sound hadith that he said: "Tonight I will go round ninety women, and each one will bear a horseman who will fight in the cause of Allah," and he did not say: "If Allah wills." It has also been said other than this.

Then He, glorified be He, explained what He punished him with, saying: ﴿And We cast upon his throne a body﴾. The accusative of (jasadan, "a body") is that it is the object of (alqayna, "We cast"). It was also said that it is in the accusative of circumstance, interpreted as a derived noun, meaning "weak" or "empty." The first is more preferable.

Most of the exegetes said: This body that Allah cast upon the throne of Solomon was a devil named Sakhr. He was rebellious against Solomon and did not enter into his obedience. Allah cast Solomon's likeness upon him, and he kept scheming until he obtained Solomon's ring. That happened when Solomon entered the privy, since he used to remove it when he entered the privy. Sakhr came in the form of Solomon and took the ring from one of Solomon's wives. He sat on Solomon's throne and remained for forty days in his kingdom, while Solomon was fleeing.

Mujahid said: A devil said to him: "Solomon, how do you subdue people?" He said: "Show me your ring and I will tell you." When Solomon gave it to him, he threw it into the sea. Thus his kingdom was lost, and the devil sat on his throne. Allah prevented him from his wives, so he did not approach them. Solomon used to beg for food, saying: "Do you know me? Feed me!" but they would deny him, until a woman gave him a fish one day. He split its belly and found his ring inside it, and so his kingdom returned to him. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Then he turned penitently﴾, that is, he returned to his kingdom after forty days. It was also said: The meaning of "turned penitently" is that he returned to Allah in repentance for his sin, and this is the correct view.

The clause ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me"﴾ may be a substitute for the clause "turned penitently" and an explanation of it, meaning: forgive me for the sin that proceeded from me, for which You tested me.

Then, having mentioned repentance and seeking forgiveness, he made them a means to the granting of his request, saying: ﴿And grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: The meaning of "that will not befit anyone after me" is: "that will not belong to anyone after me." It was also said: The meaning is: "No one should be able to strip it from me after this stripping," or: "It will not be fitting for anyone in the distant future because of its greatness." This is not a request of the Prophet of Allah Solomon (peace be upon him) for the world, its kingdom, or honour among its people. Rather, the intention of his request for kingship was that he might be empowered thereby to enforce the commands of Allah, glorified be He, and to restrain the rebellious among His servants, both jinn and humans. Even if the only reason for this request from him had been what he saw of the satanic judgments taking place among the servants of Allah when the devil sat on his throne, that would have been enough. The clause ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾ is a justification for what preceded it, of what he asked: forgiveness from Allah and the granting of a kingdom that will not befit anyone after him. That is, indeed You are abundant in gifts and great in what is given.

Then He, glorified be He, mentioned His answer to his supplication and His granting of his request, saying: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾, that is, We made it submissive to him and made it compliant with his command.

Then He explained the manner of its subjection by His saying: ﴿blowing gently by his command﴾, that is, mild in its blowing, not violent, derived from softness (rukhawah). The meaning is that it was a gentle wind that does not shake or storm, despite the strength of its blowing and the speed of its course. This does not contradict His saying in another verse: ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, blowing violently, running by his command﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 81], because the meaning is that it was of the strength of a storm, yet it did not storm.

It was also said: It was sometimes gentle and sometimes violent, according to what Solomon willed and desired. This is better for reconciling the two verses. ﴿Wherever he directed it﴾ (p-1265), that is, wherever he intended.

Al-Zajjaj said: The consensus of the linguists and exegetes is that the meaning of "wherever he directed it" is "wherever he intended," and its literal meaning is "wherever he sat."

Al-Asma'i and Ibn al-A'rabi said: The Arabs say: "He hit the right thing (asaba al-sawab) and erred in the answer (akhta' al-jawab)."

It was also said: The meaning of asaba in the language of Himyar is "intended," and it is not from the language of the Arabs. It was also said: It is in the dialect of Hajar. The first is preferable, and it is derived from an arrow hitting its target.

And "the devils" is coordinated with "the wind," meaning: We subjected to him the devils. His saying ﴿every builder and diver﴾ is an apposition to "the devils," meaning: every builder among them and every diver among them, who build for him whatever structures he wills and dive into the sea to extract pearls for him. From this is the saying of the poet:

Except Solomon, when the Majestic said to him:
"Stand in the wilderness and mark its boundaries against the desert."

And inform the jinn that I have permitted them
To build Tadmur with stone blocks and pillars.

﴿And others bound together in shackles﴾ is coordinated with "every" and falls under the same ruling as the apposition. They are the rebellious devils, who were subjected to him until he bound them together in shackles.

It is said: He bound them with ropes when they were a large group. The word "al-asfad" means fetters, and its singular is "safad."

Al-Zajjaj said: They are chains. Whatever you tie firmly with iron or other things, you have fettered (safadta).

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "I fettered the man (safadtu al-rajul), so he is maf'ud (fettered); and I shackled him heavily (saffadtahu), so he is musaffad (heavily shackled)." From this is the saying of 'Amr ibn Kulthum in his mu'allaqah:

They returned with plunder and captives,
And we returned with kings shackled.

Yahya ibn Salam said: He would not do this except to their unbelievers. When they believed, he released them and did not subject them.

The reference in His saying "this" is to what was mentioned before: the subjection of the wind and the devils to him.

It is by implication of a saying, meaning: And We said to him: ﴿This is Our gift﴾, which We have given you, of the great kingdom you asked for. ﴿So bestow or withhold﴾. Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and others said: That is, give to whom you wish and withhold from whom you wish. ﴿Without account﴾: there is no account upon you in that giving or withholding. Or: Our gift to you is without account, because of its abundance and greatness.

Qatadah said: His saying ﴿This is Our gift﴾ refers to what he was given of sexual potency. There is no justification for restricting the verse to this, even if we assume it was mentioned before among those things. How can one claim that the verse is specific to it when it is not mentioned?

﴿And indeed for him with Us is a nearness﴾, that is, a closeness in the Hereafter, ﴿and a good final return﴾, a good place of return, which is Paradise.

Al-Firyabi, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And We had certainly tested Solomon and We cast upon his throne a body﴾ that he said: It is the devil who was upon his throne judging between the people for forty days. Solomon had a wife called Jaradah, and there was a dispute between some of her people and a group of people. He judged between them with the truth, except that he wished the truth had been for her people. Allah revealed to him that a trial would befall him. He did not know whether it would come to him from the sky or from the earth.

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported, as al-Suyuti said with a strong chain, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Solomon wished to enter the lavatory, so he gave his ring to Jaradah, who was his wife and the most beloved of his wives to him. The devil came in the form of Solomon and said to her: "Give me my ring!" and she gave it to him. When he put it on, humans, jinn and devils submitted to him. When Solomon came out of the lavatory he said: "Give me my ring!" She said: "I have given it to Solomon." He said: "I am Solomon!" She said: "You lie, you are not Solomon!" So he began to go to anyone and say: "I am Solomon," and they would deny him, until the children began to pelt him with stones. When he saw this, he knew it was from the command of Allah. The devil stood judging among the people. When Allah wished to restore Solomon's authority, He cast into the hearts of the people the rejection of that devil. They sent to the wives of Solomon and said to them: "Do you notice anything strange about Solomon's conduct?" They said: "Yes, he comes to us while we are menstruating, and he did not used to come to us before that." When the devil saw that he had been detected, he thought his affair had come to an end. They wrote books containing sorcery and disbelief and buried them beneath Solomon's throne. Then they dug them up and read them to the people, saying: "With this Solomon used to dominate the people and overcome them." So the people declared Solomon an unbeliever and continued to call him an unbeliever. That devil sent the ring and threw it into the sea, and a fish swallowed it. Solomon used to work on the seashore for wages. A man came and bought fish, among which was that fish that had the ring in its belly. Solomon was called by him, who said: "Will you carry this fish for me?" He said: "Yes." He asked: "For how much?" He said: "For one fish from this fish." So Solomon carried the fish and then went with it to his home. When the man reached the door of his house, he gave him that fish which had the ring in its belly. Solomon took it, split its belly, and found the ring inside it. He took it and put it on. When he put it on, the jinn, humans and devils submitted to him, and he returned to his former state. The devil fled until he reached an island among the islands of the sea. Solomon sent for him. He was a rebellious devil, and they kept searching for him but could not find him, until one day they found him sleeping. They came and built over him a structure of lead. When he woke up and leapt, he could not leap in any place of the house without the lead moving with him. They seized him, bound him, and brought him to Solomon. He ordered that a chest of marble be hollowed out for him, placed him inside it, bound it with copper, and then ordered that it be thrown into the sea. That is His saying: ﴿And We had certainly tested Solomon and We cast upon his throne a body﴾, meaning the devil who had been empowered over him.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿and We cast upon his throne a body﴾ that he said: Sakhr the jinn appeared upon his throne in his form.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed an 'Ifrit from the jinn kept attacking me last night to cut off my prayer, but Allah gave me power over him. I was determined to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque until you all arise and look at him, but I remembered the saying of my brother Solomon: ﴿Grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me﴾, so Allah sent him back humiliated."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So bestow﴾ that he said: Free from the jinn whomever you wish and keep whomever you wish of them.

(p-1266) His words: ﴿And remember Our servant Job﴾ are coordinated with His words ﴿And remember Our servant David﴾ [Sad: 17]. "Job" is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān), and ﴿when he called out to his Lord﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from ("Our servant"). ﴿"Indeed, adversity has touched me, and Satan has afflicted me with hardship"﴾. The majority of readers recited with a fatḥa on the hamza (Anna), as a quotation of his words with which he called out to his Lord; had he not quoted them, it would have said: "that it had touched him." ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited it with a kasra, on the presumption of an implied verb of saying (al-qawl).

In the story of Job there is guidance for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to follow his example in patience through hardships.

The majority of readers recited ﴿bi-nuṣbin﴾ with a ḍamma on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād. It is said that it is the plural of naṣab (with two fatḥas), like asad and usud; and it is said that it is a dialectal form of al-naṣab, like rashad and rushd.

Abū Jaʿfar Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ, Shaybah, Ḥafṣ, and Nāfiʿ in one of the transmissions from him recited it with two ḍammas, and this reading is also reported from al-Ḥasan.

Abū Ḥaywah, Yaʿqūb, and Ḥafṣ in one transmission recited it with a fatḥa and a sukūn. All these readings have one meaning; the readings differ only according to differences of dialect.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: "Naṣab with two fatḥas means weariness and exhaustion; and in the rest of the readings it means evil and affliction." The meaning of "and torment" (ʿadhāb) is pain.

Qatādah and Muqātil said: "Naṣab refers to the body, and ʿadhāb to property." al-Naḥḥās said: "In it there is more to be said; that is what he said." The better course is to explain naṣab by its linguistic meaning, which is weariness and exhaustion, and to explain ʿadhāb by what truly fits the notion of torment, which is pain; and both refer to the body.

﴿Strike with your foot﴾: this is by way of an implied verb of saying, i.e., "We said to him: strike with your foot." Thus al-Kisāʾī said: "al-Rakḍ is pushing with the foot. It is said: he struck (rakaḍa) the animal with his foot, when he hit it with it."

al-Mubarrad said: "al-Rakḍ is moving." al-Aṣmaʿī said: "It is said: I made the animal strike (rakaḍtu al-dābbah), but one does not say: she struck (rakaḍat hiya), because rakḍ is only the rider moving his legs, and the animal has no action in that." Sībawayh related: "I made the animal strike (rakaḍtu al-dābbah), so she struck (fa-rakaḍat)," like "I set the bone, so it set (jabartu al-ʿaẓma fa-jabar)."

﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾: this too is part of the implied speech. "al-Mughtasal" is the water with which one bathes, and "al-sharāb" is the drink one drinks from it. It is also said that "al-mughtasal" is the place in which one bathes.

Qatādah said: "They are two springs in the land of Syria, in a land called al-Jābiyah. He bathed in one of them, and Allah removed the outward part of his disease; and he drank from the other, and Allah removed the inward part of his disease." al-Ḥasan said likewise.

Muqātil said: "A flowing spring gushed forth, and he bathed in it and came out healthy. Then another spring gushed forth, and he drank from it fresh, cool water."

There is an ellipsis in the speech; the estimate is: "So he struck with his foot, and a spring gushed forth; then We said to him: this is a cool bath, etc."

The attribution of touching to Satan, although it was Allah, glorified is He, who touched him with it, is either because when he acted on Satan's whisperings he was punished with that naṣab and ʿadhāb.

It has been said: he was impressed by the abundance of his wealth. It has been said: a wronged man sought his help and he did not help him. It has been said: he said that in the manner of good manners (adab). It has been said: he said that because Satan whispered to his followers, and they rejected him and expelled him from their homes. It has been said that what is meant by it is what Satan whispered to him during his illness and trial, of beautifying impatience and not bearing the calamity with patience. Other explanations have also been given.

His words: ﴿And We gave him his family﴾ are coordinated with an implied clause, as if it were said: "So he bathed and drank, and by that We removed from him the harm he had, and We gave him his family."

It is said: Allah revived them after He had caused them to die. It is said: He gathered them after their dispersal. It is said: He changed them to be like themselves, then increased him by a like number with them; and this is the meaning of His words: ﴿and a like number with them﴾. Thus they became as they had been before his trial. The accusative of His words: ﴿as a mercy from Us and a reminder for people of understanding﴾ is by way of the object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi): i.e., "We gave them to him for the sake of Our mercy toward him, and so that people of understanding might be reminded of his condition and endure hardships with patience as he did." This verse was already explained fully in Surah al-Anbiyāʾ, so we do not repeat it.

﴿And take in your hand a bundle﴾ is coordinated with "strike" (irkuḍ), or with "We gave him," or the estimate is: "And We said to him: and take in your hand a bundle." Al-ḍighth is a cluster of palm-fronds with their stalks; it is also said: it is a handful of mixed grass whose green and dry parts are together; and it is also said: a large bundle of twigs. The root of the word indicates gathering mixed things together.

al-Wāḥidī said: al-ḍighth is a handful of trees, grass, and stalks.

﴿Strike with it and do not break your oath﴾: i.e., strike with that bundle, and do not break your oath. al-ḥinth is sin, and it is also applied to doing what one swore to abandon. Job had sworn during his illness that he would strike his wife one hundred lashes.

The cause of this has been disputed. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab said: she had brought him more bread than she used to bring, and he feared she had embezzled, so he swore that he would strike her. Yaḥyā ibn Sallām and others said: Satan had seduced her to get Job to slaughter a lamb as an offering to him, for if he did that he would be healed; so he swore that he would strike her one hundred lashes if he recovered. It has also been said: she sold her forelock for two loaves when she found nothing else, and Job used to lean on her when he wished to stand up; so for this reason he swore that he would strike her. It has also been said: Iblīs came to her in the form of a physician, and she asked him to treat Job; he said: "I will treat him on condition that when he is healed he says: 'You healed me,' and I want no reward other than that." She said: "Yes." So she advised Job accordingly, and he swore that he would strike her.

The scholars have differed as to whether this ruling is specific to Job or general for all people, and whether one who has sworn is released from his oath by the same means.

al-Shāfiʿī said: if one swears that he will strike so-and-so one hundred lashes, or a beating, without saying "a severe beating" and without intending it in his heart, then a beating like the one mentioned in the verse suffices for him. Ibn al-Mundhir related this from him, and from Abū Thawr and the Companions of opinion (aṣḥāb al-raʾy).

ʿAṭāʾ said: it is specific to Job, and Ibn al-Qāsim related it from Mālik.

Then Allah, glorified is He, praised Job, saying: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ (p-1267), i.e., in the face of the trial with which We tested him, for he was tested with a severe illness in his body, and the loss of his property, his family, and his children, and he was patient. ﴿An excellent servant﴾, i.e., Job. ﴿Indeed he was one who turned back (awwāb)﴾, i.e., one who returns to Allah in seeking forgiveness and repentance.

﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob﴾: the majority read "ʿibādanā" in the plural. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ḥumayd, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Ibn Kathīr read "ʿabdanā" in the singular.

According to the majority's reading, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are explicative appositions; according to the other reading, Abraham is an explicative apposition, and what follows it is coordinated with "ʿabdanā," not with Abraham.

It may be said: since the intended meaning of "ʿabdanā" is the category, it is permissible to substitute the plural group for it.

It has also been said: Abraham and what follows him are a substitution (badal), or they are in the accusative by an implied "I mean" (aʿnī). The explicative apposition is the clearest, and the majority's reading is the most explicit; Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred it.

﴿Possessors of hands and sight﴾: al-Aydī is the plural of yad in the sense of strength and power. Qatādah said: "They were given strength in worship and victory in religion." al-Wāḥidī said: Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and the exegetes said likewise.

al-Naḥḥās said: As for al-abṣār (sight), there is agreement that it means insight in religion and knowledge. As for al-aydī (hands), its interpretation is disputed: the people of tafsir say it means strength in religion; and some say al-aydī is the plural of yad, meaning favor, i.e., they are possessors of favors, those upon whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestowed favor; and it has been said: they are possessors of favors upon people and of benevolence toward them, for they did good and sent forward good deeds. Ibn Jarīr preferred this.

The majority read "ulī al-aydī" with the ya' affirmed in al-aydī. Ibn Masʿūd, al-Aʿmash, al-Ḥasan, and ʿĪsā read al-ayd without the ya'; it is said its meaning is the same as the first reading, and the ya' was dropped because the kasra on the dal indicates it. It is also said: al-ayd means strength.

The clause ﴿Indeed We purified them with a pure quality, the remembrance of the Abode﴾ is a reason (taʿlīl) for what they were described with.

The majority read "bi-khāliṣatin" with tanwīn and without an annexation, taking it as a verbal noun in the sense of sincere devotion (al-ikhlāṣ), so that "dhikrā" is in the accusative governed by it; or in the sense of purity (al-khulūṣ), so that "dhikrā" is in the nominative governed by it; or "khāliṣah" is an active participle in its proper form, and "dhikrā" is a substitution for it, or an explanation of it, or by an implied "I mean," or in the nominative by an implied subject. "al-Dār" may be a direct object of "dhikrā," and it may be an adverbial complement, either by extension or by dropping the preposition. In every estimate, "khāliṣah" is an attribute of an omitted noun, and the bāʾ is causal, i.e., "by means of a pure quality."

Nāfiʿ, Shaybah, Abū Jaʿfar, and Hishām from Ibn ʿĀmir read "khāliṣah" annexed to "dhikrā," with the annexation being explanatory, because the pure quality may be remembrance or other than remembrance; or because "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun annexed to its object, with the agent omitted, i.e., "by their sincerely devoting the remembrance of the Abode"; or a verbal noun in the sense of purity annexed to its agent.

Mujāhid said: the meaning of the verse is: We chose them by mentioning the Hereafter, and so We purified them through its remembrance. Qatādah said: they used to call to the Hereafter and to Allah. al-Suddī said: they were purified by fear of the Hereafter.

al-Wāḥidī said: whoever reads with tanwīn in "khāliṣah," the meaning is: We made them sincere to Us, in that the remembrance of the Abode was purely theirs; "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun in the sense of purity, and "dhikrā" in the sense of remembrance, i.e., the remembrance of the Abode was purely theirs, namely that they remembered preparation for it and were detached from this world, which is characteristic of the prophets.

As for whoever annexes, the meaning is: We purified them by having the remembrance of the Abode purely theirs; "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun annexed to its agent, and "dhikrā" in this sense means the mention.

﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and the good﴾: al-iṣṭifāʾ is choosing; al-akhyār is the plural of khayyir, with shadda or without, as amwāt is the plural of mayyit, with shadda or without. The meaning: they are with Us among those chosen from the good of their kind.

﴿And remember Ismāʿīl﴾: it has been said that the reason for singling him out for mention after his father, his brother, and his nephew is to indicate that he was steadfast in patience, which is the purpose of the reminder here. ﴿And al-Yasaʿ and Dhū al-Kifl﴾: al-Yasaʿ has already been mentioned, and what is said about him was discussed in al-Anʿām; Dhū al-Kifl has already been mentioned, and what is said about him was discussed in Surah al-Anbiyāʾ. The purpose of mentioning these is that they were among those prophets who were patient and bore hardships in the religion of Allah.

Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to mention them so that he might follow their path in patience. ﴿And all of them are among the good ones﴾, i.e., those whom Allah chose for His prophethood and selected from His creation.

﴿This is a remembrance﴾: the demonstrative refers to what was mentioned before of their attributes, i.e., this is a fine remembrance in this world and a nobility by which they will be remembered forever. ﴿And indeed for the God-fearing there is a good return﴾, i.e., along with this fine remembrance they have a good return in the Hereafter. al-Maʾāb is the place of return, and the meaning is that in the Hereafter they will return to Allah's forgiveness, His good pleasure, and the bliss of His Garden.

Then He described the excellence of the final return, saying: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. The majority of reciters read *jannāti* in the accusative case as a substitute (*badal*) for *ḥusna maʾāb* ("the excellent place of return"). This holds whether *jannāti ʿadnin* is definite or indefinite, because a definite noun may substitute for an indefinite one and vice versa. It is also permissible for *jannāti* to be an explicative apposition (*ʿatf bayān*) if it is indefinite, but this is not permissible if it is definite according to the view of the majority of grammarians, although some have permitted it. The accusative of *jannāti* may also be due to an implied verb. *ʿAdn* originally means "staying," as in the expression ʿadana bi-l-makān, "he resided in the place." It is also said to be the name of a palace in Paradise. It was also read with *jannātu* in the nominative, as the subject (*mubtadaʾ*) whose predicate is *mufattaḥatan* ("opened"), or as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning "they are Gardens of Eden." The phrase ﴿with the gates opened for them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to *jannāt*, and its governing element is the meaning of the verb contained in *al-muttaqīn* ("the God-conscious"). *Al-abwāb* ("the gates") is raised as the subject of the passive participle, as in His saying: ﴿and its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. The link between the circumstantial clause and its referent is a pronoun that is understood, meaning "from them," or the definite article *al-*, which stands in place of the pronoun, since the original form is *abwābuhā* ("its gates").

It is also said that *al-abwāb* is raised as a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *mufattaḥatun*, which refers back to *jannāt*. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī held this view, meaning: "opened are the gates themselves."

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning is "its gates are opened," and the Arabs use the definite article as a substitute for the possessive pronoun. Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is "the gates are opened for them from within them." Al-Ḥasan said: it is said to the gates, "Open!" and they open, "Close!" and they close. It is also said that the angels open the gates for them.

The accusative of ﴿reclining therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *lahum* ("for them"), and its governing element is *mufattaḥatan*. It is also said that it is a circumstantial clause from *yadʿūna* ("they call for"), placed before its governing element, meaning: "they call for [fruit] in the Gardens, while reclining therein." ﴿Therein, they call for abundant fruit﴾, meaning, for fruits of many kinds and abundance, and drink in abundance. *Kathīran* ("abundant") was omitted from the second part because the first indicates it. If *muttakiʾīna* is taken as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *lahum*, governed by *mufattaḥatan*, then the clause *yadʿūna* is a resumptive clause (*mustaʾnafa*) explaining their state.

It is also said that *yadʿūna* is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *muttakiʾīna*.

﴿And with them are those restraining their glances, equals in age﴾, meaning, restraining their glances to their husbands, not looking at anyone else. Its explanation has already been given in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt.

*Atrāb* means those who are of the same age, or who are equal in beauty.

Mujāhid said: the meaning of *atrāb* is that they are companions who do not hate or envy one another. It is also said that *atrāban* is for the husbands. *Atrāb* is the plural of *tirb*, and its derivation is from *turāb* ("dust"), because they reach [adulthood] at the same time, owing to the unity of their birth.

﴿This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning﴾, meaning, this is the reward you were promised for the sake of the Day of Reckoning, since the reckoning is the cause for reaching the reward. Or the meaning is "on the Day of Reckoning."

The majority read *mā tūʿadūna* with the second person (*tāʾ fawqiyya*), as address. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Yaʿqūb read it with the third person (*yāʾ taḥtiyya*), as report. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this reading because of His saying: ﴿and indeed for the God-conscious﴾, since that is a report.

﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾, meaning: indeed this which has been mentioned of blessings and honors is Our provision which We have bestowed upon you, ﴿which has no end﴾, meaning, no cessation, and it never perishes. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿a gift never cut off﴾ [Hūd: 108]. So the blessings of Paradise never cease for its people.

Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Satan ascended to the heaven and said: "O Lord, give me power over Ayyūb." God said: "I have given you power over his wealth and his children, but I have not given you power over his body." So he descended and gathered his troops, and said to them: "I have been given power over Ayyūb, so show me your power." They became fire, then became water. While they were in the east, they suddenly were in the west, and while they were in the west, they suddenly were in the east.

He sent a group of them to his crops, a group to his family, a group to his cattle, and a group to his sheep, and said: "He will not be protected from you except by what is good." So they brought him calamities one upon another. The owner of the crops came and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent fire upon your crops, and it burned them?" Then came the owner of the camels and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your camels, and it took them away?" Then came the owner of the cattle and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your cattle, and it took them away?" Then came the owner of the sheep and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your sheep, and it took them away?" And he was alone with his sons, so he gathered them in the house of the eldest. While they were eating and drinking, a wind blew and seized the corners of the house and dropped it upon them. Then Satan came to Ayyūb in the form of a boy with two earrings in his ears, and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord gathered your sons in the house of the eldest, and while they were eating and drinking, a wind blew upon them and seized the corners of the house and dropped it upon them? If only you had seen them when their blood and flesh mixed with their food and drink!" Ayyūb said to him: "Where were you?" He said: "I was with them." He asked: "How did you escape?" He said: "I escaped." Ayyūb said: "You are Satan." Then Ayyūb said: "Today I am like the day my mother bore me." He stood, shaved his head, and began to pray. Iblīs let out a cry that was heard by the people of the heavens and the people of the earth. Then he ascended to the heaven and said: "O Lord, he has been protected, so give me power over him, for I cannot overcome him except by Your authority." He said: "I have given you power over his body, but I have not given you power over his heart." So he descended and blew beneath his foot a blast that ulcerated everything between his two feet up to his head, and it became one sore. He was thrown onto the ash until the membrane of his heart appeared. His wife would go about tending him until she said to him: "Do you not see, O Ayyūb, that by God, hardship and poverty have come upon me such that if I sold my hair for a loaf of bread to feed you...? So pray to God that He may heal you and relieve you." He said: "Woe to you! We were in bliss for seventy years, so be patient until we are in adversity for seventy years." He was in affliction for seven years, and he supplicated. Then Jibrīl came one day, and struck with his hand, then said: "Stand up," so he stood, and he moved him from his place, and said: "Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and drink." He struck with his foot, and a spring gushed forth. He said: "Bathe," and he bathed in it. Then he came again and said: "Strike with your foot," and another spring gushed forth, and he said to him: "Drink from it." This is His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot; here is a cool bath and drink﴾. And God clothed him in a garment from Paradise. Ayyūb withdrew and sat in a corner. His wife came and did not recognize him, and said: "O servant of God, where is the afflicted man who was here? Perhaps the dogs or wolves have taken him." She kept speaking with him for a while. He said: "Woe to you, I am Ayyūb. God has restored my body to me, and restored to me my wealth and my children in person, and the like of them with them, and rained upon him locusts of gold." He began taking the locusts in his hand, then placing them in his garment, and spreading his cloak and taking them and putting them in it. God revealed to him: "O Ayyūb, have you not had enough?" He said: "O Lord, who could have enough of Your bounty and mercy?"

In this report there is a severe strangeness, for God—glorified is He—does not give Satan power over one of His prophets to this extent of great domination.

Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd*, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Iblīs sat on the road and took a chest to treat people. Ayyūb's wife said: "O servant of God, there is here a man afflicted in such-and-such a way; would you treat him?" He said: "Yes, on condition that if I cure him, he says: 'You cured me,' and I want no reward from him other than this." She came to Ayyūb and told him about it. He said: "Woe to you, that is Satan. By God, if God cures me, I will flog you one hundred lashes." When God healed him, He commanded him to take a bundle and strike her with it. He took a palm-frond with one hundred stalks and struck her with one blow.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿Take in your hand a bundle﴾, that it is the *asal* (a reed/thin branch). Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him: "*al-ḍighth* is a handful of green pasture." Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated from him: "*al-ḍighth* is a bundle."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated, through the chain of Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, who said: "A slave girl among the Banū Sāʿida conceived from fornication, and she was asked: 'By whom are you pregnant?' She said: 'By so-and-so the paralyzed man.' The paralyzed man was asked, and he said: 'She has told the truth.' This was brought to the Messenger of God—may God bless him and his family and grant him peace—and he said: 'Take a cluster with one hundred stalks and strike her with it, one blow.'"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated something similar through another chain, from Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, from Saʿīd ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda. Al-Ṭabarānī narrated something similar from Sahl ibn Saʿd.

Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "Ayyūb is the chief of the patient on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn Masʿūd concerning His saying: ﴿possessors of strength﴾, that he said: "the strength in worship, and the insight," and he said: "understanding of the religion."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him: ﴿possessors of strength﴾, he said: "blessing."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure [quality]: remembrance of the Abode﴾, he said: "They were purified by remembering the Abode of the Hereafter, so that they would work for it."

(p-1266) His words: ﴿And remember Our servant Job﴾ are coordinated with His words ﴿And remember Our servant David﴾ [Sad: 17].
