al-Naḥḥās said: As for al-abṣār (sight), there is agreement that it means insight in religion and knowledge. As for al-aydī (hands), its interpretation is disputed: the people of tafsir say it means strength in religion; and some say al-aydī is the plural of yad, meaning favor, i.e., they are possessors of favors, those upon whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestowed favor; and it has been said: they are possessors of favors upon people and of benevolence toward them, for they did good and sent forward good deeds. Ibn Jarīr preferred this.

The majority read "ulī al-aydī" with the ya' affirmed in al-aydī. Ibn Masʿūd, al-Aʿmash, al-Ḥasan, and ʿĪsā read al-ayd without the ya'; it is said its meaning is the same as the first reading, and the ya' was dropped because the kasra on the dal indicates it. It is also said: al-ayd means strength.

The clause ﴿Indeed We purified them with a pure quality, the remembrance of the Abode﴾ is a reason (taʿlīl) for what they were described with.

The majority read "bi-khāliṣatin" with tanwīn and without an annexation, taking it as a verbal noun in the sense of sincere devotion (al-ikhlāṣ), so that "dhikrā" is in the accusative governed by it; or in the sense of purity (al-khulūṣ), so that "dhikrā" is in the nominative governed by it; or "khāliṣah" is an active participle in its proper form, and "dhikrā" is a substitution for it, or an explanation of it, or by an implied "I mean," or in the nominative by an implied subject. "al-Dār" may be a direct object of "dhikrā," and it may be an adverbial complement, either by extension or by dropping the preposition. In every estimate, "khāliṣah" is an attribute of an omitted noun, and the bāʾ is causal, i.e., "by means of a pure quality."

Nāfiʿ, Shaybah, Abū Jaʿfar, and Hishām from Ibn ʿĀmir read "khāliṣah" annexed to "dhikrā," with the annexation being explanatory, because the pure quality may be remembrance or other than remembrance; or because "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun annexed to its object, with the agent omitted, i.e., "by their sincerely devoting the remembrance of the Abode"; or a verbal noun in the sense of purity annexed to its agent.

Mujāhid said: the meaning of the verse is: We chose them by mentioning the Hereafter, and so We purified them through its remembrance. Qatādah said: they used to call to the Hereafter and to Allah. al-Suddī said: they were purified by fear of the Hereafter.

al-Wāḥidī said: whoever reads with tanwīn in "khāliṣah," the meaning is: We made them sincere to Us, in that the remembrance of the Abode was purely theirs; "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun in the sense of purity, and "dhikrā" in the sense of remembrance, i.e., the remembrance of the Abode was purely theirs, namely that they remembered preparation for it and were detached from this world, which is characteristic of the prophets.

As for whoever annexes, the meaning is: We purified them by having the remembrance of the Abode purely theirs; "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun annexed to its agent, and "dhikrā" in this sense means the mention.

﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and the good﴾: al-iṣṭifāʾ is choosing; al-akhyār is the plural of khayyir, with shadda or without, as amwāt is the plural of mayyit, with shadda or without. The meaning: they are with Us among those chosen from the good of their kind.

﴿And remember Ismāʿīl﴾: it has been said that the reason for singling him out for mention after his father, his brother, and his nephew is to indicate that he was steadfast in patience, which is the purpose of the reminder here. ﴿And al-Yasaʿ and Dhū al-Kifl﴾: al-Yasaʿ has already been mentioned, and what is said about him was discussed in al-Anʿām; Dhū al-Kifl has already been mentioned, and what is said about him was discussed in Surah al-Anbiyāʾ. The purpose of mentioning these is that they were among those prophets who were patient and bore hardships in the religion of Allah.

Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to mention them so that he might follow their path in patience. ﴿And all of them are among the good ones﴾, i.e., those whom Allah chose for His prophethood and selected from His creation.

﴿This is a remembrance﴾: the demonstrative refers to what was mentioned before of their attributes, i.e., this is a fine remembrance in this world and a nobility by which they will be remembered forever. ﴿And indeed for the God-fearing there is a good return﴾, i.e., along with this fine remembrance they have a good return in the Hereafter. al-Maʾāb is the place of return, and the meaning is that in the Hereafter they will return to Allah's forgiveness, His good pleasure, and the bliss of His Garden.

Then He described the excellence of the final return, saying: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. The majority of reciters read *jannāti* in the accusative case as a substitute (*badal*) for *ḥusna maʾāb* ("the excellent place of return"). This holds whether *jannāti ʿadnin* is definite or indefinite, because a definite noun may substitute for an indefinite one and vice versa. It is also permissible for *jannāti* to be an explicative apposition (*ʿatf bayān*) if it is indefinite, but this is not permissible if it is definite according to the view of the majority of grammarians, although some have permitted it. The accusative of *jannāti* may also be due to an implied verb. *ʿAdn* originally means "staying," as in the expression ʿadana bi-l-makān, "he resided in the place." It is also said to be the name of a palace in Paradise. It was also read with *jannātu* in the nominative, as the subject (*mubtadaʾ*) whose predicate is *mufattaḥatan* ("opened"), or as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning "they are Gardens of Eden." The phrase ﴿with the gates opened for them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to *jannāt*, and its governing element is the meaning of the verb contained in *al-muttaqīn* ("the God-conscious"). *Al-abwāb* ("the gates") is raised as the subject of the passive participle, as in His saying: ﴿and its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. The link between the circumstantial clause and its referent is a pronoun that is understood, meaning "from them," or the definite article *al-*, which stands in place of the pronoun, since the original form is *abwābuhā* ("its gates").

It is also said that *al-abwāb* is raised as a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *mufattaḥatun*, which refers back to *jannāt*. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī held this view, meaning: "opened are the gates themselves."

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning is "its gates are opened," and the Arabs use the definite article as a substitute for the possessive pronoun. Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is "the gates are opened for them from within them." Al-Ḥasan said: it is said to the gates, "Open!" and they open, "Close!" and they close. It is also said that the angels open the gates for them.

The accusative of ﴿reclining therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *lahum* ("for them"), and its governing element is *mufattaḥatan*. It is also said that it is a circumstantial clause from *yadʿūna* ("they call for"), placed before its governing element, meaning: "they call for [fruit] in the Gardens, while reclining therein." ﴿Therein, they call for abundant fruit﴾, meaning, for fruits of many kinds and abundance, and drink in abundance. *Kathīran* ("abundant") was omitted from the second part because the first indicates it. If *muttakiʾīna* is taken as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *lahum*, governed by *mufattaḥatan*, then the clause *yadʿūna* is a resumptive clause (*mustaʾnafa*) explaining their state.

It is also said that *yadʿūna* is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *muttakiʾīna*.

﴿And with them are those restraining their glances, equals in age﴾, meaning, restraining their glances to their husbands, not looking at anyone else. Its explanation has already been given in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt.

*Atrāb* means those who are of the same age, or who are equal in beauty.

Mujāhid said: the meaning of *atrāb* is that they are companions who do not hate or envy one another. It is also said that *atrāban* is for the husbands. *Atrāb* is the plural of *tirb*, and its derivation is from *turāb* ("dust"), because they reach [adulthood] at the same time, owing to the unity of their birth.

﴿This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning﴾, meaning, this is the reward you were promised for the sake of the Day of Reckoning, since the reckoning is the cause for reaching the reward. Or the meaning is "on the Day of Reckoning."

The majority read *mā tūʿadūna* with the second person (*tāʾ fawqiyya*), as address. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Yaʿqūb read it with the third person (*yāʾ taḥtiyya*), as report. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this reading because of His saying: ﴿and indeed for the God-conscious﴾, since that is a report.

﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾, meaning: indeed this which has been mentioned of blessings and honors is Our provision which We have bestowed upon you, ﴿which has no end﴾, meaning, no cessation, and it never perishes. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿a gift never cut off﴾ [Hūd: 108]. So the blessings of Paradise never cease for its people.

Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Satan ascended to the heaven and said: "O Lord, give me power over Ayyūb." God said: "I have given you power over his wealth and his children, but I have not given you power over his body." So he descended and gathered his troops, and said to them: "I have been given power over Ayyūb, so show me your power." They became fire, then became water. While they were in the east, they suddenly were in the west, and while they were in the west, they suddenly were in the east.

He sent a group of them to his crops, a group to his family, a group to his cattle, and a group to his sheep, and said: "He will not be protected from you except by what is good." So they brought him calamities one upon another. The owner of the crops came and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent fire upon your crops, and it burned them?" Then came the owner of the camels and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your camels, and it took them away?" Then came the owner of the cattle and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your cattle, and it took them away?" Then came the owner of the sheep and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your sheep, and it took them away?" And he was alone with his sons, so he gathered them in the house of the eldest. While they were eating and drinking, a wind blew and seized the corners of the house and dropped it upon them. Then Satan came to Ayyūb in the form of a boy with two earrings in his ears, and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord gathered your sons in the house of the eldest, and while they were eating and drinking, a wind blew upon them and seized the corners of the house and dropped it upon them? If only you had seen them when their blood and flesh mixed with their food and drink!" Ayyūb said to him: "Where were you?" He said: "I was with them." He asked: "How did you escape?" He said: "I escaped." Ayyūb said: "You are Satan." Then Ayyūb said: "Today I am like the day my mother bore me." He stood, shaved his head, and began to pray. Iblīs let out a cry that was heard by the people of the heavens and the people of the earth. Then he ascended to the heaven and said: "O Lord, he has been protected, so give me power over him, for I cannot overcome him except by Your authority." He said: "I have given you power over his body, but I have not given you power over his heart." So he descended and blew beneath his foot a blast that ulcerated everything between his two feet up to his head, and it became one sore. He was thrown onto the ash until the membrane of his heart appeared. His wife would go about tending him until she said to him: "Do you not see, O Ayyūb, that by God, hardship and poverty have come upon me such that if I sold my hair for a loaf of bread to feed you...? So pray to God that He may heal you and relieve you." He said: "Woe to you! We were in bliss for seventy years, so be patient until we are in adversity for seventy years." He was in affliction for seven years, and he supplicated. Then Jibrīl came one day, and struck with his hand, then said: "Stand up," so he stood, and he moved him from his place, and said: "Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and drink." He struck with his foot, and a spring gushed forth. He said: "Bathe," and he bathed in it. Then he came again and said: "Strike with your foot," and another spring gushed forth, and he said to him: "Drink from it." This is His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot; here is a cool bath and drink﴾. And God clothed him in a garment from Paradise. Ayyūb withdrew and sat in a corner. His wife came and did not recognize him, and said: "O servant of God, where is the afflicted man who was here? Perhaps the dogs or wolves have taken him." She kept speaking with him for a while. He said: "Woe to you, I am Ayyūb. God has restored my body to me, and restored to me my wealth and my children in person, and the like of them with them, and rained upon him locusts of gold." He began taking the locusts in his hand, then placing them in his garment, and spreading his cloak and taking them and putting them in it. God revealed to him: "O Ayyūb, have you not had enough?" He said: "O Lord, who could have enough of Your bounty and mercy?"

In this report there is a severe strangeness, for God—glorified is He—does not give Satan power over one of His prophets to this extent of great domination.

Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd*, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Iblīs sat on the road and took a chest to treat people. Ayyūb's wife said: "O servant of God, there is here a man afflicted in such-and-such a way; would you treat him?" He said: "Yes, on condition that if I cure him, he says: 'You cured me,' and I want no reward from him other than this." She came to Ayyūb and told him about it. He said: "Woe to you, that is Satan. By God, if God cures me, I will flog you one hundred lashes." When God healed him, He commanded him to take a bundle and strike her with it. He took a palm-frond with one hundred stalks and struck her with one blow.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿Take in your hand a bundle﴾, that it is the *asal* (a reed/thin branch). Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him: "*al-ḍighth* is a handful of green pasture." Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated from him: "*al-ḍighth* is a bundle."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated, through the chain of Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, who said: "A slave girl among the Banū Sāʿida conceived from fornication, and she was asked: 'By whom are you pregnant?' She said: 'By so-and-so the paralyzed man.' The paralyzed man was asked, and he said: 'She has told the truth.' This was brought to the Messenger of God—may God bless him and his family and grant him peace—and he said: 'Take a cluster with one hundred stalks and strike her with it, one blow.'"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated something similar through another chain, from Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, from Saʿīd ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda. Al-Ṭabarānī narrated something similar from Sahl ibn Saʿd.

Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "Ayyūb is the chief of the patient on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn Masʿūd concerning His saying: ﴿possessors of strength﴾, that he said: "the strength in worship, and the insight," and he said: "understanding of the religion."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him: ﴿possessors of strength﴾, he said: "blessing."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure [quality]: remembrance of the Abode﴾, he said: "They were purified by remembering the Abode of the Hereafter, so that they would work for it."

(p-1266) His words: ﴿And remember Our servant Job﴾ are coordinated with His words ﴿And remember Our servant David﴾ [Sad: 17]. "Job" is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān), and ﴿when he called out to his Lord﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from ("Our servant"). ﴿"Indeed, adversity has touched me, and Satan has afflicted me with hardship"﴾. The majority of readers recited with a fatḥa on the hamza (Anna), as a quotation of his words with which he called out to his Lord; had he not quoted them, it would have said: "that it had touched him." ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited it with a kasra, on the presumption of an implied verb of saying (al-qawl).

In the story of Job there is guidance for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to follow his example in patience through hardships.

The majority of readers recited ﴿bi-nuṣbin﴾ with a ḍamma on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād. It is said that it is the plural of naṣab (with two fatḥas), like asad and usud; and it is said that it is a dialectal form of al-naṣab, like rashad and rushd.

Abū Jaʿfar Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ, Shaybah, Ḥafṣ, and Nāfiʿ in one of the transmissions from him recited it with two ḍammas, and this reading is also reported from al-Ḥasan.

Abū Ḥaywah, Yaʿqūb, and Ḥafṣ in one transmission recited it with a fatḥa and a sukūn. All these readings have one meaning; the readings differ only according to differences of dialect.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: "Naṣab with two fatḥas means weariness and exhaustion; and in the rest of the readings it means evil and affliction." The meaning of "and torment" (ʿadhāb) is pain.

Qatādah and Muqātil said: "Naṣab refers to the body, and ʿadhāb to property." al-Naḥḥās said: "In it there is more to be said; that is what he said." The better course is to explain naṣab by its linguistic meaning, which is weariness and exhaustion, and to explain ʿadhāb by what truly fits the notion of torment, which is pain; and both refer to the body.

﴿Strike with your foot﴾: this is by way of an implied verb of saying, i.e., "We said to him: strike with your foot." Thus al-Kisāʾī said: "al-Rakḍ is pushing with the foot. It is said: he struck (rakaḍa) the animal with his foot, when he hit it with it."

al-Mubarrad said: "al-Rakḍ is moving." al-Aṣmaʿī said: "It is said: I made the animal strike (rakaḍtu al-dābbah), but one does not say: she struck (rakaḍat hiya), because rakḍ is only the rider moving his legs, and the animal has no action in that." Sībawayh related: "I made the animal strike (rakaḍtu al-dābbah), so she struck (fa-rakaḍat)," like "I set the bone, so it set (jabartu al-ʿaẓma fa-jabar)."

﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾: this too is part of the implied speech. "al-Mughtasal" is the water with which one bathes, and "al-sharāb" is the drink one drinks from it. It is also said that "al-mughtasal" is the place in which one bathes.

Qatādah said: "They are two springs in the land of Syria, in a land called al-Jābiyah. He bathed in one of them, and Allah removed the outward part of his disease; and he drank from the other, and Allah removed the inward part of his disease." al-Ḥasan said likewise.

Muqātil said: "A flowing spring gushed forth, and he bathed in it and came out healthy. Then another spring gushed forth, and he drank from it fresh, cool water."

There is an ellipsis in the speech; the estimate is: "So he struck with his foot, and a spring gushed forth; then We said to him: this is a cool bath, etc."

The attribution of touching to Satan, although it was Allah, glorified is He, who touched him with it, is either because when he acted on Satan's whisperings he was punished with that naṣab and ʿadhāb.

It has been said: he was impressed by the abundance of his wealth. It has been said: a wronged man sought his help and he did not help him. It has been said: he said that in the manner of good manners (adab). It has been said: he said that because Satan whispered to his followers, and they rejected him and expelled him from their homes. It has been said that what is meant by it is what Satan whispered to him during his illness and trial, of beautifying impatience and not bearing the calamity with patience. Other explanations have also been given.

His words: ﴿And We gave him his family﴾ are coordinated with an implied clause, as if it were said: "So he bathed and drank, and by that We removed from him the harm he had, and We gave him his family."

It is said: Allah revived them after He had caused them to die. It is said: He gathered them after their dispersal. It is said: He changed them to be like themselves, then increased him by a like number with them; and this is the meaning of His words: ﴿and a like number with them﴾. Thus they became as they had been before his trial. The accusative of His words: ﴿as a mercy from Us and a reminder for people of understanding﴾ is by way of the object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi): i.e., "We gave them to him for the sake of Our mercy toward him, and so that people of understanding might be reminded of his condition and endure hardships with patience as he did." This verse was already explained fully in Surah al-Anbiyāʾ, so we do not repeat it.

﴿And take in your hand a bundle﴾ is coordinated with "strike" (irkuḍ), or with "We gave him," or the estimate is: "And We said to him: and take in your hand a bundle." Al-ḍighth is a cluster of palm-fronds with their stalks; it is also said: it is a handful of mixed grass whose green and dry parts are together; and it is also said: a large bundle of twigs. The root of the word indicates gathering mixed things together.

al-Wāḥidī said: al-ḍighth is a handful of trees, grass, and stalks.

﴿Strike with it and do not break your oath﴾: i.e., strike with that bundle, and do not break your oath. al-ḥinth is sin, and it is also applied to doing what one swore to abandon. Job had sworn during his illness that he would strike his wife one hundred lashes.

The cause of this has been disputed. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab said: she had brought him more bread than she used to bring, and he feared she had embezzled, so he swore that he would strike her. Yaḥyā ibn Sallām and others said: Satan had seduced her to get Job to slaughter a lamb as an offering to him, for if he did that he would be healed; so he swore that he would strike her one hundred lashes if he recovered. It has also been said: she sold her forelock for two loaves when she found nothing else, and Job used to lean on her when he wished to stand up; so for this reason he swore that he would strike her. It has also been said: Iblīs came to her in the form of a physician, and she asked him to treat Job; he said: "I will treat him on condition that when he is healed he says: 'You healed me,' and I want no reward other than that." She said: "Yes." So she advised Job accordingly, and he swore that he would strike her.

The scholars have differed as to whether this ruling is specific to Job or general for all people, and whether one who has sworn is released from his oath by the same means.

al-Shāfiʿī said: if one swears that he will strike so-and-so one hundred lashes, or a beating, without saying "a severe beating" and without intending it in his heart, then a beating like the one mentioned in the verse suffices for him. Ibn al-Mundhir related this from him, and from Abū Thawr and the Companions of opinion (aṣḥāb al-raʾy).

ʿAṭāʾ said: it is specific to Job, and Ibn al-Qāsim related it from Mālik.

Then Allah, glorified is He, praised Job, saying: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ (p-1267), i.e., in the face of the trial with which We tested him, for he was tested with a severe illness in his body, and the loss of his property, his family, and his children, and he was patient. ﴿An excellent servant﴾, i.e., Job. ﴿Indeed he was one who turned back (awwāb)﴾, i.e., one who returns to Allah in seeking forgiveness and repentance.

﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob﴾: the majority read "ʿibādanā" in the plural. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ḥumayd, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Ibn Kathīr read "ʿabdanā" in the singular.

According to the majority's reading, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are explicative appositions; according to the other reading, Abraham is an explicative apposition, and what follows it is coordinated with "ʿabdanā," not with Abraham.

It may be said: since the intended meaning of "ʿabdanā" is the category, it is permissible to substitute the plural group for it.

It has also been said: Abraham and what follows him are a substitution (badal), or they are in the accusative by an implied "I mean" (aʿnī). The explicative apposition is the clearest, and the majority's reading is the most explicit; Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred it.

﴿Possessors of hands and sight﴾: al-Aydī is the plural of yad in the sense of strength and power. Qatādah said: "They were given strength in worship and victory in religion." al-Wāḥidī said: Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and the exegetes said likewise.

al-Naḥḥās said: As for al-abṣār (sight), there is agreement that it means insight in religion and knowledge. As for al-aydī (hands), its interpretation is disputed: the people of tafsir say it means strength in religion; and some say al-aydī is the plural of yad, meaning favor, i.e., they are possessors of favors, those upon whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestowed favor; and it has been said: they are possessors of favors upon people and of benevolence toward them, for they did good and sent forward good deeds. Ibn Jarīr preferred this.

The majority read "ulī al-aydī" with the ya' affirmed in al-aydī. Ibn Masʿūd, al-Aʿmash, al-Ḥasan, and ʿĪsā read al-ayd without the ya'; it is said its meaning is the same as the first reading, and the ya' was dropped because the kasra on the dal indicates it. It is also said: al-ayd means strength.

The clause ﴿Indeed We purified them with a pure quality, the remembrance of the Abode﴾ is a reason (taʿlīl) for what they were described with.

The majority read "bi-khāliṣatin" with tanwīn and without an annexation, taking it as a verbal noun in the sense of sincere devotion (al-ikhlāṣ), so that "dhikrā" is in the accusative governed by it; or in the sense of purity (al-khulūṣ), so that "dhikrā" is in the nominative governed by it; or "khāliṣah" is an active participle in its proper form, and "dhikrā" is a substitution for it, or an explanation of it, or by an implied "I mean," or in the nominative by an implied subject. "al-Dār" may be a direct object of "dhikrā," and it may be an adverbial complement, either by extension or by dropping the preposition. In every estimate, "khāliṣah" is an attribute of an omitted noun, and the bāʾ is causal, i.e., "by means of a pure quality."

Nāfiʿ, Shaybah, Abū Jaʿfar, and Hishām from Ibn ʿĀmir read "khāliṣah" annexed to "dhikrā," with the annexation being explanatory, because the pure quality may be remembrance or other than remembrance; or because "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun annexed to its object, with the agent omitted, i.e., "by their sincerely devoting the remembrance of the Abode"; or a verbal noun in the sense of purity annexed to its agent.

Mujāhid said: the meaning of the verse is: We chose them by mentioning the Hereafter, and so We purified them through its remembrance. Qatādah said: they used to call to the Hereafter and to Allah. al-Suddī said: they were purified by fear of the Hereafter.

al-Wāḥidī said: whoever reads with tanwīn in "khāliṣah," the meaning is: We made them sincere to Us, in that the remembrance of the Abode was purely theirs; "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun in the sense of purity, and "dhikrā" in the sense of remembrance, i.e., the remembrance of the Abode was purely theirs, namely that they remembered preparation for it and were detached from this world, which is characteristic of the prophets.

As for whoever annexes, the meaning is: We purified them by having the remembrance of the Abode purely theirs; "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun annexed to its agent, and "dhikrā" in this sense means the mention.

﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and the good﴾: al-iṣṭifāʾ is choosing; al-akhyār is the plural of khayyir, with shadda or without, as amwāt is the plural of mayyit, with shadda or without. The meaning: they are with Us among those chosen from the good of their kind.

﴿And remember Ismāʿīl﴾: it has been said that the reason for singling him out for mention after his father, his brother, and his nephew is to indicate that he was steadfast in patience, which is the purpose of the reminder here. ﴿And al-Yasaʿ and Dhū al-Kifl﴾: al-Yasaʿ has already been mentioned, and what is said about him was discussed in al-Anʿām; Dhū al-Kifl has already been mentioned, and what is said about him was discussed in Surah al-Anbiyāʾ. The purpose of mentioning these is that they were among those prophets who were patient and bore hardships in the religion of Allah.

Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to mention them so that he might follow their path in patience. ﴿And all of them are among the good ones﴾, i.e., those whom Allah chose for His prophethood and selected from His creation.

﴿This is a remembrance﴾: the demonstrative refers to what was mentioned before of their attributes, i.e., this is a fine remembrance in this world and a nobility by which they will be remembered forever. ﴿And indeed for the God-fearing there is a good return﴾, i.e., along with this fine remembrance they have a good return in the Hereafter. al-Maʾāb is the place of return, and the meaning is that in the Hereafter they will return to Allah's forgiveness, His good pleasure, and the bliss of His Garden.

Then He described the excellence of the final return, saying: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. The majority of reciters read *jannāti* in the accusative case as a substitute (*badal*) for *ḥusna maʾāb* ("the excellent place of return"). This holds whether *jannāti ʿadnin* is definite or indefinite, because a definite noun may substitute for an indefinite one and vice versa. It is also permissible for *jannāti* to be an explicative apposition (*ʿatf bayān*) if it is indefinite, but this is not permissible if it is definite according to the view of the majority of grammarians, although some have permitted it. The accusative of *jannāti* may also be due to an implied verb. *ʿAdn* originally means "staying," as in the expression ʿadana bi-l-makān, "he resided in the place." It is also said to be the name of a palace in Paradise. It was also read with *jannātu* in the nominative, as the subject (*mubtadaʾ*) whose predicate is *mufattaḥatan* ("opened"), or as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning "they are Gardens of Eden." The phrase ﴿with the gates opened for them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to *jannāt*, and its governing element is the meaning of the verb contained in *al-muttaqīn* ("the God-conscious"). *Al-abwāb* ("the gates") is raised as the subject of the passive participle, as in His saying: ﴿and its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. The link between the circumstantial clause and its referent is a pronoun that is understood, meaning "from them," or the definite article *al-*, which stands in place of the pronoun, since the original form is *abwābuhā* ("its gates").

It is also said that *al-abwāb* is raised as a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *mufattaḥatun*, which refers back to *jannāt*. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī held this view, meaning: "opened are the gates themselves."

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning is "its gates are opened," and the Arabs use the definite article as a substitute for the possessive pronoun. Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is "the gates are opened for them from within them." Al-Ḥasan said: it is said to the gates, "Open!" and they open, "Close!" and they close. It is also said that the angels open the gates for them.

The accusative of ﴿reclining therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *lahum* ("for them"), and its governing element is *mufattaḥatan*. It is also said that it is a circumstantial clause from *yadʿūna* ("they call for"), placed before its governing element, meaning: "they call for [fruit] in the Gardens, while reclining therein." ﴿Therein, they call for abundant fruit﴾, meaning, for fruits of many kinds and abundance, and drink in abundance. *Kathīran* ("abundant") was omitted from the second part because the first indicates it. If *muttakiʾīna* is taken as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *lahum*, governed by *mufattaḥatan*, then the clause *yadʿūna* is a resumptive clause (*mustaʾnafa*) explaining their state.

It is also said that *yadʿūna* is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *muttakiʾīna*.

﴿And with them are those restraining their glances, equals in age﴾, meaning, restraining their glances to their husbands, not looking at anyone else. Its explanation has already been given in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt.

*Atrāb* means those who are of the same age, or who are equal in beauty.

Mujāhid said: the meaning of *atrāb* is that they are companions who do not hate or envy one another. It is also said that *atrāban* is for the husbands. *Atrāb* is the plural of *tirb*, and its derivation is from *turāb* ("dust"), because they reach [adulthood] at the same time, owing to the unity of their birth.

﴿This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning﴾, meaning, this is the reward you were promised for the sake of the Day of Reckoning, since the reckoning is the cause for reaching the reward. Or the meaning is "on the Day of Reckoning."

The majority read *mā tūʿadūna* with the second person (*tāʾ fawqiyya*), as address. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Yaʿqūb read it with the third person (*yāʾ taḥtiyya*), as report. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this reading because of His saying: ﴿and indeed for the God-conscious﴾, since that is a report.

﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾, meaning: indeed this which has been mentioned of blessings and honors is Our provision which We have bestowed upon you, ﴿which has no end﴾, meaning, no cessation, and it never perishes. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿a gift never cut off﴾ [Hūd: 108]. So the blessings of Paradise never cease for its people.

Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Satan ascended to the heaven and said: "O Lord, give me power over Ayyūb." God said: "I have given you power over his wealth and his children, but I have not given you power over his body." So he descended and gathered his troops, and said to them: "I have been given power over Ayyūb, so show me your power." They became fire, then became water. While they were in the east, they suddenly were in the west, and while they were in the west, they suddenly were in the east.

He sent a group of them to his crops, a group to his family, a group to his cattle, and a group to his sheep, and said: "He will not be protected from you except by what is good." So they brought him calamities one upon another. The owner of the crops came and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent fire upon your crops, and it burned them?" Then came the owner of the camels and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your camels, and it took them away?" Then came the owner of the cattle and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your cattle, and it took them away?" Then came the owner of the sheep and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your sheep, and it took them away?" And he was alone with his sons, so he gathered them in the house of the eldest. While they were eating and drinking, a wind blew and seized the corners of the house and dropped it upon them. Then Satan came to Ayyūb in the form of a boy with two earrings in his ears, and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord gathered your sons in the house of the eldest, and while they were eating and drinking, a wind blew upon them and seized the corners of the house and dropped it upon them? If only you had seen them when their blood and flesh mixed with their food and drink!" Ayyūb said to him: "Where were you?" He said: "I was with them." He asked: "How did you escape?" He said: "I escaped." Ayyūb said: "You are Satan." Then Ayyūb said: "Today I am like the day my mother bore me." He stood, shaved his head, and began to pray. Iblīs let out a cry that was heard by the people of the heavens and the people of the earth. Then he ascended to the heaven and said: "O Lord, he has been protected, so give me power over him, for I cannot overcome him except by Your authority." He said: "I have given you power over his body, but I have not given you power over his heart." So he descended and blew beneath his foot a blast that ulcerated everything between his two feet up to his head, and it became one sore. He was thrown onto the ash until the membrane of his heart appeared. His wife would go about tending him until she said to him: "Do you not see, O Ayyūb, that by God, hardship and poverty have come upon me such that if I sold my hair for a loaf of bread to feed you...? So pray to God that He may heal you and relieve you." He said: "Woe to you! We were in bliss for seventy years, so be patient until we are in adversity for seventy years." He was in affliction for seven years, and he supplicated. Then Jibrīl came one day, and struck with his hand, then said: "Stand up," so he stood, and he moved him from his place, and said: "Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and drink." He struck with his foot, and a spring gushed forth. He said: "Bathe," and he bathed in it. Then he came again and said: "Strike with your foot," and another spring gushed forth, and he said to him: "Drink from it." This is His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot; here is a cool bath and drink﴾. And God clothed him in a garment from Paradise. Ayyūb withdrew and sat in a corner. His wife came and did not recognize him, and said: "O servant of God, where is the afflicted man who was here? Perhaps the dogs or wolves have taken him." She kept speaking with him for a while. He said: "Woe to you, I am Ayyūb. God has restored my body to me, and restored to me my wealth and my children in person, and the like of them with them, and rained upon him locusts of gold." He began taking the locusts in his hand, then placing them in his garment, and spreading his cloak and taking them and putting them in it. God revealed to him: "O Ayyūb, have you not had enough?" He said: "O Lord, who could have enough of Your bounty and mercy?"

In this report there is a severe strangeness, for God—glorified is He—does not give Satan power over one of His prophets to this extent of great domination.

Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd*, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Iblīs sat on the road and took a chest to treat people. Ayyūb's wife said: "O servant of God, there is here a man afflicted in such-and-such a way; would you treat him?" He said: "Yes, on condition that if I cure him, he says: 'You cured me,' and I want no reward from him other than this." She came to Ayyūb and told him about it. He said: "Woe to you, that is Satan. By God, if God cures me, I will flog you one hundred lashes." When God healed him, He commanded him to take a bundle and strike her with it. He took a palm-frond with one hundred stalks and struck her with one blow.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿Take in your hand a bundle﴾, that it is the *asal* (a reed/thin branch). Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him: "*al-ḍighth* is a handful of green pasture." Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated from him: "*al-ḍighth* is a bundle."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated, through the chain of Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, who said: "A slave girl among the Banū Sāʿida conceived from fornication, and she was asked: 'By whom are you pregnant?' She said: 'By so-and-so the paralyzed man.' The paralyzed man was asked, and he said: 'She has told the truth.' This was brought to the Messenger of God—may God bless him and his family and grant him peace—and he said: 'Take a cluster with one hundred stalks and strike her with it, one blow.'"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated something similar through another chain, from Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, from Saʿīd ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda. Al-Ṭabarānī narrated something similar from Sahl ibn Saʿd.

Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "Ayyūb is the chief of the patient on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn Masʿūd concerning His saying: ﴿possessors of strength﴾, that he said: "the strength in worship, and the insight," and he said: "understanding of the religion."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him: ﴿possessors of strength﴾, he said: "blessing."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure [quality]: remembrance of the Abode﴾, he said: "They were purified by remembering the Abode of the Hereafter, so that they would work for it."

(p-1266) His words: ﴿And remember Our servant Job﴾ are coordinated with His words ﴿And remember Our servant David﴾ [Sad: 17]. "Job" is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān), and ﴿when he called out to his Lord﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from ("Our servant"). ﴿"Indeed, adversity has touched me, and Satan has afflicted me with hardship"﴾. The majority of readers recited with a fatḥa on the hamza (Anna), as a quotation of his words with which he called out to his Lord; had he not quoted them, it would have said: "that it had touched him." ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited it with a kasra, on the presumption of an implied verb of saying (al-qawl).

In the story of Job there is guidance for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to follow his example in patience through hardships.

The majority of readers recited ﴿bi-nuṣbin﴾ with a ḍamma on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād. It is said that it is the plural of naṣab (with two fatḥas), like asad and usud; and it is said that it is a dialectal form of al-naṣab, like rashad and rushd.

Abū Jaʿfar Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ, Shaybah, Ḥafṣ, and Nāfiʿ in one of the transmissions from him recited it with two ḍammas, and this reading is also reported from al-Ḥasan.

Abū Ḥaywah, Yaʿqūb, and Ḥafṣ in one transmission recited it with a fatḥa and a sukūn. All these readings have one meaning; the readings differ only according to differences of dialect.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: "Naṣab with two fatḥas means weariness and exhaustion; and in the rest of the readings it means evil and affliction." The meaning of "and torment" (ʿadhāb) is pain.

Qatādah and Muqātil said: "Naṣab refers to the body, and ʿadhāb to property." al-Naḥḥās said: "In it there is more to be said; that is what he said." The better course is to explain naṣab by its linguistic meaning, which is weariness and exhaustion, and to explain ʿadhāb by what truly fits the notion of torment, which is pain; and both refer to the body.

﴿Strike with your foot﴾: this is by way of an implied verb of saying, i.e., "We said to him: strike with your foot." Thus al-Kisāʾī said: "al-Rakḍ is pushing with the foot. It is said: he struck (rakaḍa) the animal with his foot, when he hit it with it."

al-Mubarrad said: "al-Rakḍ is moving." al-Aṣmaʿī said: "It is said: I made the animal strike (rakaḍtu al-dābbah), but one does not say: she struck (rakaḍat hiya), because rakḍ is only the rider moving his legs, and the animal has no action in that." Sībawayh related: "I made the animal strike (rakaḍtu al-dābbah), so she struck (fa-rakaḍat)," like "I set the bone, so it set (jabartu al-ʿaẓma fa-jabar)."

﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾: this too is part of the implied speech. "al-Mughtasal" is the water with which one bathes, and "al-sharāb" is the drink one drinks from it. It is also said that "al-mughtasal" is the place in which one bathes.

Qatādah said: "They are two springs in the land of Syria, in a land called al-Jābiyah. He bathed in one of them, and Allah removed the outward part of his disease; and he drank from the other, and Allah removed the inward part of his disease." al-Ḥasan said likewise.

Muqātil said: "A flowing spring gushed forth, and he bathed in it and came out healthy. Then another spring gushed forth, and he drank from it fresh, cool water."

There is an ellipsis in the speech; the estimate is: "So he struck with his foot, and a spring gushed forth; then We said to him: this is a cool bath, etc."

The attribution of touching to Satan, although it was Allah, glorified is He, who touched him with it, is either because when he acted on Satan's whisperings he was punished with that naṣab and ʿadhāb.

It has been said: he was impressed by the abundance of his wealth. It has been said: a wronged man sought his help and he did not help him. It has been said: he said that in the manner of good manners (adab). It has been said: he said that because Satan whispered to his followers, and they rejected him and expelled him from their homes. It has been said that what is meant by it is what Satan whispered to him during his illness and trial, of beautifying impatience and not bearing the calamity with patience. Other explanations have also been given.

His words: ﴿And We gave him his family﴾ are coordinated with an implied clause, as if it were said: "So he bathed and drank, and by that We removed from him the harm he had, and We gave him his family."

It is said: Allah revived them after He had caused them to die. It is said: He gathered them after their dispersal. It is said: He changed them to be like themselves, then increased him by a like number with them; and this is the meaning of His words: ﴿and a like number with them﴾. Thus they became as they had been before his trial. The accusative of His words: ﴿as a mercy from Us and a reminder for people of understanding﴾ is by way of the object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi): i.e., "We gave them to him for the sake of Our mercy toward him, and so that people of understanding might be reminded of his condition and endure hardships with patience as he did." This verse was already explained fully in Surah al-Anbiyāʾ, so we do not repeat it.

﴿And take in your hand a bundle﴾ is coordinated with "strike" (irkuḍ), or with "We gave him," or the estimate is: "And We said to him: and take in your hand a bundle." Al-ḍighth is a cluster of palm-fronds with their stalks; it is also said: it is a handful of mixed grass whose green and dry parts are together; and it is also said: a large bundle of twigs. The root of the word indicates gathering mixed things together.

al-Wāḥidī said: al-ḍighth is a handful of trees, grass, and stalks.

﴿Strike with it and do not break your oath﴾: i.e., strike with that bundle, and do not break your oath. al-ḥinth is sin, and it is also applied to doing what one swore to abandon. Job had sworn during his illness that he would strike his wife one hundred lashes.

The cause of this has been disputed. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab said: she had brought him more bread than she used to bring, and he feared she had embezzled, so he swore that he would strike her. Yaḥyā ibn Sallām and others said: Satan had seduced her to get Job to slaughter a lamb as an offering to him, for if he did that he would be healed; so he swore that he would strike her one hundred lashes if he recovered. It has also been said: she sold her forelock for two loaves when she found nothing else, and Job used to lean on her when he wished to stand up; so for this reason he swore that he would strike her. It has also been said: Iblīs came to her in the form of a physician, and she asked him to treat Job; he said: "I will treat him on condition that when he is healed he says: 'You healed me,' and I want no reward other than that." She said: "Yes." So she advised Job accordingly, and he swore that he would strike her.

The scholars have differed as to whether this ruling is specific to Job or general for all people, and whether one who has sworn is released from his oath by the same means.

al-Shāfiʿī said: if one swears that he will strike so-and-so one hundred lashes, or a beating, without saying "a severe beating" and without intending it in his heart, then a beating like the one mentioned in the verse suffices for him. Ibn al-Mundhir related this from him, and from Abū Thawr and the Companions of opinion (aṣḥāb al-raʾy).

ʿAṭāʾ said: it is specific to Job, and Ibn al-Qāsim related it from Mālik.

Then Allah, glorified is He, praised Job, saying: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ (p-1267), i.e., in the face of the trial with which We tested him, for he was tested with a severe illness in his body, and the loss of his property, his family, and his children, and he was patient. ﴿An excellent servant﴾, i.e., Job. ﴿Indeed he was one who turned back (awwāb)﴾, i.e., one who returns to Allah in seeking forgiveness and repentance.

﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob﴾: the majority read "ʿibādanā" in the plural. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ḥumayd, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Ibn Kathīr read "ʿabdanā" in the singular.

According to the majority's reading, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are explicative appositions; according to the other reading, Abraham is an explicative apposition, and what follows it is coordinated with "ʿabdanā," not with Abraham.

It may be said: since the intended meaning of "ʿabdanā" is the category, it is permissible to substitute the plural group for it.

It has also been said: Abraham and what follows him are a substitution (badal), or they are in the accusative by an implied "I mean" (aʿnī). The explicative apposition is the clearest, and the majority's reading is the most explicit; Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred it.

﴿Possessors of hands and sight﴾: al-Aydī is the plural of yad in the sense of strength and power. Qatādah said: "They were given strength in worship and victory in religion." al-Wāḥidī said: Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and the exegetes said likewise.

al-Naḥḥās said: As for al-abṣār (sight), there is agreement that it means insight in religion and knowledge. As for al-aydī (hands), its interpretation is disputed: the people of tafsir say it means strength in religion; and some say al-aydī is the plural of yad, meaning favor, i.e., they are possessors of favors, those upon whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestowed favor; and it has been said: they are possessors of favors upon people and of benevolence toward them, for they did good and sent forward good deeds. Ibn Jarīr preferred this.

The majority read "ulī al-aydī" with the ya' affirmed in al-aydī. Ibn Masʿūd, al-Aʿmash, al-Ḥasan, and ʿĪsā read al-ayd without the ya'; it is said its meaning is the same as the first reading, and the ya' was dropped because the kasra on the dal indicates it. It is also said: al-ayd means strength.

The clause ﴿Indeed We purified them with a pure quality, the remembrance of the Abode﴾ is a reason (taʿlīl) for what they were described with.

The majority read "bi-khāliṣatin" with tanwīn and without an annexation, taking it as a verbal noun in the sense of sincere devotion (al-ikhlāṣ), so that "dhikrā" is in the accusative governed by it; or in the sense of purity (al-khulūṣ), so that "dhikrā" is in the nominative governed by it; or "khāliṣah" is an active participle in its proper form, and "dhikrā" is a substitution for it, or an explanation of it, or by an implied "I mean," or in the nominative by an implied subject. "al-Dār" may be a direct object of "dhikrā," and it may be an adverbial complement, either by extension or by dropping the preposition. In every estimate, "khāliṣah" is an attribute of an omitted noun, and the bāʾ is causal, i.e., "by means of a pure quality."

Nāfiʿ, Shaybah, Abū Jaʿfar, and Hishām from Ibn ʿĀmir read "khāliṣah" annexed to "dhikrā," with the annexation being explanatory, because the pure quality may be remembrance or other than remembrance; or because "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun annexed to its object, with the agent omitted, i.e., "by their sincerely devoting the remembrance of the Abode"; or a verbal noun in the sense of purity annexed to its agent.

Mujāhid said: the meaning of the verse is: We chose them by mentioning the Hereafter, and so We purified them through its remembrance. Qatādah said: they used to call to the Hereafter and to Allah. al-Suddī said: they were purified by fear of the Hereafter.

al-Wāḥidī said: whoever reads with tanwīn in "khāliṣah," the meaning is: We made them sincere to Us, in that the remembrance of the Abode was purely theirs; "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun in the sense of purity, and "dhikrā" in the sense of remembrance, i.e., the remembrance of the Abode was purely theirs, namely that they remembered preparation for it and were detached from this world, which is characteristic of the prophets.

As for whoever annexes, the meaning is: We purified them by having the remembrance of the Abode purely theirs; "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun annexed to its agent, and "dhikrā" in this sense means the mention.

﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and the good﴾: al-iṣṭifāʾ is choosing; al-akhyār is the plural of khayyir, with shadda or without, as amwāt is the plural of mayyit, with shadda or without. The meaning: they are with Us among those chosen from the good of their kind.

﴿And remember Ismāʿīl﴾: it has been said that the reason for singling him out for mention after his father, his brother, and his nephew is to indicate that he was steadfast in patience, which is the purpose of the reminder here. ﴿And al-Yasaʿ and Dhū al-Kifl﴾: al-Yasaʿ has already been mentioned, and what is said about him was discussed in al-Anʿām; Dhū al-Kifl has already been mentioned, and what is said about him was discussed in Surah al-Anbiyāʾ. The purpose of mentioning these is that they were among those prophets who were patient and bore hardships in the religion of Allah.

Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to mention them so that he might follow their path in patience. ﴿And all of them are among the good ones﴾, i.e., those whom Allah chose for His prophethood and selected from His creation.

﴿This is a remembrance﴾: the demonstrative refers to what was mentioned before of their attributes, i.e., this is a fine remembrance in this world and a nobility by which they will be remembered forever. ﴿And indeed for the God-fearing there is a good return﴾, i.e., along with this fine remembrance they have a good return in the Hereafter. al-Maʾāb is the place of return, and the meaning is that in the Hereafter they will return to Allah's forgiveness, His good pleasure, and the bliss of His Garden.

Then He described the excellence of the final return, saying: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. The majority of reciters read *jannāti* in the accusative case as a substitute (*badal*) for *ḥusna maʾāb* ("the excellent place of return"). This holds whether *jannāti ʿadnin* is definite or indefinite, because a definite noun may substitute for an indefinite one and vice versa. It is also permissible for *jannāti* to be an explicative apposition (*ʿatf bayān*) if it is indefinite, but this is not permissible if it is definite according to the view of the majority of grammarians, although some have permitted it. The accusative of *jannāti* may also be due to an implied verb. *ʿAdn* originally means "staying," as in the expression ʿadana bi-l-makān, "he resided in the place." It is also said to be the name of a palace in Paradise. It was also read with *jannātu* in the nominative, as the subject (*mubtadaʾ*) whose predicate is *mufattaḥatan* ("opened"), or as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning "they are Gardens of Eden." The phrase ﴿with the gates opened for them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to *jannāt*, and its governing element is the meaning of the verb contained in *al-muttaqīn* ("the God-conscious"). *Al-abwāb* ("the gates") is raised as the subject of the passive participle, as in His saying: ﴿and its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. The link between the circumstantial clause and its referent is a pronoun that is understood, meaning "from them," or the definite article *al-*, which stands in place of the pronoun, since the original form is *abwābuhā* ("its gates").

It is also said that *al-abwāb* is raised as a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *mufattaḥatun*, which refers back to *jannāt*. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī held this view, meaning: "opened are the gates themselves."

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning is "its gates are opened," and the Arabs use the definite article as a substitute for the possessive pronoun. Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is "the gates are opened for them from within them." Al-Ḥasan said: it is said to the gates, "Open!" and they open, "Close!" and they close. It is also said that the angels open the gates for them.

The accusative of ﴿reclining therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *lahum* ("for them"), and its governing element is *mufattaḥatan*. It is also said that it is a circumstantial clause from *yadʿūna* ("they call for"), placed before its governing element, meaning: "they call for [fruit] in the Gardens, while reclining therein." ﴿Therein, they call for abundant fruit﴾, meaning, for fruits of many kinds and abundance, and drink in abundance. *Kathīran* ("abundant") was omitted from the second part because the first indicates it. If *muttakiʾīna* is taken as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *lahum*, governed by *mufattaḥatan*, then the clause *yadʿūna* is a resumptive clause (*mustaʾnafa*) explaining their state.

It is also said that *yadʿūna* is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *muttakiʾīna*.

﴿And with them are those restraining their glances, equals in age﴾, meaning, restraining their glances to their husbands, not looking at anyone else. Its explanation has already been given in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt.

*Atrāb* means those who are of the same age, or who are equal in beauty.

Mujāhid said: the meaning of *atrāb* is that they are companions who do not hate or envy one another. It is also said that *atrāban* is for the husbands. *Atrāb* is the plural of *tirb*, and its derivation is from *turāb* ("dust"), because they reach [adulthood] at the same time, owing to the unity of their birth.

﴿This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning﴾, meaning, this is the reward you were promised for the sake of the Day of Reckoning, since the reckoning is the cause for reaching the reward. Or the meaning is "on the Day of Reckoning."

The majority read *mā tūʿadūna* with the second person (*tāʾ fawqiyya*), as address. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Yaʿqūb read it with the third person (*yāʾ taḥtiyya*), as report. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred this reading because of His saying: ﴿and indeed for the God-conscious﴾, since that is a report.

﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾, meaning: indeed this which has been mentioned of blessings and honors is Our provision which We have bestowed upon you, ﴿which has no end﴾, meaning, no cessation, and it never perishes. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿a gift never cut off﴾ [Hūd: 108]. So the blessings of Paradise never cease for its people.

Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Satan ascended to the heaven and said: "O Lord, give me power over Ayyūb." God said: "I have given you power over his wealth and his children, but I have not given you power over his body." So he descended and gathered his troops, and said to them: "I have been given power over Ayyūb, so show me your power." They became fire, then became water. While they were in the east, they suddenly were in the west, and while they were in the west, they suddenly were in the east.

He sent a group of them to his crops, a group to his family, a group to his cattle, and a group to his sheep, and said: "He will not be protected from you except by what is good." So they brought him calamities one upon another. The owner of the crops came and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent fire upon your crops, and it burned them?" Then came the owner of the camels and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your camels, and it took them away?" Then came the owner of the cattle and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your cattle, and it took them away?" Then came the owner of the sheep and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord sent an enemy upon your sheep, and it took them away?" And he was alone with his sons, so he gathered them in the house of the eldest. While they were eating and drinking, a wind blew and seized the corners of the house and dropped it upon them. Then Satan came to Ayyūb in the form of a boy with two earrings in his ears, and said: "O Ayyūb, did you not see that your Lord gathered your sons in the house of the eldest, and while they were eating and drinking, a wind blew upon them and seized the corners of the house and dropped it upon them? If only you had seen them when their blood and flesh mixed with their food and drink!" Ayyūb said to him: "Where were you?" He said: "I was with them." He asked: "How did you escape?" He said: "I escaped." Ayyūb said: "You are Satan." Then Ayyūb said: "Today I am like the day my mother bore me." He stood, shaved his head, and began to pray. Iblīs let out a cry that was heard by the people of the heavens and the people of the earth. Then he ascended to the heaven and said: "O Lord, he has been protected, so give me power over him, for I cannot overcome him except by Your authority." He said: "I have given you power over his body, but I have not given you power over his heart." So he descended and blew beneath his foot a blast that ulcerated everything between his two feet up to his head, and it became one sore. He was thrown onto the ash until the membrane of his heart appeared. His wife would go about tending him until she said to him: "Do you not see, O Ayyūb, that by God, hardship and poverty have come upon me such that if I sold my hair for a loaf of bread to feed you...? So pray to God that He may heal you and relieve you." He said: "Woe to you! We were in bliss for seventy years, so be patient until we are in adversity for seventy years." He was in affliction for seven years, and he supplicated. Then Jibrīl came one day, and struck with his hand, then said: "Stand up," so he stood, and he moved him from his place, and said: "Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and drink." He struck with his foot, and a spring gushed forth. He said: "Bathe," and he bathed in it. Then he came again and said: "Strike with your foot," and another spring gushed forth, and he said to him: "Drink from it." This is His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot; here is a cool bath and drink﴾. And God clothed him in a garment from Paradise. Ayyūb withdrew and sat in a corner. His wife came and did not recognize him, and said: "O servant of God, where is the afflicted man who was here? Perhaps the dogs or wolves have taken him." She kept speaking with him for a while. He said: "Woe to you, I am Ayyūb. God has restored my body to me, and restored to me my wealth and my children in person, and the like of them with them, and rained upon him locusts of gold." He began taking the locusts in his hand, then placing them in his garment, and spreading his cloak and taking them and putting them in it. God revealed to him: "O Ayyūb, have you not had enough?" He said: "O Lord, who could have enough of Your bounty and mercy?"

In this report there is a severe strangeness, for God—glorified is He—does not give Satan power over one of His prophets to this extent of great domination.

Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd*, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Iblīs sat on the road and took a chest to treat people. Ayyūb's wife said: "O servant of God, there is here a man afflicted in such-and-such a way; would you treat him?" He said: "Yes, on condition that if I cure him, he says: 'You cured me,' and I want no reward from him other than this." She came to Ayyūb and told him about it. He said: "Woe to you, that is Satan. By God, if God cures me, I will flog you one hundred lashes." When God healed him, He commanded him to take a bundle and strike her with it. He took a palm-frond with one hundred stalks and struck her with one blow.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿Take in your hand a bundle﴾, that it is the *asal* (a reed/thin branch). Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him: "*al-ḍighth* is a handful of green pasture." Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated from him: "*al-ḍighth* is a bundle."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated, through the chain of Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, who said: "A slave girl among the Banū Sāʿida conceived from fornication, and she was asked: 'By whom are you pregnant?' She said: 'By so-and-so the paralyzed man.' The paralyzed man was asked, and he said: 'She has told the truth.' This was brought to the Messenger of God—may God bless him and his family and grant him peace—and he said: 'Take a cluster with one hundred stalks and strike her with it, one blow.'"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated something similar through another chain, from Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, from Saʿīd ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda. Al-Ṭabarānī narrated something similar from Sahl ibn Saʿd.

Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "Ayyūb is the chief of the patient on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn Masʿūd concerning His saying: ﴿possessors of strength﴾, that he said: "the strength in worship, and the insight," and he said: "understanding of the religion."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him: ﴿possessors of strength﴾, he said: "blessing."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure [quality]: remembrance of the Abode﴾, he said: "They were purified by remembering the Abode of the Hereafter, so that they would work for it."

(p-1266) His words: ﴿And remember Our servant Job﴾ are coordinated with His words ﴿And remember Our servant David﴾ [Sad: 17]. "Job" is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān), and ﴿when he called out to his Lord﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from ("Our servant"). ﴿"Indeed, adversity has touched me, and Satan has afflicted me with hardship"﴾. The majority of readers recited with a fatḥa on the hamza (Anna), as a quotation of his words with which he called out to his Lord; had he not quoted them, it would have said: "that it had touched him." ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited it with a kasra, on the presumption of an implied verb of saying (al-qawl).

In the story of Job there is guidance for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to follow his example in patience through hardships.

The majority of readers recited ﴿bi-nuṣbin﴾ with a ḍamma on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād. It is said that it is the plural of naṣab (with two fatḥas), like asad and usud; and it is said that it is a dialectal form of al-naṣab, like rashad and rushd.

Abū Jaʿfar Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ, Shaybah, Ḥafṣ, and Nāfiʿ in one of the transmissions from him recited it with two ḍammas, and this reading is also reported from al-Ḥasan.

Abū Ḥaywah, Yaʿqūb, and Ḥafṣ in one transmission recited it with a fatḥa and a sukūn. All these readings have one meaning; the readings differ only according to differences of dialect.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: "Naṣab with two fatḥas means weariness and exhaustion; and in the rest of the readings it means evil and affliction." The meaning of "and torment" (ʿadhāb) is pain.

Qatādah and Muqātil said: "Naṣab refers to the body, and ʿadhāb to property." al-Naḥḥās said: "In it there is more to be said; that is what he said." The better course is to explain naṣab by its linguistic meaning, which is weariness and exhaustion, and to explain ʿadhāb by what truly fits the notion of torment, which is pain; and both refer to the body.

﴿Strike with your foot﴾: this is by way of an implied verb of saying, i.e., "We said to him: strike with your foot." Thus al-Kisāʾī said: "al-Rakḍ is pushing with the foot. It is said: he struck (rakaḍa) the animal with his foot, when he hit it with it."

al-Mubarrad said: "al-Rakḍ is moving." al-Aṣmaʿī said: "It is said: I made the animal strike (rakaḍtu al-dābbah), but one does not say: she struck (rakaḍat hiya), because rakḍ is only the rider moving his legs, and the animal has no action in that." Sībawayh related: "I made the animal strike (rakaḍtu al-dābbah), so she struck (fa-rakaḍat)," like "I set the bone, so it set (jabartu al-ʿaẓma fa-jabar)."

﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾: this too is part of the implied speech. "al-Mughtasal" is the water with which one bathes, and "al-sharāb" is the drink one drinks from it. It is also said that "al-mughtasal" is the place in which one bathes.

Qatādah said: "They are two springs in the land of Syria, in a land called al-Jābiyah. He bathed in one of them, and Allah removed the outward part of his disease; and he drank from the other, and Allah removed the inward part of his disease." al-Ḥasan said likewise.

Muqātil said: "A flowing spring gushed forth, and he bathed in it and came out healthy. Then another spring gushed forth, and he drank from it fresh, cool water."

There is an ellipsis in the speech; the estimate is: "So he struck with his foot, and a spring gushed forth; then We said to him: this is a cool bath, etc."

The attribution of touching to Satan, although it was Allah, glorified is He, who touched him with it, is either because when he acted on Satan's whisperings he was punished with that naṣab and ʿadhāb.

It has been said: he was impressed by the abundance of his wealth. It has been said: a wronged man sought his help and he did not help him. It has been said: he said that in the manner of good manners (adab). It has been said: he said that because Satan whispered to his followers, and they rejected him and expelled him from their homes. It has been said that what is meant by it is what Satan whispered to him during his illness and trial, of beautifying impatience and not bearing the calamity with patience. Other explanations have also been given.

His words: ﴿And We gave him his family﴾ are coordinated with an implied clause, as if it were said: "So he bathed and drank, and by that We removed from him the harm he had, and We gave him his family."

It is said: Allah revived them after He had caused them to die. It is said: He gathered them after their dispersal. It is said: He changed them to be like themselves, then increased him by a like number with them; and this is the meaning of His words: ﴿and a like number with them﴾. Thus they became as they had been before his trial. The accusative of His words: ﴿as a mercy from Us and a reminder for people of understanding﴾ is by way of the object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi): i.e., "We gave them to him for the sake of Our mercy toward him, and so that people of understanding might be reminded of his condition and endure hardships with patience as he did." This verse was already explained fully in Surah al-Anbiyāʾ, so we do not repeat it.

﴿And take in your hand a bundle﴾ is coordinated with "strike" (irkuḍ), or with "We gave him," or the estimate is: "And We said to him: and take in your hand a bundle." Al-ḍighth is a cluster of palm-fronds with their stalks; it is also said: it is a handful of mixed grass whose green and dry parts are together; and it is also said: a large bundle of twigs. The root of the word indicates gathering mixed things together.

al-Wāḥidī said: al-ḍighth is a handful of trees, grass, and stalks.

﴿Strike with it and do not break your oath﴾: i.e., strike with that bundle, and do not break your oath. al-ḥinth is sin, and it is also applied to doing what one swore to abandon. Job had sworn during his illness that he would strike his wife one hundred lashes.

The cause of this has been disputed. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab said: she had brought him more bread than she used to bring, and he feared she had embezzled, so he swore that he would strike her. Yaḥyā ibn Sallām and others said: Satan had seduced her to get Job to slaughter a lamb as an offering to him, for if he did that he would be healed; so he swore that he would strike her one hundred lashes if he recovered. It has also been said: she sold her forelock for two loaves when she found nothing else, and Job used to lean on her when he wished to stand up; so for this reason he swore that he would strike her. It has also been said: Iblīs came to her in the form of a physician, and she asked him to treat Job; he said: "I will treat him on condition that when he is healed he says: 'You healed me,' and I want no reward other than that." She said: "Yes." So she advised Job accordingly, and he swore that he would strike her.

The scholars have differed as to whether this ruling is specific to Job or general for all people, and whether one who has sworn is released from his oath by the same means.

al-Shāfiʿī said: if one swears that he will strike so-and-so one hundred lashes, or a beating, without saying "a severe beating" and without intending it in his heart, then a beating like the one mentioned in the verse suffices for him. Ibn al-Mundhir related this from him, and from Abū Thawr and the Companions of opinion (aṣḥāb al-raʾy).

ʿAṭāʾ said: it is specific to Job, and Ibn al-Qāsim related it from Mālik.

Then Allah, glorified is He, praised Job, saying: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ (p-1267), i.e., in the face of the trial with which We tested him, for he was tested with a severe illness in his body, and the loss of his property, his family, and his children, and he was patient. ﴿An excellent servant﴾, i.e., Job. ﴿Indeed he was one who turned back (awwāb)﴾, i.e., one who returns to Allah in seeking forgiveness and repentance.

﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob﴾: the majority read "ʿibādanā" in the plural. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ḥumayd, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Ibn Kathīr read "ʿabdanā" in the singular.

According to the majority's reading, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are explicative appositions; according to the other reading, Abraham is an explicative apposition, and what follows it is coordinated with "ʿabdanā," not with Abraham.

It may be said: since the intended meaning of "ʿabdanā" is the category, it is permissible to substitute the plural group for it.

It has also been said: Abraham and what follows him are a substitution (badal), or they are in the accusative by an implied "I mean" (aʿnī). The explicative apposition is the clearest, and the majority's reading is the most explicit; Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred it.

﴿Possessors of hands and sight﴾: al-Aydī is the plural of yad in the sense of strength and power. Qatādah said: "They were given strength in worship and victory in religion." al-Wāḥidī said: Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and the exegetes said likewise.

al-Naḥḥās said: As for al-abṣār (sight), there is agreement that it means insight in religion and knowledge. As for al-aydī (hands), its interpretation is disputed: the people of tafsir say it means strength in religion; and some say al-aydī is the plural of yad, meaning favor, i.e., they are possessors of favors, those upon whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestowed favor; and it has been said: they are possessors of favors upon people and of benevolence toward them, for they did good and sent forward good deeds. Ibn Jarīr preferred this.

The majority read "ulī al-aydī" with the ya' affirmed in al-aydī. Ibn Masʿūd, al-Aʿmash, al-Ḥasan, and ʿĪsā read al-ayd without the ya'; it is said its meaning is the same as the first reading, and the ya' was dropped because the kasra on the dal indicates it. It is also said: al-ayd means strength.

The clause ﴿Indeed We purified them with a pure quality, the remembrance of the Abode﴾ is a reason (taʿlīl) for what they were described with.

The majority read "bi-khāliṣatin" with tanwīn and without an annexation, taking it as a verbal noun in the sense of sincere devotion (al-ikhlāṣ), so that "dhikrā" is in the accusative governed by it; or in the sense of purity (al-khulūṣ), so that "dhikrā" is in the nominative governed by it; or "khāliṣah" is an active participle in its proper form, and "dhikrā" is a substitution for it, or an explanation of it, or by an implied "I mean," or in the nominative by an implied subject. "al-Dār" may be a direct object of "dhikrā," and it may be an adverbial complement, either by extension or by dropping the preposition. In every estimate, "khāliṣah" is an attribute of an omitted noun, and the bāʾ is causal, i.e., "by means of a pure quality."

Nāfiʿ, Shaybah, Abū Jaʿfar, and Hishām from Ibn ʿĀmir read "khāliṣah" annexed to "dhikrā," with the annexation being explanatory, because the pure quality may be remembrance or other than remembrance; or because "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun annexed to its object, with the agent omitted, i.e., "by their sincerely devoting the remembrance of the Abode"; or a verbal noun in the sense of purity annexed to its agent.

Mujāhid said: the meaning of the verse is: We chose them by mentioning the Hereafter, and so We purified them through its remembrance. Qatādah said: they used to call to the Hereafter and to Allah. al-Suddī said: they were purified by fear of the Hereafter.

al-Wāḥidī said: whoever reads with tanwīn in "khāliṣah," the meaning is: We made them sincere to Us, in that the remembrance of the Abode was purely theirs; "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun in the sense of purity, and "dhikrā" in the sense of remembrance, i.e., the remembrance of the Abode was purely theirs, namely that they remembered preparation for it and were detached from this world, which is characteristic of the prophets.

As for whoever annexes, the meaning is: We purified them by having the remembrance of the Abode purely theirs; "khāliṣah" is a verbal noun annexed to its agent, and "dhikrā" in this sense means the mention.

﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and the good﴾: al-iṣṭifāʾ is choosing; al-akhyār is the plural of khayyir, with shadda or without, as amwāt is the plural of mayyit, with shadda or without. The meaning: they are with Us among those chosen from the good of their kind.

﴿And remember Ismāʿīl﴾: it has been said that the reason for singling him out for mention after his father, his brother, and his nephew is to indicate that he was steadfast in patience, which is the purpose of the reminder here. ﴿And al-Yasaʿ and Dhū al-Kifl﴾: al-Yasaʿ has already been mentioned, and what is said about him was discussed in al-Anʿām; Dhū al-Kifl has already been mentioned, and what is said about him was discussed in Surah al-Anbiyāʾ. The purpose of mentioning these is that they were among those prophets who were patient and bore hardships in the religion of Allah.

Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to mention them so that he might follow their path in patience. ﴿And all of them are among the good ones﴾, i.e., those whom Allah chose for His prophethood and selected from His creation.
