When the guardians said that to them, they said: "No welcome to them," i.e., may their dwellings in the Fire not be spacious. "Rahb" is spaciousness, and the meaning is: there is no honor for them. This is an announcement from Allah, glory be to Him, of the severing of affection among the disbelievers, and that the affection that existed among them turns into enmity.

The clause "no welcome to them" is a supplicatory clause with no place in grammatical analysis, or it is an attribute of "troop," or a circumstantial clause from it, or with an implied "saying," i.e., "said concerning them: no welcome to them." It was also said that it is part of the speech of the guardians. The first is preferable, as the following reply of the followers indicates. The clause ﴿Indeed, they are burning in the Fire﴾ is a reason from the side of those who said "no welcome to them," i.e., they are those who will burn in the Fire just as we burned in it, and they deserve it just as we deserved it.

The clause ﴿They will say: Rather you—no welcome to you!﴾ is a resumed clause answering an implied question, i.e., the followers said upon hearing what the leaders said to them: "Rather you—no welcome to you," i.e., no honor for you. Then they gave a reason for that in their saying: ﴿You brought it upon us﴾, i.e., you brought the punishment or the burning upon us, made us fall into it, and invited us to it by what you used to tell us: that the truth is what you are upon, and that the prophets were not truthful in what they brought. ﴿So wretched is the settlement﴾, i.e., how wretched is the abode, Hell, for us and for you.

Then He related from the followers also that they followed this statement with another statement, which is: ﴿They will say: Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, add to him a double punishment in the Fire﴾, i.e., increase him in punishment with a double, and "double" means adding its like to it. The meaning of "whoever brought this upon us" is whoever invited us to it and made it appealing to us.

al-Farra' said: The meaning is: whoever made this appealing to us and set its precedent. It was said: its meaning is: he brought this punishment upon us by his calling us to disbelief, so add to him a double punishment in the Fire, i.e., punishment for his disbelief and punishment for his calling us, so that becomes double. A similar example is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Our Lord, these have misled us, so give them a double punishment from the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 38], and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, give them a double punishment from the punishment﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68]. It was said: the intended "double" here is the serpents and scorpions.

﴿And they will say: What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ It was said: this is from the words of the leaders, and it was said: from the words of the transgressors mentioned earlier.

al-Kalbi said: They look in the Fire and do not see those who used to oppose them among the believers, who were with them there. At that they said: "What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?"

It was said: they mean the poor believers, such as 'Ammar, Khabbab, Suhayb, Bilal, Salim, and Salman. It was said: they meant the companions of Muhammad in general.

﴿Did we take them in ridicule, or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ Mujahid said: The meaning is: "Did we take them in ridicule in the world and were we wrong, or have our eyes turned away from them so that we did not know their place?" The denial understood from the interrogative is directed at each of the two matters.

al-Hasan said: All of that they did: they took them in ridicule, and their eyes turned away from them.

al-Farra' said: The interrogative here carries the meaning of rebuke and wonder.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Kathir, and al-A'mash read with the elision of the hamzah of "ittakhadhnahum" in connected speech. This reading allows that the utterance is a pure statement, and the clause is in the accusative position as a second attribute of "rijalan." It also allows that the intended meaning is the interrogative, with its particle deleted, since "am" indicates it. On the first view, "am" is disjunctive, meaning "bal" and the hamzah, i.e., "rather, our eyes turned away from them," in the sense of rebuking themselves for mocking, then shifting from that to rebuke for contempt and belittling. On the second view, "am" is the connected one.

The rest read with an interrogative hamzah, by which the hamzah of connection fell away. The clause then has no place in grammar, and in it is rebuke of themselves for both matters together, because "am" in this reading is for equalization.

Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Shaybah, al-Mufaddal, Hubayrah, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin. The rest read it with a kasra. Abu 'Ubaydah said: whoever reads with a kasra makes it from mockery (al-hazw), and whoever reads with a damma makes it from subjugation (al-taskhir).

The reference of "inna dhalika" is to what was previously mentioned of their state. The predicate of "inna" is His saying: ﴿is truly (laqqun)﴾, i.e., it is an event that is established and certain in the Last Abode, not differing at all. ﴿The quarrelling of the people of the Fire﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is an explanation of that. It was said: it is an explanation of "truth." It was said: it is a substitute for it. It was said: a substitute for the place of "dhalika." It is also possible that it is a predicate after a predicate. This is according to the majority's reading with "tukhasimu" in the nominative. The meaning: that which Allah related of them is truly something that must be spoken of, namely the quarrelling of the people of the Fire therein, in the Fire, and what the leaders said to the followers, and what the followers said to them.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "takhasumu" in the accusative, as a substitute for "dhalika" or by an implied "I mean." Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "takhasama" with the past tense, so it is a resumed clause.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say a statement combining warning and guidance to monotheism, so He said: ﴿Say: I am only a warner﴾, i.e., one who frightens you of the punishment and chastisement of Allah. ﴿And there is no god﴾ worthy of worship ﴿except Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾, who has no partner, the Overpowering over everything other than Him.

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ of the created things, the Mighty, whom none can overpower, the Forgiving to whoever obeys Him. It was said: the meaning of "al-'Aziz" is the Unassailable, who has no like, and the meaning of "al-Ghaffar" is the Concealer of the sins of His creation.

Then He, glory be to Him, commanded him to exaggerate in warning them and to make clear to them the greatness and majesty of the matter, so He said: ﴿Say: It is a great news﴾, i.e., what I have warned you of regarding punishment and what I have explained to you regarding monotheism is a great report and a magnificent tidings, deserving attention to it, veneration of it, and not treating it lightly. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 1–2].

Mujahid, Qatadah, and Muqatil said: It is the Qur'an, for it is a great news because it is the speech of Allah.

al-Zajjaj said: "Say: the news I have informed you of from Allah is a great news": meaning what He informed them of regarding the stories of the earlier peoples is proof of his prophethood, and that is proof of his truthfulness and prophethood, because he would not have known that except by revelation from Allah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verse 55–70 (part 2 of 2):

The clause ﴿You are turning away from it﴾ is a rebuke and reproach directed at them, because they turned away from it and did not reflect upon it, so that they might know its truthfulness and use it as evidence for what they denied of the Resurrection.

His saying: ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly [al-mala' al-a'la] when they disputed﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought to establish that it is a momentous report. The Exalted Assembly (al-mala' al-a'la) are the angels. ﴿When they disputed﴾ means: at the time of their disputing. So His saying ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly﴾ is connected to "knowledge" ('ilm) on the basis of its being implicitly construed with the meaning of "comprehension" (ihatah), and His saying "when they disputed" (idh yakhtasimun) is connected to an implied element, meaning: I had no knowledge in what preceded, in any respect, of the state of the Exalted Assembly at the time of their disputing. The pronoun in "yakhtasimun" refers to the Exalted Assembly, and the dispute that took place among them concerned the matter of Adam, as what comes shortly after indicates.

The clause ﴿It is only revealed to me that I am a plain warner﴾ is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between their general disputing and its detailed explanation in His saying ﴿When your Lord said to the angels...﴾ [Sad: 71]. The meaning is: what is revealed to me is only that I am a plain warner. Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: what is revealed to me is only that I am a plain warner, who makes clear to you what you do of the obligatory duties and the sunan, and what you refrain from of the forbidden and disobedience. He said: It is as if you had said: What is revealed to me is only the warning. Al-Nahhas said: It is also permissible that it be in a position of accusative case, meaning: what is revealed to me is only because I am a plain warner.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read the hamza of "innama" with a fatha, on the basis that it and what follows it are in a position of nominative case, as it stands in the place of the subject (na'ib al-fa'il), meaning: what is revealed to me is only the warning, or only my being a plain warner. Or it is in a position of accusative or genitive case after the removal of the preposition of cause (lam al-'illah), and the element standing in the place of the subject on this view is the prepositional phrase. Abu Ja'far read the hamza with a kasra, because revelation (al-wahy) contains the meaning of speech (al-qawl), and it (the clause) stands in the place of the subject by way of quotation (hikayah), as if it were said: What is revealed to me is only this sentence, containing this report, namely that I should say to you: Indeed I am a plain warner.

It has also been said that the pronoun in "yakhtasimun" refers to the Quraysh, meaning the saying of whoever among them said: The angels are the daughters of God. The meaning would then be: I had no knowledge of the angels when the Quraysh dispute concerning them. But the first view is preferable.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿and ghassaq﴾, that he said: "It is the zamharir (extreme cold). ﴿And other of its kind﴾: from its like. ﴿Pairs﴾: kinds of punishment."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If a bucketful of ghassaq were poured out in this world, it would make the people of the world stink."

al-Tirmidhi said after transmitting it: "We do not know it except from the hadith of Rishdin ibn Sa'd." I say: Rishdin has a well-known controversy concerning him.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Tabarani related from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying ﴿so increase him in punishment twofold in the Fire﴾, that he said: "Vipers and serpents."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿the Exalted Assembly﴾, that he said: "The angels, when they were consulted about the creation of Adam, and they disputed concerning it, and said: Do not place in the earth one who will be a successor (khalifah)."

Muhammad ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salat, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding His saying ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they disputed﴾, that he said: "It is the dispute concerning the affair of Adam, when they said ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, and Ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salat related that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "My Lord came to me last night in the best of forms, I think he said: in a dream, and said: O Muhammad, do you know about what the Exalted Assembly dispute? I said: No. So He placed His hand between my shoulders until I felt its coolness between my breasts, or in my chest, and I knew what is in the heavens and the earth. Then He said to me: O Muhammad, do you know about what the Exalted Assembly dispute? I said: Yes, concerning the expiations (kaffarat). The expiations are: remaining in the mosques after the prayers, walking on foot to the congregations, and completing the ablution in difficult conditions..." and the hadith continues.

al-Tirmidhi, who declared it sound, Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal something similar to it, but longer, and he said: "And perfecting the ablution in the hot periods (al-sabarat)."

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from the hadith of Jabir ibn Samurah something similar to it, but shorter.

They (al-Bukhari and Muslim) also related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah something similar to it, and on this topic there are other hadiths.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verses 55–70 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "This" (hadha). Al-Zajjaj said: "This" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "the matter is this," so one stops at "this." Ibn al-Anbari said: This is a good place to pause, and then one begins with "And indeed for the transgressors" (wa inna lil-taghin). It is also permissible for "this" (hadha) to be the subject, with an omitted predicate, i.e., "this is as it has been mentioned," or "this has been mentioned."

Then, after mentioning what is for the people of goodness, He—glory be to Him—mentioned what is for the people of evil, saying: ﴿And indeed for the transgressors is the worst of destinations﴾, i.e., those who transgressed against Allah and denied His messengers, ﴿the worst of destinations﴾: the worst place of return to which they will return.

Then He explained that, saying: ﴿Hell, which they will burn in﴾. The accusative of "Hell" (jahannam) is either as an apposition (badal) to "the worst of destinations," or it is accusative by an implied "I mean" (a'ni). It is also permissible that it be an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) according to the view of some, as preceded shortly before. It is also permissible that it be accusative by the construction of the verb's object pronoun being attached (ishtighal), i.e., "they burn Hell, they burn in it." The meaning of "yaslawnaha" is "they enter it," and it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿So wretched is the resting place﴾, i.e., how wretched is what they have prepared for themselves. "Mihad" is the bedding, derived from the cradle of a child (mahd al-sabiy). It is also permissible that "mihad" means the place, and the object of the dispraise is omitted, i.e., "how wretched is the resting place it is," as in His saying: ﴿For them from Hell is a bed (mihad)﴾ [al-A'raf: 41]. Allah, glory be to Him, likened what is beneath them of the fire of Hell to a bed.

﴿This, so let them taste it: boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid (ghassaq)﴾. "This" is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is "hamim," and "ghassaq" is by inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), i.e., "this is boiling water and ghassaq, so let them taste it."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: The estimate of the verse: "This is boiling water and ghassaq, so let them taste it"; or it is said to them on that day this statement.

"Hamim" is boiling water whose heat has reached its extreme. "Ghassaq" is what flows from the skins of the people of the Fire of pus and discharge, from their saying: "his eye became watery (ghasaqat)" when it poured out, and "al-ghasaqan" is pouring out.

Al-Nahhas said: It is also possible that the meaning is: "the matter is this," and the nominativity of "hamim wa ghassaq" is because they are two predicates of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is hamim and ghassaq." It is also possible that "this" is in the accusative position by an implied verb explained by what follows, i.e., "let them taste this, so let them taste it." It is also possible that "hamim" is nominative as a subject whose predicate is understood before it, i.e., "from it is hamim and from it is ghassaq." A similar example is the poet's saying:

"Until, when the lightning flashed in the darkness, and the herbs were left, some twisted and some crushed."

i.e., from it is something twisted and from it is something crushed.

It was said: Ghassaq is what kills by its coldness, and from it is said of the night: "ghasiq," because it is colder than the day. It was said: It is the zamharir (extreme cold). It was said: Ghassaq is the foul-smelling. It was said: Ghassaq is a spring in Hell from which flows every melted substance of a snake and a scorpion.

Qatadah said: It is what flows from the private parts of adulterous women and from the stench of the flesh and skins of the disbelievers. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: It is the essence of the people of the Fire. Al-Suddi said: Ghassaq is what flows from the tears of the people of the Fire, which they are given to drink along with the hamim. Ibn Zayd said the same.

Mujahid and Muqatil said: It is cold ice whose coldness has reached its extreme. Interpreting ghassaq as "cold" is more fitting with what the Arabic language requires, and from it is the poet's saying:

"When I remember life and its pleasures, a tear of the night (ghasiq) flowed toward me."

i.e., cold. It is also more fitting for its contrast with hamim.

The people of Madinah, the people of Basrah, and some of the Kufans read "ghassaq" with the letter sin lightened (ghasaq). Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Hamzah read it with the shaddah (ghassaq). These are two dialects with one meaning, as al-Akhfash said.

It was also said: their meanings differ. Whoever lightens it, it is a noun like "adhab," "jawab," and "sawab." Whoever doubles it says it is an active participle of intensity, like "darrab" and "qattal."

﴿And other (punishments) of its kind﴾. The majority read "wa akhar" in the singular masculine. Abu 'Amr read "wa ukhar" with a damma on the hamzah, as a plural. Asim al-Jahdari rejected Abu 'Amr's reading and said: If it were as he reads, it would say "min shaklihā" (of its kind, feminine). "Akhar" is nominative as a subject whose predicate is "azwaj." It is also possible that "min shaklihi" is a fronted predicate and "azwaj" a delayed subject, and the clause is the predicate of "akhar." It is also possible that the predicate of "akhar" is omitted, i.e., "and another is for them," and "min shaklihi azwaj" is an independent clause.

The meaning of the verse according to the majority's reading: "and a different punishment or a different taste, or another type of the kind of that taste or the first type." The "shakl" is the similar kind. According to the second reading, the meaning is: "and other tastes, or other types of the kind of that taste or the type previously mentioned." The singular pronoun in "shaklihi" is by interpreting it as "of the aforementioned," i.e., "of the kind of the aforementioned." "Azwaj" means kinds, types, and similar things.

The summary of the meaning of the verse: the people of the Fire have hamim, ghassaq, and various kinds of punishment of the same sort as the hamim and ghassaq.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: it is the zamharir. This statement he attributed to the exegetes is only complete if the zamharir consists of different types and varied kinds to correspond with the meaning of "azwaj," or on the assumption that each individual of the people of the Fire has a zamharir.

al-Zajjaj said: "Say: the news I have informed you of from Allah is a great news": meaning what He informed them of regarding the stories of the earlier peoples is proof of his prophethood, and that is proof of his truthfulness and prophethood, because he would not have known that except by revelation from Allah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verse 55–70 (part 2 of 2):

The clause ﴿You are turning away from it﴾ is a rebuke and reproach directed at them, because they turned away from it and did not reflect upon it, so that they might know its truthfulness and use it as evidence for what they denied of the Resurrection.

His saying: ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly [al-mala' al-a'la] when they disputed﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought to establish that it is a momentous report. The Exalted Assembly (al-mala' al-a'la) are the angels. ﴿When they disputed﴾ means: at the time of their disputing. So His saying ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly﴾ is connected to "knowledge" ('ilm) on the basis of its being implicitly construed with the meaning of "comprehension" (ihatah), and His saying "when they disputed" (idh yakhtasimun) is connected to an implied element, meaning: I had no knowledge in what preceded, in any respect, of the state of the Exalted Assembly at the time of their disputing. The pronoun in "yakhtasimun" refers to the Exalted Assembly, and the dispute that took place among them concerned the matter of Adam, as what comes shortly after indicates.

The clause ﴿It is only revealed to me that I am a plain warner﴾ is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between their general disputing and its detailed explanation in His saying ﴿When your Lord said to the angels...﴾ [Sad: 71]. The meaning is: what is revealed to me is only that I am a plain warner. Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: what is revealed to me is only that I am a plain warner, who makes clear to you what you do of the obligatory duties and the sunan, and what you refrain from of the forbidden and disobedience. He said: It is as if you had said: What is revealed to me is only the warning. Al-Nahhas said: It is also permissible that it be in a position of accusative case, meaning: what is revealed to me is only because I am a plain warner.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read the hamza of "innama" with a fatha, on the basis that it and what follows it are in a position of nominative case, as it stands in the place of the subject (na'ib al-fa'il), meaning: what is revealed to me is only the warning, or only my being a plain warner. Or it is in a position of accusative or genitive case after the removal of the preposition of cause (lam al-'illah), and the element standing in the place of the subject on this view is the prepositional phrase. Abu Ja'far read the hamza with a kasra, because revelation (al-wahy) contains the meaning of speech (al-qawl), and it (the clause) stands in the place of the subject by way of quotation (hikayah), as if it were said: What is revealed to me is only this sentence, containing this report, namely that I should say to you: Indeed I am a plain warner.

It has also been said that the pronoun in "yakhtasimun" refers to the Quraysh, meaning the saying of whoever among them said: The angels are the daughters of God. The meaning would then be: I had no knowledge of the angels when the Quraysh dispute concerning them. But the first view is preferable.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿and ghassaq﴾, that he said: "It is the zamharir (extreme cold). ﴿And other of its kind﴾: from its like. ﴿Pairs﴾: kinds of punishment."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If a bucketful of ghassaq were poured out in this world, it would make the people of the world stink."

al-Tirmidhi said after transmitting it: "We do not know it except from the hadith of Rishdin ibn Sa'd." I say: Rishdin has a well-known controversy concerning him.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Tabarani related from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying ﴿so increase him in punishment twofold in the Fire﴾, that he said: "Vipers and serpents."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿the Exalted Assembly﴾, that he said: "The angels, when they were consulted about the creation of Adam, and they disputed concerning it, and said: Do not place in the earth one who will be a successor (khalifah)."

Muhammad ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salat, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding His saying ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they disputed﴾, that he said: "It is the dispute concerning the affair of Adam, when they said ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, and Ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salat related that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "My Lord came to me last night in the best of forms, I think he said: in a dream, and said: O Muhammad, do you know about what the Exalted Assembly dispute? I said: No. So He placed His hand between my shoulders until I felt its coolness between my breasts, or in my chest, and I knew what is in the heavens and the earth. Then He said to me: O Muhammad, do you know about what the Exalted Assembly dispute? I said: Yes, concerning the expiations (kaffarat). The expiations are: remaining in the mosques after the prayers, walking on foot to the congregations, and completing the ablution in difficult conditions..." and the hadith continues.

al-Tirmidhi, who declared it sound, Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal something similar to it, but longer, and he said: "And perfecting the ablution in the hot periods (al-sabarat)."

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from the hadith of Jabir ibn Samurah something similar to it, but shorter.

They (al-Bukhari and Muslim) also related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah something similar to it, and on this topic there are other hadiths.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verses 55–70 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "This" (hadha). Al-Zajjaj said: "This" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "the matter is this," so one stops at "this." Ibn al-Anbari said: This is a good place to pause, and then one begins with "And indeed for the transgressors" (wa inna lil-taghin). It is also permissible for "this" (hadha) to be the subject, with an omitted predicate, i.e., "this is as it has been mentioned," or "this has been mentioned."

Then, after mentioning what is for the people of goodness, He—glory be to Him—mentioned what is for the people of evil, saying: ﴿And indeed for the transgressors is the worst of destinations﴾, i.e., those who transgressed against Allah and denied His messengers, ﴿the worst of destinations﴾: the worst place of return to which they will return.

Then He explained that, saying: ﴿Hell, which they will burn in﴾. The accusative of "Hell" (jahannam) is either as an apposition (badal) to "the worst of destinations," or it is accusative by an implied "I mean" (a'ni). It is also permissible that it be an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) according to the view of some, as preceded shortly before. It is also permissible that it be accusative by the construction of the verb's object pronoun being attached (ishtighal), i.e., "they burn Hell, they burn in it." The meaning of "yaslawnaha" is "they enter it," and it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿So wretched is the resting place﴾, i.e., how wretched is what they have prepared for themselves. "Mihad" is the bedding, derived from the cradle of a child (mahd al-sabiy). It is also permissible that "mihad" means the place, and the object of the dispraise is omitted, i.e., "how wretched is the resting place it is," as in His saying: ﴿For them from Hell is a bed (mihad)﴾ [al-A'raf: 41]. Allah, glory be to Him, likened what is beneath them of the fire of Hell to a bed.

﴿This, so let them taste it: boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid (ghassaq)﴾. "This" is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is "hamim," and "ghassaq" is by inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), i.e., "this is boiling water and ghassaq, so let them taste it."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: The estimate of the verse: "This is boiling water and ghassaq, so let them taste it"; or it is said to them on that day this statement.

"Hamim" is boiling water whose heat has reached its extreme. "Ghassaq" is what flows from the skins of the people of the Fire of pus and discharge, from their saying: "his eye became watery (ghasaqat)" when it poured out, and "al-ghasaqan" is pouring out.

Al-Nahhas said: It is also possible that the meaning is: "the matter is this," and the nominativity of "hamim wa ghassaq" is because they are two predicates of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is hamim and ghassaq." It is also possible that "this" is in the accusative position by an implied verb explained by what follows, i.e., "let them taste this, so let them taste it." It is also possible that "hamim" is nominative as a subject whose predicate is understood before it, i.e., "from it is hamim and from it is ghassaq." A similar example is the poet's saying:

"Until, when the lightning flashed in the darkness, and the herbs were left, some twisted and some crushed."

i.e., from it is something twisted and from it is something crushed.

It was said: Ghassaq is what kills by its coldness, and from it is said of the night: "ghasiq," because it is colder than the day. It was said: It is the zamharir (extreme cold). It was said: Ghassaq is the foul-smelling. It was said: Ghassaq is a spring in Hell from which flows every melted substance of a snake and a scorpion.

Qatadah said: It is what flows from the private parts of adulterous women and from the stench of the flesh and skins of the disbelievers. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: It is the essence of the people of the Fire. Al-Suddi said: Ghassaq is what flows from the tears of the people of the Fire, which they are given to drink along with the hamim. Ibn Zayd said the same.

Mujahid and Muqatil said: It is cold ice whose coldness has reached its extreme. Interpreting ghassaq as "cold" is more fitting with what the Arabic language requires, and from it is the poet's saying:

"When I remember life and its pleasures, a tear of the night (ghasiq) flowed toward me."

i.e., cold. It is also more fitting for its contrast with hamim.

The people of Madinah, the people of Basrah, and some of the Kufans read "ghassaq" with the letter sin lightened (ghasaq). Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Hamzah read it with the shaddah (ghassaq). These are two dialects with one meaning, as al-Akhfash said.

It was also said: their meanings differ. Whoever lightens it, it is a noun like "adhab," "jawab," and "sawab." Whoever doubles it says it is an active participle of intensity, like "darrab" and "qattal."

﴿And other (punishments) of its kind﴾. The majority read "wa akhar" in the singular masculine. Abu 'Amr read "wa ukhar" with a damma on the hamzah, as a plural. Asim al-Jahdari rejected Abu 'Amr's reading and said: If it were as he reads, it would say "min shaklihā" (of its kind, feminine). "Akhar" is nominative as a subject whose predicate is "azwaj." It is also possible that "min shaklihi" is a fronted predicate and "azwaj" a delayed subject, and the clause is the predicate of "akhar." It is also possible that the predicate of "akhar" is omitted, i.e., "and another is for them," and "min shaklihi azwaj" is an independent clause.

The meaning of the verse according to the majority's reading: "and a different punishment or a different taste, or another type of the kind of that taste or the first type." The "shakl" is the similar kind. According to the second reading, the meaning is: "and other tastes, or other types of the kind of that taste or the type previously mentioned." The singular pronoun in "shaklihi" is by interpreting it as "of the aforementioned," i.e., "of the kind of the aforementioned." "Azwaj" means kinds, types, and similar things.

The summary of the meaning of the verse: the people of the Fire have hamim, ghassaq, and various kinds of punishment of the same sort as the hamim and ghassaq.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: it is the zamharir. This statement he attributed to the exegetes is only complete if the zamharir consists of different types and varied kinds to correspond with the meaning of "azwaj," or on the assumption that each individual of the people of the Fire has a zamharir.

(p-1270) ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you﴾. "Fawj" is a group, and "iqtiham" is entering. This is a quotation of the words of the angels who are the guardians of the Fire, because when the leaders and chiefs enter the Fire, and the followers enter after them, the guardians say to the leaders: "This is a troop," meaning the followers, ﴿rushing in with you﴾, i.e., entering the Fire with you.

His saying: ﴿No welcome to them﴾ is from the words of the leaders and chiefs. When the guardians said that to them, they said: "No welcome to them," i.e., may their dwellings in the Fire not be spacious. "Rahb" is spaciousness, and the meaning is: there is no honor for them. This is an announcement from Allah, glory be to Him, of the severing of affection among the disbelievers, and that the affection that existed among them turns into enmity.

The clause "no welcome to them" is a supplicatory clause with no place in grammatical analysis, or it is an attribute of "troop," or a circumstantial clause from it, or with an implied "saying," i.e., "said concerning them: no welcome to them." It was also said that it is part of the speech of the guardians. The first is preferable, as the following reply of the followers indicates. The clause ﴿Indeed, they are burning in the Fire﴾ is a reason from the side of those who said "no welcome to them," i.e., they are those who will burn in the Fire just as we burned in it, and they deserve it just as we deserved it.

The clause ﴿They will say: Rather you—no welcome to you!﴾ is a resumed clause answering an implied question, i.e., the followers said upon hearing what the leaders said to them: "Rather you—no welcome to you," i.e., no honor for you. Then they gave a reason for that in their saying: ﴿You brought it upon us﴾, i.e., you brought the punishment or the burning upon us, made us fall into it, and invited us to it by what you used to tell us: that the truth is what you are upon, and that the prophets were not truthful in what they brought. ﴿So wretched is the settlement﴾, i.e., how wretched is the abode, Hell, for us and for you.

Then He related from the followers also that they followed this statement with another statement, which is: ﴿They will say: Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, add to him a double punishment in the Fire﴾, i.e., increase him in punishment with a double, and "double" means adding its like to it. The meaning of "whoever brought this upon us" is whoever invited us to it and made it appealing to us.

al-Farra' said: The meaning is: whoever made this appealing to us and set its precedent. It was said: its meaning is: he brought this punishment upon us by his calling us to disbelief, so add to him a double punishment in the Fire, i.e., punishment for his disbelief and punishment for his calling us, so that becomes double. A similar example is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Our Lord, these have misled us, so give them a double punishment from the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 38], and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, give them a double punishment from the punishment﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68]. It was said: the intended "double" here is the serpents and scorpions.

﴿And they will say: What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ It was said: this is from the words of the leaders, and it was said: from the words of the transgressors mentioned earlier.

al-Kalbi said: They look in the Fire and do not see those who used to oppose them among the believers, who were with them there. At that they said: "What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?"

It was said: they mean the poor believers, such as 'Ammar, Khabbab, Suhayb, Bilal, Salim, and Salman. It was said: they meant the companions of Muhammad in general.

﴿Did we take them in ridicule, or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ Mujahid said: The meaning is: "Did we take them in ridicule in the world and were we wrong, or have our eyes turned away from them so that we did not know their place?" The denial understood from the interrogative is directed at each of the two matters.

al-Hasan said: All of that they did: they took them in ridicule, and their eyes turned away from them.

al-Farra' said: The interrogative here carries the meaning of rebuke and wonder.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Kathir, and al-A'mash read with the elision of the hamzah of "ittakhadhnahum" in connected speech. This reading allows that the utterance is a pure statement, and the clause is in the accusative position as a second attribute of "rijalan." It also allows that the intended meaning is the interrogative, with its particle deleted, since "am" indicates it. On the first view, "am" is disjunctive, meaning "bal" and the hamzah, i.e., "rather, our eyes turned away from them," in the sense of rebuking themselves for mocking, then shifting from that to rebuke for contempt and belittling. On the second view, "am" is the connected one.

The rest read with an interrogative hamzah, by which the hamzah of connection fell away. The clause then has no place in grammar, and in it is rebuke of themselves for both matters together, because "am" in this reading is for equalization.

Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Shaybah, al-Mufaddal, Hubayrah, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin. The rest read it with a kasra. Abu 'Ubaydah said: whoever reads with a kasra makes it from mockery (al-hazw), and whoever reads with a damma makes it from subjugation (al-taskhir).

The reference of "inna dhalika" is to what was previously mentioned of their state. The predicate of "inna" is His saying: ﴿is truly (laqqun)﴾, i.e., it is an event that is established and certain in the Last Abode, not differing at all. ﴿The quarrelling of the people of the Fire﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is an explanation of that. It was said: it is an explanation of "truth." It was said: it is a substitute for it. It was said: a substitute for the place of "dhalika." It is also possible that it is a predicate after a predicate. This is according to the majority's reading with "tukhasimu" in the nominative. The meaning: that which Allah related of them is truly something that must be spoken of, namely the quarrelling of the people of the Fire therein, in the Fire, and what the leaders said to the followers, and what the followers said to them.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "takhasumu" in the accusative, as a substitute for "dhalika" or by an implied "I mean." Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "takhasama" with the past tense, so it is a resumed clause.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say a statement combining warning and guidance to monotheism, so He said: ﴿Say: I am only a warner﴾, i.e., one who frightens you of the punishment and chastisement of Allah. ﴿And there is no god﴾ worthy of worship ﴿except Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾, who has no partner, the Overpowering over everything other than Him.

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ of the created things, the Mighty, whom none can overpower, the Forgiving to whoever obeys Him. It was said: the meaning of "al-'Aziz" is the Unassailable, who has no like, and the meaning of "al-Ghaffar" is the Concealer of the sins of His creation.

Then He, glory be to Him, commanded him to exaggerate in warning them and to make clear to them the greatness and majesty of the matter, so He said: ﴿Say: It is a great news﴾, i.e., what I have warned you of regarding punishment and what I have explained to you regarding monotheism is a great report and a magnificent tidings, deserving attention to it, veneration of it, and not treating it lightly. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 1–2].

Mujahid, Qatadah, and Muqatil said: It is the Qur'an, for it is a great news because it is the speech of Allah.

al-Zajjaj said: "Say: the news I have informed you of from Allah is a great news": meaning what He informed them of regarding the stories of the earlier peoples is proof of his prophethood, and that is proof of his truthfulness and prophethood, because he would not have known that except by revelation from Allah.

It is also permissible that it be accusative by the construction of the verb's object pronoun being attached (ishtighal), i.e., "they burn Hell, they burn in it." The meaning of "yaslawnaha" is "they enter it," and it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿So wretched is the resting place﴾, i.e., how wretched is what they have prepared for themselves. "Mihad" is the bedding, derived from the cradle of a child (mahd al-sabiy). It is also permissible that "mihad" means the place, and the object of the dispraise is omitted, i.e., "how wretched is the resting place it is," as in His saying: ﴿For them from Hell is a bed (mihad)﴾ [al-A'raf: 41]. Allah, glory be to Him, likened what is beneath them of the fire of Hell to a bed.

﴿This, so let them taste it: boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid (ghassaq)﴾. "This" is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is "hamim," and "ghassaq" is by inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), i.e., "this is boiling water and ghassaq, so let them taste it."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: The estimate of the verse: "This is boiling water and ghassaq, so let them taste it"; or it is said to them on that day this statement.

"Hamim" is boiling water whose heat has reached its extreme. "Ghassaq" is what flows from the skins of the people of the Fire of pus and discharge, from their saying: "his eye became watery (ghasaqat)" when it poured out, and "al-ghasaqan" is pouring out.

Al-Nahhas said: It is also possible that the meaning is: "the matter is this," and the nominativity of "hamim wa ghassaq" is because they are two predicates of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is hamim and ghassaq." It is also possible that "this" is in the accusative position by an implied verb explained by what follows, i.e., "let them taste this, so let them taste it." It is also possible that "hamim" is nominative as a subject whose predicate is understood before it, i.e., "from it is hamim and from it is ghassaq." A similar example is the poet's saying:

"Until, when the lightning flashed in the darkness, and the herbs were left, some twisted and some crushed."

i.e., from it is something twisted and from it is something crushed.

It was said: Ghassaq is what kills by its coldness, and from it is said of the night: "ghasiq," because it is colder than the day. It was said: It is the zamharir (extreme cold). It was said: Ghassaq is the foul-smelling. It was said: Ghassaq is a spring in Hell from which flows every melted substance of a snake and a scorpion.

Qatadah said: It is what flows from the private parts of adulterous women and from the stench of the flesh and skins of the disbelievers. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: It is the essence of the people of the Fire. Al-Suddi said: Ghassaq is what flows from the tears of the people of the Fire, which they are given to drink along with the hamim. Ibn Zayd said the same.

Mujahid and Muqatil said: It is cold ice whose coldness has reached its extreme. Interpreting ghassaq as "cold" is more fitting with what the Arabic language requires, and from it is the poet's saying:

"When I remember life and its pleasures, a tear of the night (ghasiq) flowed toward me."

i.e., cold. It is also more fitting for its contrast with hamim.

The people of Madinah, the people of Basrah, and some of the Kufans read "ghassaq" with the letter sin lightened (ghasaq). Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Hamzah read it with the shaddah (ghassaq). These are two dialects with one meaning, as al-Akhfash said.

It was also said: their meanings differ. Whoever lightens it, it is a noun like "adhab," "jawab," and "sawab." Whoever doubles it says it is an active participle of intensity, like "darrab" and "qattal."

﴿And other (punishments) of its kind﴾. The majority read "wa akhar" in the singular masculine. Abu 'Amr read "wa ukhar" with a damma on the hamzah, as a plural. Asim al-Jahdari rejected Abu 'Amr's reading and said: If it were as he reads, it would say "min shaklihā" (of its kind, feminine). "Akhar" is nominative as a subject whose predicate is "azwaj." It is also possible that "min shaklihi" is a fronted predicate and "azwaj" a delayed subject, and the clause is the predicate of "akhar." It is also possible that the predicate of "akhar" is omitted, i.e., "and another is for them," and "min shaklihi azwaj" is an independent clause.

The meaning of the verse according to the majority's reading: "and a different punishment or a different taste, or another type of the kind of that taste or the first type." The "shakl" is the similar kind. According to the second reading, the meaning is: "and other tastes, or other types of the kind of that taste or the type previously mentioned." The singular pronoun in "shaklihi" is by interpreting it as "of the aforementioned," i.e., "of the kind of the aforementioned." "Azwaj" means kinds, types, and similar things.

The summary of the meaning of the verse: the people of the Fire have hamim, ghassaq, and various kinds of punishment of the same sort as the hamim and ghassaq.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: it is the zamharir. This statement he attributed to the exegetes is only complete if the zamharir consists of different types and varied kinds to correspond with the meaning of "azwaj," or on the assumption that each individual of the people of the Fire has a zamharir.

(p-1270) ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you﴾. "Fawj" is a group, and "iqtiham" is entering. This is a quotation of the words of the angels who are the guardians of the Fire, because when the leaders and chiefs enter the Fire, and the followers enter after them, the guardians say to the leaders: "This is a troop," meaning the followers, ﴿rushing in with you﴾, i.e., entering the Fire with you.

His saying: ﴿No welcome to them﴾ is from the words of the leaders and chiefs. When the guardians said that to them, they said: "No welcome to them," i.e., may their dwellings in the Fire not be spacious. "Rahb" is spaciousness, and the meaning is: there is no honor for them. This is an announcement from Allah, glory be to Him, of the severing of affection among the disbelievers, and that the affection that existed among them turns into enmity.

The clause "no welcome to them" is a supplicatory clause with no place in grammatical analysis, or it is an attribute of "troop," or a circumstantial clause from it, or with an implied "saying," i.e., "said concerning them: no welcome to them." It was also said that it is part of the speech of the guardians. The first is preferable, as the following reply of the followers indicates. The clause ﴿Indeed, they are burning in the Fire﴾ is a reason from the side of those who said "no welcome to them," i.e., they are those who will burn in the Fire just as we burned in it, and they deserve it just as we deserved it.

The clause ﴿They will say: Rather you—no welcome to you!﴾ is a resumed clause answering an implied question, i.e., the followers said upon hearing what the leaders said to them: "Rather you—no welcome to you," i.e., no honor for you. Then they gave a reason for that in their saying: ﴿You brought it upon us﴾, i.e., you brought the punishment or the burning upon us, made us fall into it, and invited us to it by what you used to tell us: that the truth is what you are upon, and that the prophets were not truthful in what they brought. ﴿So wretched is the settlement﴾, i.e., how wretched is the abode, Hell, for us and for you.

Then He related from the followers also that they followed this statement with another statement, which is: ﴿They will say: Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, add to him a double punishment in the Fire﴾, i.e., increase him in punishment with a double, and "double" means adding its like to it. The meaning of "whoever brought this upon us" is whoever invited us to it and made it appealing to us.

al-Farra' said: The meaning is: whoever made this appealing to us and set its precedent. It was said: its meaning is: he brought this punishment upon us by his calling us to disbelief, so add to him a double punishment in the Fire, i.e., punishment for his disbelief and punishment for his calling us, so that becomes double. A similar example is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Our Lord, these have misled us, so give them a double punishment from the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 38], and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, give them a double punishment from the punishment﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68]. It was said: the intended "double" here is the serpents and scorpions.

﴿And they will say: What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ It was said: this is from the words of the leaders, and it was said: from the words of the transgressors mentioned earlier.

al-Kalbi said: They look in the Fire and do not see those who used to oppose them among the believers, who were with them there. At that they said: "What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?"

It was said: they mean the poor believers, such as 'Ammar, Khabbab, Suhayb, Bilal, Salim, and Salman. It was said: they meant the companions of Muhammad in general.

﴿Did we take them in ridicule, or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ Mujahid said: The meaning is: "Did we take them in ridicule in the world and were we wrong, or have our eyes turned away from them so that we did not know their place?" The denial understood from the interrogative is directed at each of the two matters.

al-Hasan said: All of that they did: they took them in ridicule, and their eyes turned away from them.

al-Farra' said: The interrogative here carries the meaning of rebuke and wonder.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Kathir, and al-A'mash read with the elision of the hamzah of "ittakhadhnahum" in connected speech. This reading allows that the utterance is a pure statement, and the clause is in the accusative position as a second attribute of "rijalan." It also allows that the intended meaning is the interrogative, with its particle deleted, since "am" indicates it. On the first view, "am" is disjunctive, meaning "bal" and the hamzah, i.e., "rather, our eyes turned away from them," in the sense of rebuking themselves for mocking, then shifting from that to rebuke for contempt and belittling. On the second view, "am" is the connected one.

The rest read with an interrogative hamzah, by which the hamzah of connection fell away. The clause then has no place in grammar, and in it is rebuke of themselves for both matters together, because "am" in this reading is for equalization.

Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Shaybah, al-Mufaddal, Hubayrah, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin. The rest read it with a kasra. Abu 'Ubaydah said: whoever reads with a kasra makes it from mockery (al-hazw), and whoever reads with a damma makes it from subjugation (al-taskhir).

The reference of "inna dhalika" is to what was previously mentioned of their state. The predicate of "inna" is His saying: ﴿is truly (laqqun)﴾, i.e., it is an event that is established and certain in the Last Abode, not differing at all. ﴿The quarrelling of the people of the Fire﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is an explanation of that. It was said: it is an explanation of "truth." It was said: it is a substitute for it. It was said: a substitute for the place of "dhalika." It is also possible that it is a predicate after a predicate. This is according to the majority's reading with "tukhasimu" in the nominative. The meaning: that which Allah related of them is truly something that must be spoken of, namely the quarrelling of the people of the Fire therein, in the Fire, and what the leaders said to the followers, and what the followers said to them.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "takhasumu" in the accusative, as a substitute for "dhalika" or by an implied "I mean." Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "takhasama" with the past tense, so it is a resumed clause.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say a statement combining warning and guidance to monotheism, so He said: ﴿Say: I am only a warner﴾, i.e., one who frightens you of the punishment and chastisement of Allah. ﴿And there is no god﴾ worthy of worship ﴿except Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾, who has no partner, the Overpowering over everything other than Him.

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ of the created things, the Mighty, whom none can overpower, the Forgiving to whoever obeys Him. It was said: the meaning of "al-'Aziz" is the Unassailable, who has no like, and the meaning of "al-Ghaffar" is the Concealer of the sins of His creation.

Then He, glory be to Him, commanded him to exaggerate in warning them and to make clear to them the greatness and majesty of the matter, so He said: ﴿Say: It is a great news﴾, i.e., what I have warned you of regarding punishment and what I have explained to you regarding monotheism is a great report and a magnificent tidings, deserving attention to it, veneration of it, and not treating it lightly. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 1–2].

Mujahid, Qatadah, and Muqatil said: It is the Qur'an, for it is a great news because it is the speech of Allah.

al-Zajjaj said: "Say: the news I have informed you of from Allah is a great news": meaning what He informed them of regarding the stories of the earlier peoples is proof of his prophethood, and that is proof of his truthfulness and prophethood, because he would not have known that except by revelation from Allah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verse 55–70 (part 2 of 2):

The clause ﴿You are turning away from it﴾ is a rebuke and reproach directed at them, because they turned away from it and did not reflect upon it, so that they might know its truthfulness and use it as evidence for what they denied of the Resurrection.

His saying: ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly [al-mala' al-a'la] when they disputed﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought to establish that it is a momentous report. The Exalted Assembly (al-mala' al-a'la) are the angels. ﴿When they disputed﴾ means: at the time of their disputing. So His saying ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly﴾ is connected to "knowledge" ('ilm) on the basis of its being implicitly construed with the meaning of "comprehension" (ihatah), and His saying "when they disputed" (idh yakhtasimun) is connected to an implied element, meaning: I had no knowledge in what preceded, in any respect, of the state of the Exalted Assembly at the time of their disputing. The pronoun in "yakhtasimun" refers to the Exalted Assembly, and the dispute that took place among them concerned the matter of Adam, as what comes shortly after indicates.

The clause ﴿It is only revealed to me that I am a plain warner﴾ is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between their general disputing and its detailed explanation in His saying ﴿When your Lord said to the angels...﴾ [Sad: 71]. The meaning is: what is revealed to me is only that I am a plain warner. Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: what is revealed to me is only that I am a plain warner, who makes clear to you what you do of the obligatory duties and the sunan, and what you refrain from of the forbidden and disobedience. He said: It is as if you had said: What is revealed to me is only the warning. Al-Nahhas said: It is also permissible that it be in a position of accusative case, meaning: what is revealed to me is only because I am a plain warner.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read the hamza of "innama" with a fatha, on the basis that it and what follows it are in a position of nominative case, as it stands in the place of the subject (na'ib al-fa'il), meaning: what is revealed to me is only the warning, or only my being a plain warner. Or it is in a position of accusative or genitive case after the removal of the preposition of cause (lam al-'illah), and the element standing in the place of the subject on this view is the prepositional phrase. Abu Ja'far read the hamza with a kasra, because revelation (al-wahy) contains the meaning of speech (al-qawl), and it (the clause) stands in the place of the subject by way of quotation (hikayah), as if it were said: What is revealed to me is only this sentence, containing this report, namely that I should say to you: Indeed I am a plain warner.

It has also been said that the pronoun in "yakhtasimun" refers to the Quraysh, meaning the saying of whoever among them said: The angels are the daughters of God. The meaning would then be: I had no knowledge of the angels when the Quraysh dispute concerning them. But the first view is preferable.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿and ghassaq﴾, that he said: "It is the zamharir (extreme cold). ﴿And other of its kind﴾: from its like. ﴿Pairs﴾: kinds of punishment."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If a bucketful of ghassaq were poured out in this world, it would make the people of the world stink."

al-Tirmidhi said after transmitting it: "We do not know it except from the hadith of Rishdin ibn Sa'd." I say: Rishdin has a well-known controversy concerning him.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Tabarani related from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying ﴿so increase him in punishment twofold in the Fire﴾, that he said: "Vipers and serpents."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿the Exalted Assembly﴾, that he said: "The angels, when they were consulted about the creation of Adam, and they disputed concerning it, and said: Do not place in the earth one who will be a successor (khalifah)."

Muhammad ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salat, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding His saying ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they disputed﴾, that he said: "It is the dispute concerning the affair of Adam, when they said ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, and Ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salat related that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "My Lord came to me last night in the best of forms, I think he said: in a dream, and said: O Muhammad, do you know about what the Exalted Assembly dispute? I said: No. So He placed His hand between my shoulders until I felt its coolness between my breasts, or in my chest, and I knew what is in the heavens and the earth. Then He said to me: O Muhammad, do you know about what the Exalted Assembly dispute? I said: Yes, concerning the expiations (kaffarat). The expiations are: remaining in the mosques after the prayers, walking on foot to the congregations, and completing the ablution in difficult conditions..." and the hadith continues.

al-Tirmidhi, who declared it sound, Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal something similar to it, but longer, and he said: "And perfecting the ablution in the hot periods (al-sabarat)."

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from the hadith of Jabir ibn Samurah something similar to it, but shorter.

They (al-Bukhari and Muslim) also related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah something similar to it, and on this topic there are other hadiths.

It is also permissible for "this" (hadha) to be the subject, with an omitted predicate, i.e., "this is as it has been mentioned," or "this has been mentioned."
