The meaning of "the human being" (al-insān) in His words, ﴿And We created the human being﴾, is Adam, because he is the origin of this kind. As for *al-ṣalṣāl* (الصَّلْصالُ), Abu 'Ubayda said: it is clay mixed with sand that rattles (yatalaṣlaṣu) when it is shaken; when it is baked in fire, it becomes pottery (al-fakhkhār).

This is the view of most exegetes (*mufassirūn*).

Al-Kisa'i said: it is foul-smelling clay, derived from the Arabs' saying, "ṣalla al-laḥm wa-aṣalla" (ṣalla al-laḥm wa-aṣalla), meaning the meat became putrid, whether cooked or raw.

Al-Hutay'a said:
"That is a young man who gives away his cooking pot; the rot does not spoil the meat with him."

*Al-ḥama'* (الحَمَأُ): black clay that has changed.
Or it is black clay without the restriction of having changed.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: one says of it, "ḥamaʾtu al-bi'r ḥamʾan" (with the sukun), when you remove its silt; "ḥami'at al-bi'r ḥamaʾan" (with the fatḥah), when its silt has increased; and "aḥmaytuhā iḥmā'an," when I threw silt into it.

Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-ḥamʾah* with a sukun on the mim is like *al-ḥamaʾah* with fatḥah; its plural is *ḥamʾ*, like *tamrah* and *tamr*. *Al-ḥama'* is a verbal noun, like *al-halaʿ* and *al-jazaʿ*, and then it was named by it.

*Al-masnūn* (المَسْنُونُ): al-Farra' said it is what has changed; its root is from "sanantu al-ḥajar 'alā al-ḥajar," when I rubbed one stone against another, and what comes out between two stones is called *al-sunāna* and *al-sinīn*. From this is the saying of 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥassān:
"Then she besieged it up to the red dome, walking among marble and rubbed (sunūn) stones."
That is, rubbed. It is also said, "asina al-māʾ" when the water changed. From this is His saying, ﴿it has not changed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259], and His saying, ﴿water not changing﴾ [Muḥammad: 15]. Both derivations indicate change, because what comes out between two stones is necessarily foul-smelling.

Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-masnūn* means shaped (al-muṣawwab). It comes from the Arabs' saying, "sanantu al-māʾ 'alā al-wajh," when I poured it, and *al-sann* is pouring.

Sibawayh said: *al-masnūn* means formed (al-muṣawwar), derived from *sunnat al-wajh*, which is its form. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:
"She shows you the form of a face, not blemished, smooth, with no mole or scar."

Al-Akhfash said: *al-masnūn* means upright and erect, from their saying "wajhun masnūn" when it has length in it.

The conclusion of these views is that when the dust was moistened it became clay; when it became foul it became black mud (ḥama'an masnūnan); when it dried it became *ṣalṣāl*.
So the origin of *al-ṣalṣāl* is *al-ḥama' al-masnūn*, and for this reason both are described by these two words.

﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of the scorching wind﴾. *Al-jānn* (الجانّ) is the father of the jinn according to the majority of exegetes.
ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Muqātil said: it is Iblis.
He was called *jānn* because he is hidden from the eyes. One says, "janna al-shay'" when he covered it. So the *jānn* conceals himself from the eyes of the children of Adam. The meaning of "before" (min qabl) is before the creation of Adam. *Al-samūm* is the sharp wind that penetrates the pores; it occurs by day and may also occur by night, as Abu 'Ubayda said. The creation of the human being and the jinn is mentioned in this place to show the perfection of divine power, and to show that the One who is able to originate creation is able to bring it back again.

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾: the adverbial clause (al-ẓarf) is governed by a verb understood: that is, "remember." After mentioning the creation of the human being, He explained what happened at the time of his creation. The account of this was already discussed in al-Baqarah. *Al-bashar* is derived from *al-basharah*, which is the outer surface of the skin. The explanation of *al-ṣalṣāl* and *al-ḥama' al-masnūn* has been given above in full detail.

﴿So when I have proportioned him﴾: that is, I perfected his creation, balanced his human form, and completed his parts. ﴿And breathed into him of My spirit﴾: *al-nafkh* is the moving of wind into the cavities of another body. Whoever says the spirit is a subtle body like air, its meaning is clear. Whoever says it is a simple substance, neither occupying space nor inhering in something that occupies space, then for him the meaning of breathing is the preparation of the body so that the rational soul may attach to it.

Al-Nisaburi said: there is no disagreement that the idafah (possessive construction) in "My spirit" is for honour and dignity, like "the she-camel of God" and "the House of God."

Al-Qurtubi said: the spirit is a subtle body which God has made customary to create life in the body together with that body. Its reality is the attribution of a creature to its Creator: the spirit is a creation of His which He attributed to Himself as an honour and dignity. He said: similar to it is ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 171], which was already discussed in al-Nisa'.

﴿Then fall down prostrating to him﴾: the *fa'* indicates that their prostration was obligatory upon them immediately after the proportioning and breathing, without delay. It is a command to "fall" (*waqaʿa*, *yaqaʿu*).
This indicates that what was commanded is prostration, not merely bowing, as has been said. This prostration is a prostration of greeting and honour, not a prostration of worship. God may honour whom He wills among His creatures, as He wills, with what He wills. It was also said: the prostration was to God, and Adam was a *qiblah* (direction) for them.

﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾: He informed that the angels all prostrated together at God's command to them, without delay. Al-Mubarrad said: His saying "kulluhum" removed the possibility that some of the angels did not prostrate, and His saying "ajmaʿūn" is an emphasis after an emphasis. Al-Zajjaj preferred this view.
Al-Nisaburi said: this is because *ajmaʿ* is definite, so it cannot function as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); and if it could be a ḥāl, it would be in the accusative case.

Then He excepted Iblis from the angels, saying: ﴿except Iblis; he refused to be among those who prostrate﴾. It was said: this exception is *muttaṣil* (connected), because he was of the kind of the angels, but he refused out of arrogance, self-magnification and envy of Adam, so the word of God became binding upon him. It was also said: he was not of the angels, but he was with them, so the name "angels" overpowered him and he was commanded with what they were commanded; thus the exception is connected in this sense. It was also said: the exception is *munfaṣil* (disconnected), based on his not being one of them and their not being named to include him; that is, "but Iblis refused to be among those who prostrate." This matter has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿he refused to be among those who prostrate﴾ is a new sentence (istiʾnāf) explaining the manner of his exception from non-prostration, because non-prostration may be accompanied by hesitation, so He made clear that it was by way of refusal.

The clause ﴿He said: O Iblis, what is it with you that you are not among those who prostrate?﴾ is also a new sentence, answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did God say to Iblis after he refused to prostrate?" This address to him is not for honour and dignity but for reproach and rebuke. The meaning is: what purpose do you have in refusing, and what reason moved you to it, so that you are not among those who prostrate to Adam together with the angels, while they are in nobility, high rank and nearness to God, in the position you already know?

The clause ﴿He said: I am not one to prostrate to a human being You created from clay, from black mud, moulded﴾ is a new sentence like the previous one. He made the reason for not prostrating that Adam was a human being created from *ṣalṣāl* of *ḥama' masnūn*, supposing that he himself was created from a finer element than the element of Adam. This contains an implicit hint at his claim of being better than him. It was explicitly stated elsewhere: He said, ﴿I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ [Ṣād: 76]; and He said elsewhere, ﴿Shall I prostrate to one You created from clay?﴾ [al-Isrā': 61]. The *lām* in *li-asjud* emphasises the negation: that is, it is not valid for me.

God answered him with His words: ﴿He said: Then get out of it, for you are accursed﴾ (p-762). The pronoun in "minhā" is said to refer to Paradise; it is also said to refer to the heaven; and it is said to refer to the host of angels, meaning: get out of the host of angels. ﴿For you are accursed (rajīm)﴾: that is, stoned with meteors. It is also said that the meaning of *rajīm* is cursed, that is, expelled, because one who is expelled is stoned with rocks.

﴿And upon you is the curse until the Day of Judgement﴾: that is, upon you is expulsion and distancing from God's mercy, continuing upon you and remaining with you until the Day of Recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection. Making the Day of Judgement the limit of the curse does not imply that it ends at that time, because what is meant is its continuation without cessation. The Day of Judgement is mentioned for emphasis, as in His saying, ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ [Hūd: 107]. Or it is meant that on the Day of Judgement and after it he is punished with something harsher than cursing, from various kinds of punishment, so that he finds no relief from it as he used to find before the punishment touched him.

﴿He said: My Lord, then give me respite﴾: that is, delay me and grant me time, and do not cause me to die until the Day when they are raised, meaning Adam and his offspring.
He asked to remain alive until this day. When he heard that, he knew that God had postponed his punishment until the Final Abode. It is as if he asked never to die, because if his death was deferred until that day, then that day has no death in it. It was also said that he did not ask never to die, but asked that his punishment be postponed until the Day of Resurrection and that he not be punished in this world.

﴿He said: Then you are among those given respite﴾: when he asked for respite, God granted him what he asked and informed him that he was among those He gave respite, from among those whose lifespans He delayed from His creatures, or among those whose punishment He postponed for what they committed.

Then He explained the term up to which He gave him respite. He said: ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection. The Day of Judgement, the Day when they are raised, and the Day of the Appointed Time are all expressions for the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that the Appointed Time means a time near the resurrection; at that time he will die.

﴿He said: My Lord, because You have misled me, I will surely adorn [evil] for them on earth﴾. The *bā'* is for oath, and *mā* is verbal (maṣdariyyah). The answer to the oath is ﴿I will surely adorn [evil] for them﴾; that is: I swear by Your misleading me that I will surely adorn for them on earth, meaning as long as they are in this world. The adornment is either by making sins appear good to them and causing them to fall into them, or by occupying them with the adornment of this world so that they do not turn to anything else than what God commanded them.
His oath here by God's misleading him does not contradict his oath elsewhere by God's might, which is His power and dominion, because misleading him is among the things to which might applies.

﴿And I will surely mislead them all﴾: that is, I will surely lead them astray from the path of guidance, and bring them into the path of error and compel them to it.

﴿Except Your sincere servants among them﴾: Ahl al-Madīnah and Ahl al-Kūfah read it with a fatḥah on the *lām* (al-mukhlaṣīna), meaning those whom You have chosen from among the servants. The rest read it with a kasrah on the *lām* (al-mukhliṣīna), meaning those who made their worship sincere for You, so they did not intend it for other than You.

﴿He said: This is a path upon Me, straight﴾: that is, it is a right incumbent upon Me to uphold it, which is that You will have no authority over My servants.
Al-Kisa'i said: this is in the sense of warning and threat, like your saying to one whom you threaten, "Your path is upon me and your destination is to me," and like His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. So the meaning of this statement is: this is the path of his return to Me, and I will recompense each one according to his deed. It was also said: *ʿalā* here means *ilā* (to). It was also said: the meaning is that the straight path is by clarification and proof, and it was said: by granting success and guidance.

Ibn Sirin, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan, Qays ibn ʿAbbād, Abu Raja', Ḥumayd and Yaʿqūb read "hādhā ṣirāṭun ʿaliyyun" (this is an exalted path), as a *ṣifah mushabbahah* (attributive adjective), meaning "elevated."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verses 82–88 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Indeed, My servants — you have no authority over them﴾. The servants here are meant to be the sincere ones (al-mukhlisun). The meaning is that he has no power over them to bring them into a sin through which they would perish without repenting from it. This does not contradict what occurred from Adam and Hawwa' (Eve) and the like, for that was a sin that was forgiven because repentance was made from it. ﴿Except those who follow you from among the misguided﴾. He, glorified is He, excepted from His servants these, namely those who follow Iblis — from among the misguided, those who have fallen into error, going astray from the path of truth. This agrees with what the accursed Iblis said: ﴿I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them﴾. It may be said that there is a difference between the two statements: the speech of Allah, glorified is He, contains the negation of Iblis' authority over all His servants except those among the misguided who follow him, so it includes the sincere ones and others who did not follow Iblis from among the misguided. The speech of the accursed Iblis contains the misguiding of all except the sincere ones, so there entered into them those who were neither sincere nor misguided followers of Iblis.

The conclusion is that between the sincere ones and the misguided followers of Iblis there is a group that was neither sincere nor misguided followers of Iblis. It has been said that the misguided followers of Iblis are the polytheists (mushrikun), and this is indicated by the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 100].

Then Allah, glorified is He, said, threatening the followers of Iblis: ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾.

That is, the promised place of the misguided followers. "Ajma'in" (all) is an emphasis for the pronoun or a circumstantial (ḥāl) construction.

﴿It has seven gates﴾ through which the people of the Fire enter. It has seven because of the multitude of its inhabitants. ﴿For each gate there is a portion of them﴾, that is, of the misguided followers, ﴿a designated share﴾, that is, a known measure distinguished from others. It has been said: the meaning of "gates" is "levels" (aṭbāq), one level above another, and they are: Jahannam, then Laẓā, then al-Ḥuṭama, then al-Sa‘īr, then Saqar, then al-Jaḥīm, then al-Hāwiyah. The highest of them is for the monotheists (muwaḥḥidun), the second for the Jews, the third for the Christians, the fourth for the Sabians, the fifth for the Magians, the sixth for the polytheists, and the seventh for the hypocrites (munafiqun). So Jahannam is the highest of the levels, then what follows it is beneath it, and so on. Thus it has been said.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh in al-‘Aẓama transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas, who said: Man was created from three things: from clay that clings (ṭīn lāzib), and ṣalṣāl, and ḥama' masnūn. The clay that clings: that which sticks firmly and is good. The ṣalṣāl: that which is dried and fired, from which pottery is made. The ḥama' masnūn: the clay in which there is black mud.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, who said: The ṣalṣāl is water that falls upon good earth, then it dries out from it and it cracks, then it becomes like thin pottery shards.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, who said: The ṣalṣāl is dry earth that is moistened after its drying.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, who said: The ṣalṣāl is clay mixed with sand.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him.
He said: The ṣalṣāl is that which, when you strike it, it rings (ṣalṣala).

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him.
He said: The ṣalṣāl is clay which, when you squeeze it with your hand, the water comes out from between your fingers.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him (p-763) regarding His saying: ﴿from black mud, moulded﴾ [ḥama' masnūn], he said: from moist clay. And these same transmitters also transmitted from him regarding ﴿from ḥama' masnūn﴾: from stinking clay.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, who said: The jinn is the transformed (masikh) of the jinn, like monkeys and pigs are the transformed of mankind.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, who said: The jinn is Iblis, who was created before Adam.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of samum﴾, he said: from the best of fire.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, who said: ﴿Fire of samum﴾ is the scorching heat that kills.

Al-Tayalisi, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu‘ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn Mas‘ud, who said: The samum from which the jinn was created is a part of seventy parts of the fire of Jahannam. Then he recited: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of samum﴾. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from him as a marfu' report.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿He said: My Lord, reprieve me until the day they are resurrected﴾, he said: Iblis wanted not to taste death, so it was said: "Indeed you are among those reprieved until the day of the appointed time." He said: The first blast, in which Iblis will die, and between the blast and the blast is forty years.

Abu ‘Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Sirin regarding ﴿This is a path, upon Me, straight﴾, that it means elevated (rafi‘).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted the like of it from Qatadah.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿For it there are seven gates﴾, according to the number of the levels of Jahannam, as we have previously mentioned.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Hannad, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Sifat al-Nar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba‘th transmitted through various chains from ‘Ali, who said: The levels of Jahannam are seven, some above others; the first is filled, then the second, then the third, until all of them are filled. al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ‘Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Jahannam has seven gates: one of them is for whoever draws the sword against my Ummah."

Reports and narrations have come concerning the description of the Fire.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib in his Tarikh transmitted from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said regarding His saying, Exalted: ﴿For each gate of them there is a designated share﴾: A share of those who associated partners with Allah, a share of those who doubted Allah, and a share of those who were heedless of Allah."

The meaning of "the human being" (al-insān) in His words, ﴿And We created the human being﴾, is Adam, because he is the origin of this kind. As for *al-ṣalṣāl* (الصَّلْصالُ), Abu 'Ubayda said: it is clay mixed with sand that rattles (yatalaṣlaṣu) when it is shaken; when it is baked in fire, it becomes pottery (al-fakhkhār).

So the origin of *al-ṣalṣāl* is *al-ḥama' al-masnūn*, and for this reason both are described by these two words.

﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of the scorching wind﴾. *Al-jānn* (الجانّ) is the father of the jinn according to the majority of exegetes.
ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Muqātil said: it is Iblis.
He was called *jānn* because he is hidden from the eyes. One says, "janna al-shay'" when he covered it. So the *jānn* conceals himself from the eyes of the children of Adam. The meaning of "before" (min qabl) is before the creation of Adam. *Al-samūm* is the sharp wind that penetrates the pores; it occurs by day and may also occur by night, as Abu 'Ubayda said. The creation of the human being and the jinn is mentioned in this place to show the perfection of divine power, and to show that the One who is able to originate creation is able to bring it back again.

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾: the adverbial clause (al-ẓarf) is governed by a verb understood: that is, "remember." After mentioning the creation of the human being, He explained what happened at the time of his creation. The account of this was already discussed in al-Baqarah. *Al-bashar* is derived from *al-basharah*, which is the outer surface of the skin. The explanation of *al-ṣalṣāl* and *al-ḥama' al-masnūn* has been given above in full detail.

﴿So when I have proportioned him﴾: that is, I perfected his creation, balanced his human form, and completed his parts. ﴿And breathed into him of My spirit﴾: *al-nafkh* is the moving of wind into the cavities of another body. Whoever says the spirit is a subtle body like air, its meaning is clear. Whoever says it is a simple substance, neither occupying space nor inhering in something that occupies space, then for him the meaning of breathing is the preparation of the body so that the rational soul may attach to it.

Its reality is the attribution of a creature to its Creator: the spirit is a creation of His which He attributed to Himself as an honour and dignity. He said: similar to it is ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 171], which was already discussed in al-Nisa'.

﴿Then fall down prostrating to him﴾: the *fa'* indicates that their prostration was obligatory upon them immediately after the proportioning and breathing, without delay. It is a command to "fall" (*waqaʿa*, *yaqaʿu*).
This indicates that what was commanded is prostration, not merely bowing, as has been said. This prostration is a prostration of greeting and honour, not a prostration of worship. God may honour whom He wills among His creatures, as He wills, with what He wills. It was also said: the prostration was to God, and Adam was a *qiblah* (direction) for them.

﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾: He informed that the angels all prostrated together at God's command to them, without delay. Al-Mubarrad said: His saying "kulluhum" removed the possibility that some of the angels did not prostrate, and His saying "ajmaʿūn" is an emphasis after an emphasis. Al-Zajjaj preferred this view.
Al-Nisaburi said: this is because *ajmaʿ* is definite, so it cannot function as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); and if it could be a ḥāl, it would be in the accusative case.

Then He excepted Iblis from the angels, saying: ﴿except Iblis; he refused to be among those who prostrate﴾. It was said: this exception is *muttaṣil* (connected), because he was of the kind of the angels, but he refused out of arrogance, self-magnification and envy of Adam, so the word of God became binding upon him. It was also said: he was not of the angels, but he was with them, so the name "angels" overpowered him and he was commanded with what they were commanded; thus the exception is connected in this sense. It was also said: the exception is *munfaṣil* (disconnected), based on his not being one of them and their not being named to include him; that is, "but Iblis refused to be among those who prostrate." This matter has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿he refused to be among those who prostrate﴾ is a new sentence (istiʾnāf) explaining the manner of his exception from non-prostration, because non-prostration may be accompanied by hesitation, so He made clear that it was by way of refusal.

The clause ﴿He said: O Iblis, what is it with you that you are not among those who prostrate?﴾ is also a new sentence, answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did God say to Iblis after he refused to prostrate?" This address to him is not for honour and dignity but for reproach and rebuke. The meaning is: what purpose do you have in refusing, and what reason moved you to it, so that you are not among those who prostrate to Adam together with the angels, while they are in nobility, high rank and nearness to God, in the position you already know?

The clause ﴿He said: I am not one to prostrate to a human being You created from clay, from black mud, moulded﴾ is a new sentence like the previous one. He made the reason for not prostrating that Adam was a human being created from *ṣalṣāl* of *ḥama' masnūn*, supposing that he himself was created from a finer element than the element of Adam. This contains an implicit hint at his claim of being better than him. It was explicitly stated elsewhere: He said, ﴿I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ [Ṣād: 76]; and He said elsewhere, ﴿Shall I prostrate to one You created from clay?﴾ [al-Isrā': 61]. The *lām* in *li-asjud* emphasises the negation: that is, it is not valid for me.

God answered him with His words: ﴿He said: Then get out of it, for you are accursed﴾ (p-762). The pronoun in "minhā" is said to refer to Paradise; it is also said to refer to the heaven; and it is said to refer to the host of angels, meaning: get out of the host of angels. ﴿For you are accursed (rajīm)﴾: that is, stoned with meteors. It is also said that the meaning of *rajīm* is cursed, that is, expelled, because one who is expelled is stoned with rocks.

﴿And upon you is the curse until the Day of Judgement﴾: that is, upon you is expulsion and distancing from God's mercy, continuing upon you and remaining with you until the Day of Recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection. Making the Day of Judgement the limit of the curse does not imply that it ends at that time, because what is meant is its continuation without cessation. The Day of Judgement is mentioned for emphasis, as in His saying, ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ [Hūd: 107]. Or it is meant that on the Day of Judgement and after it he is punished with something harsher than cursing, from various kinds of punishment, so that he finds no relief from it as he used to find before the punishment touched him.

﴿He said: My Lord, then give me respite﴾: that is, delay me and grant me time, and do not cause me to die until the Day when they are raised, meaning Adam and his offspring.
He asked to remain alive until this day. When he heard that, he knew that God had postponed his punishment until the Final Abode. It is as if he asked never to die, because if his death was deferred until that day, then that day has no death in it. It was also said that he did not ask never to die, but asked that his punishment be postponed until the Day of Resurrection and that he not be punished in this world.

﴿He said: Then you are among those given respite﴾: when he asked for respite, God granted him what he asked and informed him that he was among those He gave respite, from among those whose lifespans He delayed from His creatures, or among those whose punishment He postponed for what they committed.

Then He explained the term up to which He gave him respite. He said: ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection. The Day of Judgement, the Day when they are raised, and the Day of the Appointed Time are all expressions for the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that the Appointed Time means a time near the resurrection; at that time he will die.

﴿He said: My Lord, because You have misled me, I will surely adorn [evil] for them on earth﴾. The *bā'* is for oath, and *mā* is verbal (maṣdariyyah). The answer to the oath is ﴿I will surely adorn [evil] for them﴾; that is: I swear by Your misleading me that I will surely adorn for them on earth, meaning as long as they are in this world. The adornment is either by making sins appear good to them and causing them to fall into them, or by occupying them with the adornment of this world so that they do not turn to anything else than what God commanded them.
His oath here by God's misleading him does not contradict his oath elsewhere by God's might, which is His power and dominion, because misleading him is among the things to which might applies.

﴿And I will surely mislead them all﴾: that is, I will surely lead them astray from the path of guidance, and bring them into the path of error and compel them to it.

﴿Except Your sincere servants among them﴾: Ahl al-Madīnah and Ahl al-Kūfah read it with a fatḥah on the *lām* (al-mukhlaṣīna), meaning those whom You have chosen from among the servants. The rest read it with a kasrah on the *lām* (al-mukhliṣīna), meaning those who made their worship sincere for You, so they did not intend it for other than You.

﴿He said: This is a path upon Me, straight﴾: that is, it is a right incumbent upon Me to uphold it, which is that You will have no authority over My servants.
Al-Kisa'i said: this is in the sense of warning and threat, like your saying to one whom you threaten, "Your path is upon me and your destination is to me," and like His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. So the meaning of this statement is: this is the path of his return to Me, and I will recompense each one according to his deed. It was also said: *ʿalā* here means *ilā* (to). It was also said: the meaning is that the straight path is by clarification and proof, and it was said: by granting success and guidance.

Ibn Sirin, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan, Qays ibn ʿAbbād, Abu Raja', Ḥumayd and Yaʿqūb read "hādhā ṣirāṭun ʿaliyyun" (this is an exalted path), as a *ṣifah mushabbahah* (attributive adjective), meaning "elevated."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verses 82–88 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Indeed, My servants — you have no authority over them﴾. The servants here are meant to be the sincere ones (al-mukhlisun). The meaning is that he has no power over them to bring them into a sin through which they would perish without repenting from it. This does not contradict what occurred from Adam and Hawwa' (Eve) and the like, for that was a sin that was forgiven because repentance was made from it. ﴿Except those who follow you from among the misguided﴾. He, glorified is He, excepted from His servants these, namely those who follow Iblis — from among the misguided, those who have fallen into error, going astray from the path of truth. This agrees with what the accursed Iblis said: ﴿I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them﴾. It may be said that there is a difference between the two statements: the speech of Allah, glorified is He, contains the negation of Iblis' authority over all His servants except those among the misguided who follow him, so it includes the sincere ones and others who did not follow Iblis from among the misguided. The speech of the accursed Iblis contains the misguiding of all except the sincere ones, so there entered into them those who were neither sincere nor misguided followers of Iblis.

The conclusion is that between the sincere ones and the misguided followers of Iblis there is a group that was neither sincere nor misguided followers of Iblis. It has been said that the misguided followers of Iblis are the polytheists (mushrikun), and this is indicated by the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 100].

Then Allah, glorified is He, said, threatening the followers of Iblis: ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾.

That is, the promised place of the misguided followers. "Ajma'in" (all) is an emphasis for the pronoun or a circumstantial (ḥāl) construction.

﴿It has seven gates﴾ through which the people of the Fire enter. It has seven because of the multitude of its inhabitants. ﴿For each gate there is a portion of them﴾, that is, of the misguided followers, ﴿a designated share﴾, that is, a known measure distinguished from others. It has been said: the meaning of "gates" is "levels" (aṭbāq), one level above another, and they are: Jahannam, then Laẓā, then al-Ḥuṭama, then al-Sa‘īr, then Saqar, then al-Jaḥīm, then al-Hāwiyah. The highest of them is for the monotheists (muwaḥḥidun), the second for the Jews, the third for the Christians, the fourth for the Sabians, the fifth for the Magians, the sixth for the polytheists, and the seventh for the hypocrites (munafiqun). So Jahannam is the highest of the levels, then what follows it is beneath it, and so on. Thus it has been said.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh in al-‘Aẓama transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas, who said: Man was created from three things: from clay that clings (ṭīn lāzib), and ṣalṣāl, and ḥama' masnūn. The clay that clings: that which sticks firmly and is good. The ṣalṣāl: that which is dried and fired, from which pottery is made. The ḥama' masnūn: the clay in which there is black mud.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, who said: The ṣalṣāl is water that falls upon good earth, then it dries out from it and it cracks, then it becomes like thin pottery shards.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, who said: The ṣalṣāl is dry earth that is moistened after its drying.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, who said: The ṣalṣāl is clay mixed with sand.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him.
He said: The ṣalṣāl is that which, when you strike it, it rings (ṣalṣala).

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him.
He said: The ṣalṣāl is clay which, when you squeeze it with your hand, the water comes out from between your fingers.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him (p-763) regarding His saying: ﴿from black mud, moulded﴾ [ḥama' masnūn], he said: from moist clay. And these same transmitters also transmitted from him regarding ﴿from ḥama' masnūn﴾: from stinking clay.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, who said: The jinn is the transformed (masikh) of the jinn, like monkeys and pigs are the transformed of mankind.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, who said: The jinn is Iblis, who was created before Adam.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of samum﴾, he said: from the best of fire.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, who said: ﴿Fire of samum﴾ is the scorching heat that kills.

Al-Tayalisi, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu‘ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn Mas‘ud, who said: The samum from which the jinn was created is a part of seventy parts of the fire of Jahannam. Then he recited: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of samum﴾. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from him as a marfu' report.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿He said: My Lord, reprieve me until the day they are resurrected﴾, he said: Iblis wanted not to taste death, so it was said: "Indeed you are among those reprieved until the day of the appointed time." He said: The first blast, in which Iblis will die, and between the blast and the blast is forty years.

Abu ‘Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Sirin regarding ﴿This is a path, upon Me, straight﴾, that it means elevated (rafi‘).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted the like of it from Qatadah.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿For it there are seven gates﴾, according to the number of the levels of Jahannam, as we have previously mentioned.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Hannad, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Sifat al-Nar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba‘th transmitted through various chains from ‘Ali, who said: The levels of Jahannam are seven, some above others; the first is filled, then the second, then the third, until all of them are filled. al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ‘Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Jahannam has seven gates: one of them is for whoever draws the sword against my Ummah."

Reports and narrations have come concerning the description of the Fire.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib in his Tarikh transmitted from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said regarding His saying, Exalted: ﴿For each gate of them there is a designated share﴾: A share of those who associated partners with Allah, a share of those who doubted Allah, and a share of those who were heedless of Allah."

The meaning of "the human being" (al-insān) in His words, ﴿And We created the human being﴾, is Adam, because he is the origin of this kind. As for *al-ṣalṣāl* (الصَّلْصالُ), Abu 'Ubayda said: it is clay mixed with sand that rattles (yatalaṣlaṣu) when it is shaken; when it is baked in fire, it becomes pottery (al-fakhkhār).

This is the view of most exegetes (*mufassirūn*).

Al-Kisa'i said: it is foul-smelling clay, derived from the Arabs' saying, "ṣalla al-laḥm wa-aṣalla" (ṣalla al-laḥm wa-aṣalla), meaning the meat became putrid, whether cooked or raw.

Al-Hutay'a said:
"That is a young man who gives away his cooking pot; the rot does not spoil the meat with him."

*Al-ḥama'* (الحَمَأُ): black clay that has changed.
Or it is black clay without the restriction of having changed.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: one says of it, "ḥamaʾtu al-bi'r ḥamʾan" (with the sukun), when you remove its silt; "ḥami'at al-bi'r ḥamaʾan" (with the fatḥah), when its silt has increased; and "aḥmaytuhā iḥmā'an," when I threw silt into it.

Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-ḥamʾah* with a sukun on the mim is like *al-ḥamaʾah* with fatḥah; its plural is *ḥamʾ*, like *tamrah* and *tamr*. *Al-ḥama'* is a verbal noun, like *al-halaʿ* and *al-jazaʿ*, and then it was named by it.

*Al-masnūn* (المَسْنُونُ): al-Farra' said it is what has changed; its root is from "sanantu al-ḥajar 'alā al-ḥajar," when I rubbed one stone against another, and what comes out between two stones is called *al-sunāna* and *al-sinīn*. From this is the saying of 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥassān:
"Then she besieged it up to the red dome, walking among marble and rubbed (sunūn) stones."
That is, rubbed. It is also said, "asina al-māʾ" when the water changed. From this is His saying, ﴿it has not changed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259], and His saying, ﴿water not changing﴾ [Muḥammad: 15]. Both derivations indicate change, because what comes out between two stones is necessarily foul-smelling.

Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-masnūn* means shaped (al-muṣawwab). It comes from the Arabs' saying, "sanantu al-māʾ 'alā al-wajh," when I poured it, and *al-sann* is pouring.

Sibawayh said: *al-masnūn* means formed (al-muṣawwar), derived from *sunnat al-wajh*, which is its form. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:
"She shows you the form of a face, not blemished, smooth, with no mole or scar."

Al-Akhfash said: *al-masnūn* means upright and erect, from their saying "wajhun masnūn" when it has length in it.

The conclusion of these views is that when the dust was moistened it became clay; when it became foul it became black mud (ḥama'an masnūnan); when it dried it became *ṣalṣāl*.
So the origin of *al-ṣalṣāl* is *al-ḥama' al-masnūn*, and for this reason both are described by these two words.

﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of the scorching wind﴾. *Al-jānn* (الجانّ) is the father of the jinn according to the majority of exegetes.
ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Muqātil said: it is Iblis.
He was called *jānn* because he is hidden from the eyes. One says, "janna al-shay'" when he covered it. So the *jānn* conceals himself from the eyes of the children of Adam. The meaning of "before" (min qabl) is before the creation of Adam. *Al-samūm* is the sharp wind that penetrates the pores; it occurs by day and may also occur by night, as Abu 'Ubayda said. The creation of the human being and the jinn is mentioned in this place to show the perfection of divine power, and to show that the One who is able to originate creation is able to bring it back again.

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾: the adverbial clause (al-ẓarf) is governed by a verb understood: that is, "remember." After mentioning the creation of the human being, He explained what happened at the time of his creation. The account of this was already discussed in al-Baqarah. *Al-bashar* is derived from *al-basharah*, which is the outer surface of the skin. The explanation of *al-ṣalṣāl* and *al-ḥama' al-masnūn* has been given above in full detail.

﴿So when I have proportioned him﴾: that is, I perfected his creation, balanced his human form, and completed his parts. ﴿And breathed into him of My spirit﴾: *al-nafkh* is the moving of wind into the cavities of another body. Whoever says the spirit is a subtle body like air, its meaning is clear. Whoever says it is a simple substance, neither occupying space nor inhering in something that occupies space, then for him the meaning of breathing is the preparation of the body so that the rational soul may attach to it.

Al-Nisaburi said: there is no disagreement that the idafah (possessive construction) in "My spirit" is for honour and dignity, like "the she-camel of God" and "the House of God."

Al-Qurtubi said: the spirit is a subtle body which God has made customary to create life in the body together with that body. Its reality is the attribution of a creature to its Creator: the spirit is a creation of His which He attributed to Himself as an honour and dignity. He said: similar to it is ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 171], which was already discussed in al-Nisa'.

﴿Then fall down prostrating to him﴾: the *fa'* indicates that their prostration was obligatory upon them immediately after the proportioning and breathing, without delay. It is a command to "fall" (*waqaʿa*, *yaqaʿu*).
This indicates that what was commanded is prostration, not merely bowing, as has been said. This prostration is a prostration of greeting and honour, not a prostration of worship. God may honour whom He wills among His creatures, as He wills, with what He wills. It was also said: the prostration was to God, and Adam was a *qiblah* (direction) for them.

﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾: He informed that the angels all prostrated together at God's command to them, without delay. Al-Mubarrad said: His saying "kulluhum" removed the possibility that some of the angels did not prostrate, and His saying "ajmaʿūn" is an emphasis after an emphasis. Al-Zajjaj preferred this view.
Al-Nisaburi said: this is because *ajmaʿ* is definite, so it cannot function as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); and if it could be a ḥāl, it would be in the accusative case.

Then He excepted Iblis from the angels, saying: ﴿except Iblis; he refused to be among those who prostrate﴾. It was said: this exception is *muttaṣil* (connected), because he was of the kind of the angels, but he refused out of arrogance, self-magnification and envy of Adam, so the word of God became binding upon him. It was also said: he was not of the angels, but he was with them, so the name "angels" overpowered him and he was commanded with what they were commanded; thus the exception is connected in this sense. It was also said: the exception is *munfaṣil* (disconnected), based on his not being one of them and their not being named to include him; that is, "but Iblis refused to be among those who prostrate." This matter has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿he refused to be among those who prostrate﴾ is a new sentence (istiʾnāf) explaining the manner of his exception from non-prostration, because non-prostration may be accompanied by hesitation, so He made clear that it was by way of refusal.

The clause ﴿He said: O Iblis, what is it with you that you are not among those who prostrate?﴾ is also a new sentence, answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did God say to Iblis after he refused to prostrate?" This address to him is not for honour and dignity but for reproach and rebuke. The meaning is: what purpose do you have in refusing, and what reason moved you to it, so that you are not among those who prostrate to Adam together with the angels, while they are in nobility, high rank and nearness to God, in the position you already know?

The clause ﴿He said: I am not one to prostrate to a human being You created from clay, from black mud, moulded﴾ is a new sentence like the previous one. He made the reason for not prostrating that Adam was a human being created from *ṣalṣāl* of *ḥama' masnūn*, supposing that he himself was created from a finer element than the element of Adam. This contains an implicit hint at his claim of being better than him. It was explicitly stated elsewhere: He said, ﴿I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ [Ṣād: 76]; and He said elsewhere, ﴿Shall I prostrate to one You created from clay?﴾ [al-Isrā': 61]. The *lām* in *li-asjud* emphasises the negation: that is, it is not valid for me.

God answered him with His words: ﴿He said: Then get out of it, for you are accursed﴾ (p-762). The pronoun in "minhā" is said to refer to Paradise; it is also said to refer to the heaven; and it is said to refer to the host of angels, meaning: get out of the host of angels. ﴿For you are accursed (rajīm)﴾: that is, stoned with meteors. It is also said that the meaning of *rajīm* is cursed, that is, expelled, because one who is expelled is stoned with rocks.

﴿And upon you is the curse until the Day of Judgement﴾: that is, upon you is expulsion and distancing from God's mercy, continuing upon you and remaining with you until the Day of Recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection. Making the Day of Judgement the limit of the curse does not imply that it ends at that time, because what is meant is its continuation without cessation. The Day of Judgement is mentioned for emphasis, as in His saying, ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ [Hūd: 107]. Or it is meant that on the Day of Judgement and after it he is punished with something harsher than cursing, from various kinds of punishment, so that he finds no relief from it as he used to find before the punishment touched him.

﴿He said: My Lord, then give me respite﴾: that is, delay me and grant me time, and do not cause me to die until the Day when they are raised, meaning Adam and his offspring.
He asked to remain alive until this day. When he heard that, he knew that God had postponed his punishment until the Final Abode. It is as if he asked never to die, because if his death was deferred until that day, then that day has no death in it. It was also said that he did not ask never to die, but asked that his punishment be postponed until the Day of Resurrection and that he not be punished in this world.

﴿He said: Then you are among those given respite﴾: when he asked for respite, God granted him what he asked and informed him that he was among those He gave respite, from among those whose lifespans He delayed from His creatures, or among those whose punishment He postponed for what they committed.

Then He explained the term up to which He gave him respite. He said: ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection. The Day of Judgement, the Day when they are raised, and the Day of the Appointed Time are all expressions for the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that the Appointed Time means a time near the resurrection; at that time he will die.

﴿He said: My Lord, because You have misled me, I will surely adorn [evil] for them on earth﴾. The *bā'* is for oath, and *mā* is verbal (maṣdariyyah). The answer to the oath is ﴿I will surely adorn [evil] for them﴾; that is: I swear by Your misleading me that I will surely adorn for them on earth, meaning as long as they are in this world. The adornment is either by making sins appear good to them and causing them to fall into them, or by occupying them with the adornment of this world so that they do not turn to anything else than what God commanded them.
His oath here by God's misleading him does not contradict his oath elsewhere by God's might, which is His power and dominion, because misleading him is among the things to which might applies.

﴿And I will surely mislead them all﴾: that is, I will surely lead them astray from the path of guidance, and bring them into the path of error and compel them to it.

﴿Except Your sincere servants among them﴾: Ahl al-Madīnah and Ahl al-Kūfah read it with a fatḥah on the *lām* (al-mukhlaṣīna), meaning those whom You have chosen from among the servants. The rest read it with a kasrah on the *lām* (al-mukhliṣīna), meaning those who made their worship sincere for You, so they did not intend it for other than You.

﴿He said: This is a path upon Me, straight﴾: that is, it is a right incumbent upon Me to uphold it, which is that You will have no authority over My servants.
Al-Kisa'i said: this is in the sense of warning and threat, like your saying to one whom you threaten, "Your path is upon me and your destination is to me," and like His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. So the meaning of this statement is: this is the path of his return to Me, and I will recompense each one according to his deed. It was also said: *ʿalā* here means *ilā* (to). It was also said: the meaning is that the straight path is by clarification and proof, and it was said: by granting success and guidance.

Ibn Sirin, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan, Qays ibn ʿAbbād, Abu Raja', Ḥumayd and Yaʿqūb read "hādhā ṣirāṭun ʿaliyyun" (this is an exalted path), as a *ṣifah mushabbahah* (attributive adjective), meaning "elevated."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 38, verses 82–88 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Indeed, My servants — you have no authority over them﴾. The servants here are meant to be the sincere ones (al-mukhlisun). The meaning is that he has no power over them to bring them into a sin through which they would perish without repenting from it. This does not contradict what occurred from Adam and Hawwa' (Eve) and the like, for that was a sin that was forgiven because repentance was made from it. ﴿Except those who follow you from among the misguided﴾. He, glorified is He, excepted from His servants these, namely those who follow Iblis — from among the misguided, those who have fallen into error, going astray from the path of truth. This agrees with what the accursed Iblis said: ﴿I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them﴾. It may be said that there is a difference between the two statements: the speech of Allah, glorified is He, contains the negation of Iblis' authority over all His servants except those among the misguided who follow him, so it includes the sincere ones and others who did not follow Iblis from among the misguided. The speech of the accursed Iblis contains the misguiding of all except the sincere ones, so there entered into them those who were neither sincere nor misguided followers of Iblis.

The conclusion is that between the sincere ones and the misguided followers of Iblis there is a group that was neither sincere nor misguided followers of Iblis. It has been said that the misguided followers of Iblis are the polytheists (mushrikun), and this is indicated by the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 100].

Then Allah, glorified is He, said, threatening the followers of Iblis: ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾.

That is, the promised place of the misguided followers. "Ajma'in" (all) is an emphasis for the pronoun or a circumstantial (ḥāl) construction.

﴿It has seven gates﴾ through which the people of the Fire enter. It has seven because of the multitude of its inhabitants. ﴿For each gate there is a portion of them﴾, that is, of the misguided followers, ﴿a designated share﴾, that is, a known measure distinguished from others. It has been said: the meaning of "gates" is "levels" (aṭbāq), one level above another, and they are: Jahannam, then Laẓā, then al-Ḥuṭama, then al-Sa‘īr, then Saqar, then al-Jaḥīm, then al-Hāwiyah. The highest of them is for the monotheists (muwaḥḥidun), the second for the Jews, the third for the Christians, the fourth for the Sabians, the fifth for the Magians, the sixth for the polytheists, and the seventh for the hypocrites (munafiqun). So Jahannam is the highest of the levels, then what follows it is beneath it, and so on. Thus it has been said.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh in al-‘Aẓama transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas, who said: Man was created from three things: from clay that clings (ṭīn lāzib), and ṣalṣāl, and ḥama' masnūn. The clay that clings: that which sticks firmly and is good. The ṣalṣāl: that which is dried and fired, from which pottery is made. The ḥama' masnūn: the clay in which there is black mud.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, who said: The ṣalṣāl is water that falls upon good earth, then it dries out from it and it cracks, then it becomes like thin pottery shards.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, who said: The ṣalṣāl is dry earth that is moistened after its drying.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, who said: The ṣalṣāl is clay mixed with sand.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him.
He said: The ṣalṣāl is that which, when you strike it, it rings (ṣalṣala).

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him.
He said: The ṣalṣāl is clay which, when you squeeze it with your hand, the water comes out from between your fingers.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him (p-763) regarding His saying: ﴿from black mud, moulded﴾ [ḥama' masnūn], he said: from moist clay. And these same transmitters also transmitted from him regarding ﴿from ḥama' masnūn﴾: from stinking clay.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, who said: The jinn is the transformed (masikh) of the jinn, like monkeys and pigs are the transformed of mankind.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, who said: The jinn is Iblis, who was created before Adam.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of samum﴾, he said: from the best of fire.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, who said: ﴿Fire of samum﴾ is the scorching heat that kills.

Al-Tayalisi, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu‘ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn Mas‘ud, who said: The samum from which the jinn was created is a part of seventy parts of the fire of Jahannam. Then he recited: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of samum﴾. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from him as a marfu' report.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿He said: My Lord, reprieve me until the day they are resurrected﴾, he said: Iblis wanted not to taste death, so it was said: "Indeed you are among those reprieved until the day of the appointed time." He said: The first blast, in which Iblis will die, and between the blast and the blast is forty years.

Abu ‘Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Sirin regarding ﴿This is a path, upon Me, straight﴾, that it means elevated (rafi‘).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted the like of it from Qatadah.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿For it there are seven gates﴾, according to the number of the levels of Jahannam, as we have previously mentioned.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Hannad, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Sifat al-Nar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba‘th transmitted through various chains from ‘Ali, who said: The levels of Jahannam are seven, some above others; the first is filled, then the second, then the third, until all of them are filled. al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ‘Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Jahannam has seven gates: one of them is for whoever draws the sword against my Ummah."

Reports and narrations have come concerning the description of the Fire.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib in his Tarikh transmitted from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said regarding His saying, Exalted: ﴿For each gate of them there is a designated share﴾: A share of those who associated partners with Allah, a share of those who doubted Allah, and a share of those who were heedless of Allah."

The meaning of "the human being" (al-insān) in His words, ﴿And We created the human being﴾, is Adam, because he is the origin of this kind. As for *al-ṣalṣāl* (الصَّلْصالُ), Abu 'Ubayda said: it is clay mixed with sand that rattles (yatalaṣlaṣu) when it is shaken; when it is baked in fire, it becomes pottery (al-fakhkhār).

This is the view of most exegetes (*mufassirūn*).

Al-Kisa'i said: it is foul-smelling clay, derived from the Arabs' saying, "ṣalla al-laḥm wa-aṣalla" (ṣalla al-laḥm wa-aṣalla), meaning the meat became putrid, whether cooked or raw.

Al-Hutay'a said:
"That is a young man who gives away his cooking pot; the rot does not spoil the meat with him."

*Al-ḥama'* (الحَمَأُ): black clay that has changed.
Or it is black clay without the restriction of having changed.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: one says of it, "ḥamaʾtu al-bi'r ḥamʾan" (with the sukun), when you remove its silt; "ḥami'at al-bi'r ḥamaʾan" (with the fatḥah), when its silt has increased; and "aḥmaytuhā iḥmā'an," when I threw silt into it.

Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-ḥamʾah* with a sukun on the mim is like *al-ḥamaʾah* with fatḥah; its plural is *ḥamʾ*, like *tamrah* and *tamr*. *Al-ḥama'* is a verbal noun, like *al-halaʿ* and *al-jazaʿ*, and then it was named by it.

*Al-masnūn* (المَسْنُونُ): al-Farra' said it is what has changed; its root is from "sanantu al-ḥajar 'alā al-ḥajar," when I rubbed one stone against another, and what comes out between two stones is called *al-sunāna* and *al-sinīn*. From this is the saying of 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥassān:
"Then she besieged it up to the red dome, walking among marble and rubbed (sunūn) stones."
That is, rubbed. It is also said, "asina al-māʾ" when the water changed. From this is His saying, ﴿it has not changed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259], and His saying, ﴿water not changing﴾ [Muḥammad: 15]. Both derivations indicate change, because what comes out between two stones is necessarily foul-smelling.

Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-masnūn* means shaped (al-muṣawwab). It comes from the Arabs' saying, "sanantu al-māʾ 'alā al-wajh," when I poured it, and *al-sann* is pouring.

Sibawayh said: *al-masnūn* means formed (al-muṣawwar), derived from *sunnat al-wajh*, which is its form. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:
"She shows you the form of a face, not blemished, smooth, with no mole or scar."

Al-Akhfash said: *al-masnūn* means upright and erect, from their saying "wajhun masnūn" when it has length in it.

The conclusion of these views is that when the dust was moistened it became clay; when it became foul it became black mud (ḥama'an masnūnan); when it dried it became *ṣalṣāl*.
So the origin of *al-ṣalṣāl* is *al-ḥama' al-masnūn*, and for this reason both are described by these two words.

﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of the scorching wind﴾. *Al-jānn* (الجانّ) is the father of the jinn according to the majority of exegetes.
ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Muqātil said: it is Iblis.
He was called *jānn* because he is hidden from the eyes. One says, "janna al-shay'" when he covered it. So the *jānn* conceals himself from the eyes of the children of Adam. The meaning of "before" (min qabl) is before the creation of Adam. *Al-samūm* is the sharp wind that penetrates the pores; it occurs by day and may also occur by night, as Abu 'Ubayda said. The creation of the human being and the jinn is mentioned in this place to show the perfection of divine power, and to show that the One who is able to originate creation is able to bring it back again.

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾: the adverbial clause (al-ẓarf) is governed by a verb understood: that is, "remember." After mentioning the creation of the human being, He explained what happened at the time of his creation. The account of this was already discussed in al-Baqarah. *Al-bashar* is derived from *al-basharah*, which is the outer surface of the skin. The explanation of *al-ṣalṣāl* and *al-ḥama' al-masnūn* has been given above in full detail.

﴿So when I have proportioned him﴾: that is, I perfected his creation, balanced his human form, and completed his parts. ﴿And breathed into him of My spirit﴾: *al-nafkh* is the moving of wind into the cavities of another body. Whoever says the spirit is a subtle body like air, its meaning is clear. Whoever says it is a simple substance, neither occupying space nor inhering in something that occupies space, then for him the meaning of breathing is the preparation of the body so that the rational soul may attach to it.

Al-Nisaburi said: there is no disagreement that the idafah (possessive construction) in "My spirit" is for honour and dignity, like "the she-camel of God" and "the House of God."

Al-Qurtubi said: the spirit is a subtle body which God has made customary to create life in the body together with that body. Its reality is the attribution of a creature to its Creator: the spirit is a creation of His which He attributed to Himself as an honour and dignity. He said: similar to it is ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 171], which was already discussed in al-Nisa'.

﴿Then fall down prostrating to him﴾: the *fa'* indicates that their prostration was obligatory upon them immediately after the proportioning and breathing, without delay. It is a command to "fall" (*waqaʿa*, *yaqaʿu*).
This indicates that what was commanded is prostration, not merely bowing, as has been said. This prostration is a prostration of greeting and honour, not a prostration of worship. God may honour whom He wills among His creatures, as He wills, with what He wills. It was also said: the prostration was to God, and Adam was a *qiblah* (direction) for them.

﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾: He informed that the angels all prostrated together at God's command to them, without delay. Al-Mubarrad said: His saying "kulluhum" removed the possibility that some of the angels did not prostrate, and His saying "ajmaʿūn" is an emphasis after an emphasis. Al-Zajjaj preferred this view.
Al-Nisaburi said: this is because *ajmaʿ* is definite, so it cannot function as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); and if it could be a ḥāl, it would be in the accusative case.

Then He excepted Iblis from the angels, saying: ﴿except Iblis; he refused to be among those who prostrate﴾. It was said: this exception is *muttaṣil* (connected), because he was of the kind of the angels, but he refused out of arrogance, self-magnification and envy of Adam, so the word of God became binding upon him. It was also said: he was not of the angels, but he was with them, so the name "angels" overpowered him and he was commanded with what they were commanded; thus the exception is connected in this sense. It was also said: the exception is *munfaṣil* (disconnected), based on his not being one of them and their not being named to include him; that is, "but Iblis refused to be among those who prostrate." This matter has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿he refused to be among those who prostrate﴾ is a new sentence (istiʾnāf) explaining the manner of his exception from non-prostration, because non-prostration may be accompanied by hesitation, so He made clear that it was by way of refusal.

The clause ﴿He said: O Iblis, what is it with you that you are not among those who prostrate?﴾ is also a new sentence, answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did God say to Iblis after he refused to prostrate?" This address to him is not for honour and dignity but for reproach and rebuke. The meaning is: what purpose do you have in refusing, and what reason moved you to it, so that you are not among those who prostrate to Adam together with the angels, while they are in nobility, high rank and nearness to God, in the position you already know?

The clause ﴿He said: I am not one to prostrate to a human being You created from clay, from black mud, moulded﴾ is a new sentence like the previous one. He made the reason for not prostrating that Adam was a human being created from *ṣalṣāl* of *ḥama' masnūn*, supposing that he himself was created from a finer element than the element of Adam. This contains an implicit hint at his claim of being better than him. It was explicitly stated elsewhere: He said, ﴿I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ [Ṣād: 76]; and He said elsewhere, ﴿Shall I prostrate to one You created from clay?﴾ [al-Isrā': 61]. The *lām* in *li-asjud* emphasises the negation: that is, it is not valid for me.

God answered him with His words: ﴿He said: Then get out of it, for you are accursed﴾ (p-762). The pronoun in "minhā" is said to refer to Paradise; it is also said to refer to the heaven; and it is said to refer to the host of angels, meaning: get out of the host of angels. ﴿For you are accursed (rajīm)﴾: that is, stoned with meteors. It is also said that the meaning of *rajīm* is cursed, that is, expelled, because one who is expelled is stoned with rocks.

﴿And upon you is the curse until the Day of Judgement﴾: that is, upon you is expulsion and distancing from God's mercy, continuing upon you and remaining with you until the Day of Recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection. Making the Day of Judgement the limit of the curse does not imply that it ends at that time, because what is meant is its continuation without cessation. The Day of Judgement is mentioned for emphasis, as in His saying, ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ [Hūd: 107]. Or it is meant that on the Day of Judgement and after it he is punished with something harsher than cursing, from various kinds of punishment, so that he finds no relief from it as he used to find before the punishment touched him.

﴿He said: My Lord, then give me respite﴾: that is, delay me and grant me time, and do not cause me to die until the Day when they are raised, meaning Adam and his offspring.
He asked to remain alive until this day. When he heard that, he knew that God had postponed his punishment until the Final Abode. It is as if he asked never to die, because if his death was deferred until that day, then that day has no death in it. It was also said that he did not ask never to die, but asked that his punishment be postponed until the Day of Resurrection and that he not be punished in this world.

﴿He said: Then you are among those given respite﴾: when he asked for respite, God granted him what he asked and informed him that he was among those He gave respite, from among those whose lifespans He delayed from His creatures, or among those whose punishment He postponed for what they committed.

Then He explained the term up to which He gave him respite. He said: ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection. The Day of Judgement, the Day when they are raised, and the Day of the Appointed Time are all expressions for the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that the Appointed Time means a time near the resurrection; at that time he will die.

﴿He said: My Lord, because You have misled me, I will surely adorn [evil] for them on earth﴾. The *bā'* is for oath, and *mā* is verbal (maṣdariyyah). The answer to the oath is ﴿I will surely adorn [evil] for them﴾; that is: I swear by Your misleading me that I will surely adorn for them on earth, meaning as long as they are in this world. The adornment is either by making sins appear good to them and causing them to fall into them, or by occupying them with the adornment of this world so that they do not turn to anything else than what God commanded them.
His oath here by God's misleading him does not contradict his oath elsewhere by God's might, which is His power and dominion, because misleading him is among the things to which might applies.

﴿And I will surely mislead them all﴾: that is, I will surely lead them astray from the path of guidance, and bring them into the path of error and compel them to it.

﴿Except Your sincere servants among them﴾: Ahl al-Madīnah and Ahl al-Kūfah read it with a fatḥah on the *lām* (al-mukhlaṣīna), meaning those whom You have chosen from among the servants. The rest read it with a kasrah on the *lām* (al-mukhliṣīna), meaning those who made their worship sincere for You, so they did not intend it for other than You.

﴿He said: This is a path upon Me, straight﴾: that is, it is a right incumbent upon Me to uphold it, which is that You will have no authority over My servants.
Al-Kisa'i said: this is in the sense of warning and threat, like your saying to one whom you threaten, "Your path is upon me and your destination is to me," and like His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. So the meaning of this statement is: this is the path of his return to Me, and I will recompense each one according to his deed. It was also said: *ʿalā* here means *ilā* (to). It was also said: the meaning is that the straight path is by clarification and proof, and it was said: by granting success and guidance.
